subtopic_detail: toddler refusing to use one arm after axial traction with no bony tenderness or swelling
stem:
You are the resident in a regional emergency department. A 2-year-old girl is brought in by her father, who says she stopped using her right arm about an hour ago after he swung her up by both hands to lift her over a puddle. She cried for a minute at the time and has been settled since, but she will not reach for her drink bottle with that hand.

She sits comfortably on her father's lap with the right arm held slightly bent at the elbow and the palm turned in towards her body, and she reaches across herself for a toy with her left hand. There is no swelling, bruising or deformity anywhere on the limb, and she keeps playing while you palpate her collarbone, upper arm, forearm and wrist in turn. She pulls the arm away and cries when you try to turn the forearm palm-up. She is otherwise well and there have been no previous injuries or presentations.

data_table.Examination: Right arm held in slight flexion and pronation, no swelling, bruising or deformity
data_table.Palpation: No tenderness over the clavicle, humerus, radius, ulna or wrist
data_table.Provocation: Distress on attempted passive supination of the right forearm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform bedside supination of the forearm followed by flexion of the elbow
options.rationale: The traction mechanism, the pronated slightly flexed posture, absent bony tenderness and pain confined to attempted supination are the picture of radial head subluxation, and supination with flexion relocates the annular ligament at the bedside. Most children begin using the arm again within minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Immobilise the limb in an above elbow backslab and review in fracture clinic
options.rationale: A backslab is for a suspected or confirmed fracture, which the absence of swelling, deformity and bony tenderness argues strongly against here. Immobilising an unreduced subluxation simply postpones recovery. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Arrange an urgent elbow ultrasound to look for a posterior joint effusion
options.rationale: Ultrasound is useful when a septic or inflamed joint is in question, but this child is afebrile and systemically well with a clear traction mechanism. The near pair here is septic arthritis of the elbow, which holds the joint in mid-flexion with warmth and swelling and resists movement in every direction, not supination alone. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation

options.text: Request radiographs of the elbow and forearm before any manipulation
options.rationale: Imaging is the right first move when the history or examination suggests a fracture, but a pure traction mechanism with no swelling and no bony tenderness does not, and films of a subluxed radial head are almost always reported as normal. Reducing first and imaging only if the arm does not recover spares an unnecessary study. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Apply a broad arm sling and arrange orthopaedic review within a week
options.rationale: A sling treats the pain rather than the problem and leaves the annular ligament interposed, so the child continues not to use the arm for weeks. Slings are also poorly tolerated at this age and delay a reduction that takes seconds at the bedside. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

explanation.summary: Radial head subluxation follows sudden axial traction on a pronated forearm and is among the commonest upper limb injuries of early childhood, peaking between one and four years while the annular ligament is still lax. The diagnosis rests on the mechanism plus a systemically well child with no bony tenderness who resists supination rather than palpation. Radiographs are reserved for an atypical mechanism, focal bony tenderness, swelling, deformity, or failure to recover after two reduction attempts. Recurrence is common enough that parents should be warned against lifting a child by the hands or wrists. Persistent non-use after an apparently successful reduction should prompt reconsideration of an occult fracture.
key_points: Axial traction on a pronated forearm is the mechanism; a fall onto the arm is not.
The child is systemically well, holds the arm pronated, and has no bony tenderness.
Supination with flexion, or hyperpronation, reduces it at the bedside without imaging.
Radiograph for focal bony tenderness, swelling, deformity or failed reduction.
explanation.pearls: After a successful supination-flexion or hyperpronation manoeuvre most toddlers use the arm spontaneously within 5 to 15 minutes; if the arm is still not being used at 30 minutes, radiograph the elbow rather than attempting a third manipulation.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation

subtopic_detail: persistent head tilt with limited passive neck rotation and occipital flattening in a well three month old
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 3-month-old boy at his immunisation visit. His mother says his head always leans towards his right shoulder and that he only ever looks off to the left, even when she calls him from the other side. He was born at term by ventouse after a long second stage.

On examination the head is tilted to the right with the chin rotated to the left. You can passively rotate the chin towards the right only about 45 degrees before he resists, and there is a firm painless olive-shaped thickening in the lower third of the right sternocleidomastoid. The back of the head is flattened on the left with the left ear displaced forward. He fixes and follows with both eyes through a full range, the red reflex is symmetrical, and tone, power and the primitive reflexes are normal in all four limbs. He smiles responsively and is gaining weight along the 50th centile.

data_table.Neck examination: Head tilted right, chin rotated left, passive rotation to the right limited to 45 degrees
data_table.Palpation: Firm painless olive-shaped thickening in the lower right sternocleidomastoid
data_table.Head shape: Left occipital flattening with the left ear displaced anteriorly
data_table.Neurological and eye findings: Fixes and follows fully with both eyes, symmetrical red reflex, normal tone and reflexes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to paediatric ophthalmology to assess for a compensatory ocular tilt
options.rationale: Ocular torticollis is the near pair to consider, and it is distinguished by a full passive range of neck movement with no palpable muscle mass, the tilt being adopted voluntarily to fuse images. Here the range is mechanically restricted and the eye examination is normal, which points to the muscle rather than the eye. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Refer to paediatric physiotherapy for stretching and positioning advice
options.rationale: A restricted passive rotation with a palpable sternocleidomastoid mass in an otherwise normal infant is muscular in origin, and supervised stretching with positioning and tummy time is the treatment. Started before six months it resolves the great majority and the head shape remodels as the tilt corrects. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Arrange an urgent neck ultrasound to exclude a malignant soft tissue mass
options.rationale: The mass of muscular torticollis is a fibrotic segment of the sternocleidomastoid itself, firm, painless, non-growing and confined to the muscle belly. A mass that is growing, tender, outside the muscle, or accompanied by systemic symptoms would warrant imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Refer for a moulding helmet to correct the skull asymmetry at this stage
options.rationale: Helmet therapy addresses the deformational head shape but not the muscle restriction that is causing it, so the tilt recurs and the flattening returns. Positional plagiocephaly secondary to torticollis is treated by treating the torticollis first. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and the cervical spine
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is indicated when the tilt is accompanied by abnormal tone, developmental regression, a bulging fontanelle or abnormal eye movements, none of which are present. A normal neurological examination with a palpable muscle mass makes a posterior fossa or cord lesion very unlikely. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

explanation.summary: Congenital muscular torticollis affects roughly one in 250 infants and is associated with difficult or instrumental delivery, breech position and intrauterine crowding. The infant tilts towards the shortened sternocleidomastoid and rotates the chin away from it, and a fibrous mass in the muscle belly is palpable in a substantial minority. Deformational plagiocephaly follows because the infant always rests on the same part of the occiput, and it corrects as the neck range is restored rather than requiring separate treatment. The differential that must be excluded clinically is ocular torticollis, posterior fossa or cord pathology, and atlantoaxial abnormality, all of which spare the passive range or add neurological signs. Referral delayed beyond twelve months substantially raises the proportion who go on to need surgical release.
key_points: Tilt is towards the tight muscle and chin rotation is away from it.
A mechanically restricted passive rotation distinguishes muscular from ocular causes.
Plagiocephaly here is secondary and remodels once the neck range is restored.
Abnormal tone, abnormal eye movements or a growing mass change the pathway to imaging.
explanation.pearls: Physiotherapy started before six months of age resolves congenital muscular torticollis in over 90 per cent of infants, while referral after twelve months raises the surgical release rate several-fold, so the referral is made at the visit the tilt is noticed rather than at the next one.

subtopic_detail: offensive discharge from one nostril only for three weeks in an afebrile toddler
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 3-year-old boy whose mother says green gunk has been dribbling out of his right nostril for about three weeks and that it smells so bad she can notice it across the room. The left nostril has stayed dry throughout.

She has tried saline spray and a week of the antibiotic left over from his sister, and neither made any difference. He has been his usual self, playing normally and eating well, and has had no fever, no cough and no wheeze. On examination the skin below the right nostril is red and excoriated and there is thick yellow-green material at the right nasal opening, while the left nasal cavity is clear. His chest is clear on auscultation, the tympanic membranes are normal on both sides, and there is no facial swelling, no periorbital swelling and no tenderness over the cheeks or forehead. His vital signs are within normal limits. His mother mentions he plays with his older sister's craft beads.

data_table.Nasal examination: Thick offensive yellow-green discharge from the right naris with an excoriated vestibule, clear left nasal cavity
data_table.Other examination: Normal tympanic membranes bilaterally, clear chest, no facial or periorbital swelling or sinus tenderness
data_table.Course: Three weeks of strictly unilateral discharge unchanged by saline and a course of oral antibiotic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Advise saline irrigation twice daily and review the child in one month
options.rationale: Saline is a reasonable adjunct for viral or allergic rhinitis and has already been tried without effect, which makes this the near pair to reasonable conservative care. The distinction is that strict unilaterality is what separates a mechanical cause from an inflammatory one, and a month of irrigation delays removal. (Source: RCH CPG: Nasal foreign body)

options.text: Prescribe an intranasal corticosteroid spray and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid treats allergic rhinitis, which is bilateral, produces clear rather than offensive discharge and is accompanied by sneezing and itch. It will not shift an obstructing object and another four weeks risks pressure necrosis of the septum. (Source: RCH CPG: Nasal foreign body)

options.text: Examine the nasal cavity with a speculum and remove any foreign body
options.rationale: Unilateral offensive nasal discharge in a young child is a retained foreign body until proven otherwise, and the secondary infection resolves once the object is out. Direct inspection with a speculum and good light both confirms the diagnosis and permits removal at the same visit. (Source: RCH CPG: Nasal foreign body)

options.text: Start a two week course of oral amoxicillin with clavulanate today
options.rationale: Antibiotics may briefly reduce the smell but cannot clear an infection that is being sustained by a retained object, which is why the previous course failed. Bacterial sinusitis would also be bilateral in a child of this age and accompanied by fever or facial tenderness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the sinuses before any intervention
options.rationale: Sinus imaging carries radiation to the developing orbit and lens and is reserved for suspected complications of sinusitis such as orbital or intracranial spread. Most nasal foreign bodies are radiolucent, so a scan can be negative even when an object is present. (Source: RCH CPG: Nasal foreign body)

explanation.summary: Nasal foreign bodies are common between the ages of one and five, and because the insertion is frequently unwitnessed or denied the presentation is usually the secondary infection rather than the event. The cardinal sign is unilateral foul-smelling purulent nasal discharge, sometimes with epistaxis or nasal obstruction, and the strict unilaterality is what distinguishes it from rhinitis and sinusitis, which in a young child are bilateral. Removal at the bedside is attempted with a nasal speculum and good illumination using the positive pressure technique, in which the carer blows into the mouth while occluding the unaffected nostril, or with forceps for a graspable object or a curved hook passed behind a smooth one. Blind instrumentation, probing without a clear view and repeated failed attempts all risk pushing the object posteriorly, where it can be aspirated, so two attempts is a reasonable limit before referral. Button batteries and paired magnets are the exceptions that convert this into an emergency, since a battery causes liquefactive necrosis and septal perforation within hours and magnets in opposite nostrils trap and necrose the septum between them.
key_points: Unilateral offensive nasal discharge in a young child means a foreign body until excluded.
Rhinitis and paediatric sinusitis are bilateral, which is the discriminating feature.
Removal needs a speculum and good light; blind probing risks posterior displacement and aspiration.
Antibiotics cannot clear an infection sustained by a retained object.
explanation.pearls: A button battery in the nose causes liquefactive necrosis and septal perforation within hours, so a disc-shaped shiny object or a history of missing hearing aid batteries means immediate ear nose and throat referral for removal rather than a routine outpatient appointment.

subtopic_detail: greasy adherent yellow scale on the scalp and behind the ears of a thriving unbothered six week old
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-week-old boy whose parents are worried about thick yellowish flaking on the top of his head that has built up over the past fortnight. They say it looks greasy rather than dry and that some of it is now behind both ears, and they have been afraid to wash it off in case they hurt him.

On examination there are adherent greasy yellow scales over the vertex and in both retroauricular folds, with mild underlying erythema and no excoriation, weeping or crusting. The nappy area shows a faint salmon-coloured erythema in the inguinal folds without satellite lesions. He does not scratch or rub at his head while you examine him, sleeps through the night between feeds, and has gained 900 grams since birth. His mother has psoriasis affecting her elbows.

data_table.Skin examination: Adherent greasy yellow scale over the vertex and both retroauricular folds with mild erythema
data_table.Nappy area: Faint salmon erythema in the inguinal folds without satellite lesions
data_table.Growth: Weight gain of 900 grams since birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Start oral cefalexin for seven days and swab the scalp lesions for bacteria
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are for secondary bacterial infection, signalled by golden crusting, weeping, surrounding cellulitis or a systemically unwell infant, none of which are present. Uncomplicated scale carries no indication for a swab. (Source: RCH CPG: Seborrhoeic dermatitis)

options.text: Exclude cow's milk protein from the diet of the breastfeeding mother now
options.rationale: Maternal dietary exclusion is considered in proven cow's milk protein allergy, which presents with gastrointestinal symptoms, blood in the stool or poor weight gain rather than with isolated scalp scale in a thriving baby. Unnecessary exclusion risks maternal nutritional deficit. (Source: RACGP: Common infant skin conditions)

options.text: Apply a topical antifungal cream to the scalp and the nappy area every day
options.rationale: Topical antifungal is the near pair here and it has a place in extensive or persistent disease and in candidal nappy rash, but it is second line to emollient and descaling for uncomplicated scalp involvement. Candidal nappy rash is distinguished by satellite pustules beyond the margin of the main rash, which are absent. (Source: RCH CPG: Seborrhoeic dermatitis)

options.text: Apply a bland emollient to soften the scale then brush it out after bathing
options.rationale: Greasy adherent scale over the vertex and flexural folds in a thriving infant who is not itchy is infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis, and softening the scale with an emollient before gentle mechanical removal is the first-line treatment. It is self-limiting and usually clears over weeks to a few months. (Source: RCH CPG: Seborrhoeic dermatitis)

options.text: Apply a moderately potent topical corticosteroid ointment twice each day
options.rationale: A moderately potent steroid is disproportionate for scale on infant scalp skin and is the treatment for inflamed itchy eczema rather than for greasy adherent scale. A brief course of hydrocortisone 1 per cent is reasonable only if erythema persists once the scale has been cleared. (Source: RCH CPG: Seborrhoeic dermatitis)

explanation.summary: Infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis appears in the first weeks to months of life and is thought to reflect maternal androgen-driven sebum production together with Malassezia colonisation. It is distinguished from atopic dermatitis by the greasy rather than dry scale, the flexural and scalp distribution, and above all by the absence of itch in a settled infant, since atopic dermatitis makes babies miserable and they scratch. It is self-limiting, usually resolving within weeks to a few months, and carries no implication for later atopy. Treatment escalates only if simple measures fail, with hydrocortisone 1 per cent for residual inflammation and a topical antifungal for extensive or recurrent disease. Secondary bacterial or candidal infection is the reason management changes, so parents are told what weeping and golden crusting look like.
key_points: Greasy scale in a settled non-itchy infant separates this from atopic dermatitis.
Scalp vertex and flexural folds are the typical sites and the course is self-limiting.
Emollient softening with gentle mechanical removal is the first-line measure.
Satellite pustules beyond the rash margin indicate candida and change treatment.
explanation.pearls: Itch is the discriminator: infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis leaves the baby comfortable, so a six-week-old who is scratching, waking and rubbing has atopic dermatitis until proven otherwise, whatever the scale looks like.

subtopic_detail: bilateral evening leg pains in a well six year old who runs normally the following morning
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old boy whose mother says he cries with sore legs in the evening two or three nights a week, usually after he has gone to bed. She points to the front of both thighs and the backs of both calves when asked where he holds them. Rubbing his legs and a warm pack settle him within about twenty minutes and he goes back to sleep.

He plays soccer at lunchtime and runs to the car without difficulty the next morning, and his teacher has raised no concerns. He has not limped at any point, has had no fevers or sweats, and his weight and height are tracking along the 75th centile as they have since he was two. On examination he is well, with no joint swelling, warmth or restriction anywhere, no bony tenderness on firm palpation of both legs, no lymphadenopathy and no hepatosplenomegaly. His gait, including heel and toe walking, is normal.

data_table.Examination: No joint swelling, warmth or restriction, no bony tenderness on palpation of both legs
data_table.Systemic findings: No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly, normal gait including heel and toe walking
data_table.Growth: Height and weight tracking the 75th centile since age two

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request radiographs of both femora and tibiae to exclude a bone lesion
options.rationale: Radiographs are for focal bony tenderness, a limp, or pain that wakes a child and does not settle, since an osteoid osteoma or a malignant bone lesion is focal and unilateral. Bilateral muscular pain with a normal examination does not fit that pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Limb pain)

options.text: Refer to paediatric rheumatology for assessment of juvenile arthritis
options.rationale: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is the near pair and it is distinguished by joint rather than muscle pain, morning stiffness that eases through the day, and objective joint swelling or restriction. The pattern here is the mirror image, with evening pain and a normal morning. (Source: RCH CPG: Limb pain)

options.text: Start a six week trial of ibuprofen each evening and repeat the examination
options.rationale: Regular scheduled anti-inflammatory for six weeks medicalises a self-limiting condition and exposes the child to gastric and renal risk for episodic pain that responds to rubbing. Simple analgesia as needed is all that is warranted. (Source: RACGP: Growing pains in children)

options.text: Arrange a full blood count, film and inflammatory markers before reassuring
options.rationale: Blood tests are indicated when a red flag is present, such as a limp, unilateral or persistent daytime pain, fever, weight loss, bruising or organomegaly. Investigating a textbook benign pattern generates incidental abnormalities and prolongs parental anxiety rather than resolving it. (Source: RCH CPG: Limb pain)

options.text: Explain the benign pattern, advise massage and simple analgesia, and review
options.rationale: Bilateral pain confined to the evening or night, in the muscles rather than the joints, in a thriving child who is entirely well and running normally by day, is benign nocturnal limb pain and needs no investigation. Explanation, massage, heat and simple analgesia with planned review is the complete management. (Source: RCH CPG: Limb pain)

explanation.summary: Benign nocturnal limb pain, still widely called growing pains, affects up to a third of primary school aged children and is a clinical diagnosis made on pattern rather than on tests. The defining features are pain that is bilateral, muscular rather than articular, confined to the evening or night, and completely absent by morning in a child whose growth, examination and activity are normal. The conditions that must not be missed all break that pattern in a specific way, with leukaemia producing bone pain, bruising, pallor or organomegaly, osteoid osteoma producing focal unilateral night pain, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis producing morning stiffness with joint signs. Because the diagnosis rests on the absence of red flags rather than on a normal test, safety-netting and planned review carry the clinical weight. A child whose pain migrates into the day, becomes unilateral, or is accompanied by a limp is re-examined and investigated.
key_points: Bilateral, muscular, evening or night pain with a completely normal morning is the pattern.
A limp, unilateral pain, fever, weight loss, bruising or organomegaly are the red flags.
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis causes morning stiffness, the reverse of this timing.
No investigation is required when the pattern is typical and the examination is normal.
explanation.pearls: Pain that wakes a child from sleep is not by itself alarming in benign limb pain, but pain that persists into the following morning or produces a limp has left the benign pattern and warrants a full blood count, film and radiograph of the symptomatic site.

subtopic_detail: symmetrical bow legs in an eighteen month old of normal stature walking without pain
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 18-month-old girl whose grandmother has told the family her legs are bending outwards and that she needs braces. She started walking at 13 months, runs after her brother, and has never complained of leg pain or refused to weight bear.

On examination she stands with the medial malleoli together and there is a gap of about 5 cm between the medial femoral condyles, which is symmetrical on the two sides. The bowing is centred at the knees, the tibiae are not sharply angulated, and there is no lateral thrust of either knee as she walks. There is no tenderness, no swelling and no restriction of hip or knee movement. Her height and weight are both on the 50th centile and have tracked there since birth. She has a varied diet including dairy, plays outdoors daily, and takes no medications. Her wrists and costochondral junctions feel normal.

data_table.Lower limb examination: Symmetrical intercondylar distance of 5 cm with the malleoli together, bowing centred at the knees
data_table.Gait: Walks and runs without a limp and with no lateral thrust at either knee
data_table.Growth: Height and weight both on the 50th centile since birth
data_table.Other findings: No wrist or costochondral widening, full hip and knee range of movement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure, record the intercondylar distance and review the gait in six months
options.rationale: Symmetrical genu varum centred at the knees in a child of normal stature who walks without pain is the physiological pattern, which peaks around 18 months and corrects spontaneously. Documenting the intercondylar distance gives an objective measure to compare against at review. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.text: Request standing long leg alignment radiographs of both lower limbs today
options.rationale: Alignment films are reserved for bowing that is asymmetrical, progressive after the age of two, sharply angulated, painful, or accompanied by short stature. None of those applies, and radiographing physiological varus exposes a toddler to radiation for a normal result. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.text: Check serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D level
options.rationale: Nutritional rickets is the metabolic near pair and it is suggested by short stature or faltering growth, wrist and costochondral widening, delayed dentition or a restricted diet with little sun exposure. A child on the 50th centile with normal wrists and a varied diet does not warrant the panel. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.text: Refer to paediatric orthopaedics for consideration of bracing this year
options.rationale: Bracing has no role in physiological varus, which corrects without intervention, and orthopaedic referral is reserved for the patterns that do not correct. Offering a brace treats the grandmother's concern rather than the child's leg. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

options.text: Arrange a skeletal survey to look for an underlying skeletal dysplasia
options.rationale: A skeletal dysplasia declares itself with short stature, disproportion between limb and trunk length, or a family history, and normal centile tracking argues strongly against one. A skeletal survey is a substantial radiation exposure that this presentation does not justify. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

explanation.summary: Lower limb alignment follows a predictable developmental arc, with physiological varus maximal at around 18 months, a neutral axis at about two years, physiological valgus peaking near three to four years, and adult alignment reached by about seven. Parents and grandparents commonly present a toddler at the varus peak, so recognising the normal trajectory prevents a cascade of imaging and referral. The findings that take a child off the physiological pathway are asymmetry, progression after age two, sharp angulation at the proximal tibia, pain, a lateral thrust at the knee during stance, and short stature. Blount disease and nutritional rickets are the two diagnoses that account for most pathological varus, and each is suggested clinically before any test is ordered. Measuring and recording the intercondylar distance converts a subjective impression into a number that can be compared at the next visit.
key_points: Physiological varus peaks near 18 months and neutralises by about two years.
Symmetry, normal stature and a painless gait define the physiological pattern.
Asymmetry, progression after age two, or a lateral knee thrust suggests Blount disease.
Short stature with wrist or costochondral widening points instead to rickets.
explanation.pearls: Record the intercondylar distance in centimetres with the medial malleoli touching: a physiological varus shrinks at the six month review, whereas a measurement that is unchanged or larger after the second birthday is the trigger for standing alignment radiographs.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

subtopic_detail: boggy scalp swelling crossing the suture lines with tachycardia and pallor hours after a ventouse delivery
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the postnatal ward to see a 4-hour-old term boy. He was delivered by ventouse after two pulls for a prolonged second stage, with cord gases and Apgar scores that were unremarkable, and he went to the breast without difficulty. The midwife has called you because his head now feels soft and squelchy all over and because he has become pale and sleepy in the last hour.

On examination there is a diffuse fluctuant swelling over the whole scalp that crosses the sagittal suture and extends to the nape of the neck and behind both ears. Fluid shifts under your fingers when you tilt his head. His pulse rate is 194 beats per minute, blood pressure 42/22 mmHg, respiratory rate 68 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent in air and temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius. He is pale with a capillary refill of four seconds centrally. His head circumference has risen 2.5 cm since the measurement taken at birth.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 194 beats per minute, blood pressure 42/22 mmHg, respiratory rate 68 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent in air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Scalp examination: Diffuse fluctuant swelling crossing the sagittal suture, extending to the nape and behind both ears, fluid shifting on positional change
data_table.Perfusion: Pale, central capillary refill four seconds
data_table.Serial measurement: Head circumference risen 2.5 cm since birth
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (145-225 at birth), venous lactate 4.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Measure the head circumference hourly and observe on the postnatal ward
options.rationale: Serial head circumference is the right monitoring tool but it is not a treatment, and this infant has already declared himself with tachycardia, hypotension, pallor and a falling haemoglobin. Observation on a postnatal ward without venous access is how these babies exsanguinate into the scalp. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth trauma)

options.text: Transfer to the neonatal unit for volume resuscitation and transfusion
options.rationale: A swelling that crosses suture lines and shifts with position in a shocked infant after instrumental delivery is bleeding into the subaponeurotic space, which can hold the entire circulating volume. Immediate transfer with volume replacement and early red cell transfusion, alongside correction of coagulopathy, is the treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth trauma)

options.text: Arrange an urgent computed tomography scan of the head before any transfer
options.rationale: This is a clinical diagnosis made at the cot side, and taking a shocked neonate to a scanner before restoring circulating volume delays the only intervention that changes the outcome. Imaging has a place later for a suspected coexisting intracranial bleed or skull fracture. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth trauma)

options.text: Give intramuscular phytomenadione and repeat the coagulation profile
options.rationale: Vitamin K should certainly be confirmed as given and a coagulopathy corrected, but neither addresses the acute hypovolaemia and neither works fast enough to matter in the next fifteen minutes. This is an adjunct to resuscitation, not a substitute for it. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal birth trauma)

options.text: Apply a compression bandage to the scalp and recheck the haemoglobin
options.rationale: Head wrapping does not tamponade the subaponeurotic space, which communicates widely from orbit to nape, and a tight bandage obscures the serial head circumference that is being used to track ongoing bleeding. It substitutes a mechanical gesture for circulatory support. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Neonatal resuscitation)

explanation.summary: Subgaleal haemorrhage is bleeding into the loose areolar plane between the epicranial aponeurosis and the periosteum, a potential space that extends from the orbital ridges to the nape of the neck and can accommodate the whole neonatal blood volume. It complicates roughly 4 per 10000 spontaneous births and rises sharply with vacuum extraction, particularly after multiple pulls or a failed attempt followed by forceps. The bedside discriminator from the two benign mimics is anatomical, since caput succedaneum is superficial and pits while cephalhaematoma is subperiosteal and therefore stops at the suture lines, whereas subgaleal blood crosses them and shifts with gravity. Each centimetre of head circumference increase corresponds to roughly 38 mL of blood, so serial measurement is the monitoring tool while volume replacement is the treatment. Mortality approaches one in five once shock develops, which is why any infant delivered by vacuum has scalp and observation checks scheduled rather than left to chance.
key_points: Blood crossing the suture lines and shifting with position distinguishes it from cephalhaematoma.
Vacuum extraction, particularly multiple pulls or sequential instruments, is the main risk factor.
Tachycardia, pallor and a rising head circumference indicate ongoing loss into the scalp.
Treatment is volume resuscitation and transfusion in a neonatal unit, not imaging first.
explanation.pearls: Each 1 cm rise in head circumference in a subgaleal haemorrhage represents roughly 38 mL of blood, which in a 3.5 kg newborn is about 13 per cent of the circulating volume, so a 2 cm increase over a few hours is a haemorrhagic emergency however well the baby looked at birth.

subtopic_detail: firm bright red umbilical lesion unchanged after two courses of topical treatment in a five week old
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 5-week-old girl whose umbilical stump separated at day nine. Her parents were shown how to apply table salt to a small red lump at the navel three weeks ago, and when that made no difference your colleague cauterised it with silver nitrate a fortnight later. The lump is unchanged and the parents describe a clear sticky discharge that keeps staining her singlets.

On examination there is an 8 mm bright red firm lesion protruding from the umbilicus with a smooth glistening surface that looks like the inside of a lip. It does not blanch on pressure, it feels solid rather than soft, and it did not shrink or whiten with either treatment. The surrounding skin is normal in colour with no induration, no warmth and no tenderness. She is afebrile and thriving with a weight gain of 240 grams in the past week. There is no cough on handling and no leakage of urine or intestinal content from the lesion.

data_table.Umbilical examination: 8 mm firm bright red protruding lesion with a smooth glistening non-blanching surface
data_table.Surrounding skin: Normal colour without induration, warmth or tenderness
data_table.Treatment response: No change after three weeks of topical salt and one silver nitrate cauterisation
data_table.Growth: Weight gain of 240 grams over the past week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply a further course of topical salt therapy for seven more days
options.rationale: Salt desiccates the friable granulation tissue of an umbilical granuloma, which is dull pink, soft and blanching, and a lesion that has already failed salt is by definition not behaving like one. Repeating a treatment that has twice failed delays the diagnosis rather than testing it. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

options.text: Cauterise the lesion with silver nitrate again at this consultation
options.rationale: Silver nitrate works on granulation tissue and does nothing to epithelialised intestinal or urothelial mucosa, and repeated application risks chemical burns to the surrounding abdominal skin. Two failed treatments are the signal to reconsider the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for excision and histological examination
options.rationale: A firm bright red non-blanching lesion with a mucosal appearance that has resisted both salt and silver nitrate is an umbilical polyp, a persistent remnant of the omphalomesenteric or urachal duct lined by intestinal or urothelial mucosa. It requires surgical excision with histology and assessment for a deeper persistent tract. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

options.text: Swab the umbilicus and start oral cefalexin for suspected omphalitis
options.rationale: Omphalitis presents with periumbilical erythema, induration, tenderness and a systemically unwell infant, and it is a paediatric emergency in the neonatal period rather than a five week outpatient problem. The skin around this lesion is entirely normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Omphalitis)

options.text: Request an abdominal ultrasound to look for a patent urachal remnant
options.rationale: Ultrasound is a reasonable adjunct where a urachal sinus is suspected, particularly with urinary leakage, but it does not distinguish granuloma from polyp at the surface and it does not remove the lesion. Imaging is arranged by the surgical team alongside excision rather than instead of referral. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Umbilical anomalies)

explanation.summary: Most red umbilical lesions after cord separation are granulomas, which are soft, dull pink, friable, blanching masses of granulation tissue that respond to desiccation with salt or to silver nitrate cautery. An umbilical polyp is the important mimic and it is a persistent remnant of the omphalomesenteric duct or urachus lined by heterotopic intestinal or bladder mucosa, which is why it appears bright red, firm, glistening and mucosal and why it is entirely unresponsive to chemical treatment. The practical rule is that failure of adequate topical therapy reclassifies the lesion rather than earning another course. Excision is required both to remove the polyp and to exclude a deeper patent tract to the ileum or bladder, which can present later with faecal or urinary discharge, infection or volvulus around a persistent band. Histology of the excised specimen confirms the mucosal lining and directs any further imaging.
key_points: Granuloma is soft, dull pink and blanching; polyp is firm, bright red and mucosal.
Failure of salt or silver nitrate reclassifies the lesion rather than warranting repeat treatment.
A polyp is a vitellointestinal or urachal duct remnant and requires surgical excision.
A persistent deep tract can later cause discharge, infection or volvulus around a band.
explanation.pearls: Two failed treatments is the decision point: an umbilical lesion that has not shrunk after an adequate course of salt and one silver nitrate application is referred for excision rather than treated a third time, because a polyp has no granulation tissue for either agent to act on.

subtopic_detail: anterior chest wall depression in a tall adolescent with arachnodactyly and a high arched palate
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 14-year-old boy who has asked about surgery for the dip in the middle of his chest, which his parents say has deepened since he shot up in height over the past two years. He swims twice a week and says he keeps up with his friends, and he has never had chest pain, blackouts or palpitations.

On examination there is a symmetrical depression of the lower sternum. His height is on the 97th centile while both parents are of average height, his arm span exceeds his height by 6 cm, and the thumb and wrist signs are both positive. The palate is high and narrowly arched and there is bilateral pes planus. The apex beat is not displaced, both heart sounds are normal, and there is a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge that is best heard sitting forward. The lung fields are clear. His maternal uncle died suddenly at 41 years of age and the family were never told why.

data_table.Anthropometry: Height on the 97th centile, arm span exceeding height by 6 cm, positive thumb and wrist signs
data_table.Chest wall: Symmetrical depression of the lower sternum
data_table.Cardiac examination: Normal heart sounds with a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge
data_table.Other findings: High narrow palate, bilateral pes planus, clear lung fields

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Reassure him and review at the end of the pubertal growth spurt next year
options.rationale: Waiting is reasonable for an isolated chest wall depression in an otherwise unremarkable adolescent, but it is not reasonable when a diastolic murmur and a family history of unexplained sudden death in a young adult are present. Aortic root dilatation progresses silently during exactly the growth phase he is in. (Source: RCH CPG: Marfan syndrome)

options.text: Request a chest radiograph to calculate the Haller index before referral
options.rationale: The Haller index is derived from cross-sectional imaging rather than a plain film and it grades the severity of the chest wall deformity only. It is the near pair to the correct answer in that both are imaging, but it measures the cosmetic problem rather than the lethal one. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Pectus excavatum)

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for consideration of minimally invasive repair
options.rationale: A chest wall repair addresses the deformity the boy has asked about while leaving the systemic condition it is a marker of entirely unassessed. Surgical planning in a connective tissue disorder also requires the aortic dimensions to be known beforehand. (Source: RCH CPG: Marfan syndrome)

options.text: Arrange transthoracic echocardiography with aortic root measurement
options.rationale: Tall stature with disproportionate arm span, positive thumb and wrist signs, a high arched palate, chest wall deformity and an early diastolic murmur point to a heritable connective tissue disorder, and the murmur suggests aortic regurgitation from root dilatation. Echocardiography with root measurement indexed to body surface area is the investigation that determines both diagnosis and immediate risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Marfan syndrome)

options.text: Request spirometry and a formal cardiopulmonary exercise test to start
options.rationale: Lung function quantifies the restriction some deep chest wall deformities cause and is used when surgery is being planned for functional reasons, but it does not assess the aorta. A boy who swims twice a week without breathlessness is unlikely to have physiology that changes management. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Pectus excavatum)

explanation.summary: Pectus excavatum is common and usually isolated, but it is also a systemic feature in the revised Ghent criteria for Marfan syndrome, so its presence obliges a look for the other systemic features rather than a straight referral for repair. The systemic score counts findings such as wrist and thumb signs, reduced upper to lower segment ratio with increased arm span to height ratio, scoliosis, pes planus, a high arched palate and characteristic facial features. Aortic root dilatation at the sinuses of Valsalva is the feature that determines prognosis, since dissection and rupture account for most premature deaths, and it is measured by echocardiography and indexed as a Z score for body surface area. An early diastolic murmur in this setting represents aortic regurgitation from a dilated root and moves the assessment from elective to prompt. Management once confirmed includes beta blockade or an angiotensin receptor blocker, serial imaging, avoidance of isometric and contact sport, and family screening, all of which are unavailable until the echocardiogram is done.
key_points: Pectus excavatum is a systemic feature of Marfan syndrome, not only a cosmetic issue.
Arm span to height ratio, thumb and wrist signs and palate shape build the systemic score.
An early diastolic murmur suggests aortic regurgitation from root dilatation.
Echocardiography with a body surface area indexed root Z score drives all further management.
explanation.pearls: An aortic root Z score of 2 or more at the sinuses of Valsalva satisfies the aortic criterion in the revised Ghent nosology, and a root diameter approaching 45 mm in an adolescent with Marfan syndrome is the usual threshold for referral to consider prophylactic root replacement.

subtopic_detail: irreducible tender groin lump in a vomiting four month old with a previously intermittent swelling
stem:
You are the registrar in a district emergency department. A 4-month-old boy, born at 32 weeks, is brought in because he has screamed inconsolably for five hours and has vomited three times, the last of which his mother describes as bright green. She says a lump in his right groin has come and gone for weeks and has always flattened when he lay down, but this evening it has stayed up.

On examination he is unsettled and drawing up his legs. There is a firm tender 3 cm swelling in the right groin extending towards the scrotum, and you cannot define an upper border above it. The overlying skin is normal in colour. Both testes are palpable separately and are of equal size, non-tender and in the scrotum. The abdomen is distended with high-pitched bowel sounds. His pulse rate is 178 beats per minute, blood pressure 76/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 48 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air and temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 178 beats per minute, blood pressure 76/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 48 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Groin examination: Firm tender 3 cm right groin swelling extending towards the scrotum with no palpable upper border
data_table.Scrotal examination: Both testes palpable separately, equal in size, non-tender and descended
data_table.Abdominal examination: Distended abdomen with high-pitched bowel sounds
data_table.History: Born at 32 weeks gestation, intermittent reducible groin swelling for several weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Book an elective herniotomy on the next available paediatric operating list
options.rationale: Elective repair is what should have happened when the reducible lump was first noticed, and it is the correct pathway for a hernia that reduces easily. Once incarceration with obstruction has occurred the timeframe is hours, not weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

options.text: Start intravenous antibiotics for a presumed strangulated bowel segment
options.rationale: Antibiotics are given as part of preparation for theatre when strangulation is suspected, but they are an adjunct and do not relieve the obstruction. The near pair to keep in mind is an infected or necrotic segment already perforated, which would show peritonism, fever and shock rather than this picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Apply ice and review the swelling in the morning if he settles overnight
options.rationale: Delay is the single most dangerous choice here because incarcerated bowel becomes ischaemic within hours and the testicular vessels sharing the inguinal canal are compressed at the same time. Bilious vomiting with a distended abdomen indicates obstruction that is already established. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

options.text: Arrange an urgent scrotal ultrasound with Doppler before touching the lump
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the right test when the diagnosis is in doubt between a hydrocele, a torted testis and a hernia, but here both testes are normal and separately palpable and there is no upper border to the swelling. Waiting for imaging in an obstructed infant costs the bowel time it does not have. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

options.text: Give analgesia and attempt gentle reduction with urgent surgical involvement
options.rationale: An irreducible groin swelling with no upper border, bilious vomiting and abdominal distension in an ex-premature infant is an incarcerated inguinal hernia, and adequate analgesia with gentle sustained taxis succeeds in the majority. Surgical involvement is contemporaneous because failure of reduction mandates immediate operation and successful reduction still requires repair on the same admission. (Source: RCH CPG: Inguinal hernia)

explanation.summary: Indirect inguinal hernia in infancy results from a patent processus vaginalis and carries a far higher incarceration risk than in adults, concentrated in the first year and highest in ex-premature infants, which is why repair is arranged promptly rather than deferred. The bedside discriminators are that a hernia has no palpable upper border because it extends through the external ring into the abdomen, while a hydrocele transilluminates, has an upper border and does not obstruct, and a torted testis presents with an abnormal tender testis rather than a separate groin mass. Incarceration announces itself with irreducibility, pain, and then bilious vomiting and distension as bowel obstruction develops. Adequate opioid analgesia and sedation allow gentle sustained taxis to succeed in most cases, after which repair proceeds on the same admission once oedema settles, typically within 24 to 48 hours. Failed reduction, peritonism or systemic compromise means immediate operation, and the ipsilateral testis is at risk throughout because the cord structures are compressed at the external ring.
key_points: Inability to define an upper border distinguishes a hernia from a hydrocele or testicular problem.
Prematurity markedly increases the risk of incarceration in the first year of life.
Analgesia with gentle sustained taxis reduces most incarcerated infant hernias.
Repair follows on the same admission, and failed reduction means immediate operation.
explanation.pearls: In an incarcerated infant inguinal hernia the ipsilateral testis is at risk from cord compression as well as the bowel, so the operation note and the discharge examination both record testicular size, and a testis that is smaller at six week review prompts surgical re-referral.

subtopic_detail: unilateral in-toeing with a painless limp and reduced hip abduction in a three year old
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 3-year-old girl whose parents say her right foot turns in when she runs and that she has walked with a slight dip to one side since she started walking at 15 months. They say she has never complained of pain and has never stopped playing because of it.

On examination she in-toes on the right only, and the left foot points straight ahead. There is a painless dip of the trunk to the right during the stance phase of each step. Hip abduction in flexion is 70 degrees on the left and 40 degrees on the right. With the hips and knees flexed and the feet flat on the couch, the right knee sits lower than the left. Internal rotation of the right hip is increased and external rotation reduced compared with the left. The thigh-foot axis and the shape of the lateral border of each foot are normal on both sides. She is afebrile and systemically well, and her height and weight are on the 50th centile.

data_table.Gait: Right sided in-toeing with a painless trunk dip to the right in stance phase
data_table.Hip examination: Abduction in flexion 70 degrees left and 40 degrees right, increased right internal rotation
data_table.Leg length: Right knee lower than left with hips and knees flexed and feet flat
data_table.Distal examination: Normal thigh-foot axis and normal lateral foot border bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Request an anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis and both hips
options.rationale: Unilateral in-toeing with a painless Trendelenburg gait, restricted abduction in flexion and a positive Galeazzi sign is late-presenting developmental dysplasia, in which the femur internally rotates to keep the head in a shallow acetabulum. After the femoral head has ossified a plain pelvic radiograph is the diagnostic test. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Prescribe a night time derotation brace and review her in twelve months
options.rationale: Derotation devices and twister cables have no evidence of benefit even for the benign rotational variants they were designed for, and they treat the visible foot position rather than the hip driving it. Bracing an undiagnosed dysplastic hip wastes a year of growth. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

options.text: Refer for gait analysis and in-shoe orthotics through podiatry services
options.rationale: Orthotics address the foot and would be considered for a metatarsus adductus, which is excluded here by the normal lateral foot border. They cannot influence acetabular development and the referral delays the radiograph. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

options.text: Arrange an ultrasound of both hips to assess the acetabular alpha angle
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the imaging of choice for developmental dysplasia but only while the femoral head is still cartilaginous, conventionally under about four to six months of age. This is the near pair to the correct answer, and the distinguishing point is that after the ossific nucleus appears the head casts an acoustic shadow and a plain radiograph becomes the accurate study. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Reassure the parents that rotational profiles correct with skeletal growth
options.rationale: Benign rotational variants are symmetrical, involve no limp and leave hip abduction and leg length untouched, whereas this child has unilateral findings with restricted abduction and apparent shortening. Reassurance here would allow a treatable hip to deteriorate through the years when treatment works best. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

explanation.summary: In-toeing in a toddler is usually one of three benign rotational variants, namely metatarsus adductus in infancy, internal tibial torsion in the second year and increased femoral anteversion from around three years, all of which are symmetrical, painless and self-correcting. The clinical value of a rotational profile is that it localises the level of the problem, with the lateral foot border assessing the forefoot, the thigh-foot axis assessing the tibia, and hip rotation assessing the femur. A unilateral pattern is the finding that takes a child off that pathway, because a dysplastic hip produces compensatory femoral internal rotation along with a Trendelenburg gait, reduced abduction in flexion and apparent femoral shortening. Late-presenting developmental dysplasia is missed by newborn examination and neonatal ultrasound in a meaningful minority, and it presents exactly like this once walking is established. Treatment after walking age generally requires closed or open reduction with femoral or pelvic osteotomy rather than a harness, and outcomes deteriorate with every year of delay.
key_points: Benign rotational variants are symmetrical, painless and leave hip examination normal.
Unilateral in-toeing with a Trendelenburg gait points to the hip, not the foot or tibia.
Restricted abduction in flexion plus a positive Galeazzi sign is dysplasia until excluded.
Ultrasound is accurate only before the femoral ossific nucleus appears; then use radiography.
explanation.pearls: Hip ultrasound loses accuracy once the femoral ossific nucleus appears at around four to six months, so a walking child with suspected developmental dysplasia is imaged with an anteroposterior pelvic radiograph rather than the ultrasound used in the newborn period.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

subtopic_detail: postauricular swelling pushing the ear outwards five days into oral treatment for an ear infection
stem:
You are the registrar in a regional emergency department seeing a 4-year-old girl who was started on oral amoxicillin five days ago for a painful right ear. Her mother says the pain settled for two days and then came back worse, and that since yesterday the area behind the ear has puffed up.

She has been off her food, is hot to touch and has not wanted to play. On examination there is a tender fluctuant red swelling behind the right ear with loss of the crease where the ear meets the skull, and the right pinna sits lower and further out from the head than the left. The right ear canal skin is sagging at its roof and the tympanic membrane is red and bulging. She has no neck stiffness, no photophobia and no facial asymmetry, and the neurological examination is normal. Her pulse rate is 148 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air and temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius. White cell count is 19.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0) and C-reactive protein 128 mg/L (less than 5).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Postauricular findings: Tender fluctuant erythematous swelling with loss of the postauricular crease, right pinna displaced inferiorly and laterally
data_table.Otoscopy: Sagging of the posterosuperior canal wall with a red bulging tympanic membrane
data_table.Neurological examination: No neck stiffness or photophobia, no facial asymmetry, otherwise normal
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), C-reactive protein 128 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Change to oral cefalexin and review the child again in two days
options.rationale: Swapping one oral agent for another concedes that the first has failed while leaving the child on a route that cannot achieve adequate concentrations in infected bone. Cefalexin also has poorer activity against the pneumococcus and Streptococcus pyogenes that predominate here. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis)

options.text: Admit for intravenous antibiotics with urgent ear nose and throat review
options.rationale: Postauricular swelling with loss of the crease and a displaced pinna in a febrile child with a bulging drum is acute mastoiditis, a suppurative complication of otitis media involving the mastoid air cells. Admission for high dose intravenous antibiotics with same-day otolaryngology involvement for possible myringotomy or cortical mastoidectomy is the standard of care. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis)

options.text: Prescribe topical ciprofloxacin ear drops and continue the oral course
options.rationale: Topical quinolone drops treat otitis externa and discharging grommets, and otitis externa is the near pair because it also causes canal changes and postauricular tenderness. The distinction is that otitis externa spares the middle ear, gives pain on tragal pressure with a normal drum, and does not displace the pinna or obliterate the postauricular crease. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis)

options.text: Arrange an outpatient computed tomography scan of the temporal bones
options.rationale: Imaging has a definite role in suspected intracranial extension, subperiosteal abscess or a poor response to treatment, but this is a clinical diagnosis and an outpatient appointment introduces a delay of days. Antibiotics are started first and imaging arranged from the ward if needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis)

options.text: Aspirate the swelling in the clinic and send the fluid for culture
options.rationale: Needle aspiration of a postauricular collection without imaging or surgical support risks injuring the facial nerve and the sigmoid sinus, both of which lie in the operative field. Drainage, where required, is a theatre procedure performed by an otolaryngologist. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute mastoiditis)

explanation.summary: Acute mastoiditis is the commonest suppurative complication of acute otitis media and follows spread of infection from the middle ear into the mastoid air cells, which communicate with it directly through the aditus ad antrum. Incidence has fallen in the antibiotic era but the diagnosis persists and is now often seen in children who have been on oral therapy, so recent antibiotic treatment is no reassurance at all. The clinical triad is postauricular erythema, tenderness and swelling with loss of the postauricular crease, protrusion of the pinna inferiorly and laterally, and signs of middle ear infection such as a bulging drum or sagging of the posterosuperior canal wall. Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus are the usual organisms, and treatment is intravenous antibiotics with otolaryngology involvement, proceeding to myringotomy with or without grommet insertion, or cortical mastoidectomy, where there is a subperiosteal abscess or failure to improve. The complications that make this a same-day problem are facial nerve palsy, sigmoid sinus thrombosis, subperiosteal or Bezold abscess, labyrinthitis, meningitis and intracranial abscess, so any new focal neurological sign, altered conscious state or neck stiffness prompts urgent contrast imaging.
key_points: Loss of the postauricular crease with a displaced pinna is the defining physical sign.
Recent or current oral antibiotic treatment does not exclude the diagnosis.
Otitis externa spares the middle ear and does not displace the pinna.
Facial palsy, neck stiffness or altered conscious state signal intracranial extension.
explanation.pearls: Compare the two ears from behind and above with the child sitting up: the loss of the postauricular crease and the forward and downward displacement of the pinna are far more obvious from that angle than from the front, and they are what separate mastoiditis from simple postauricular lymphadenitis.

subtopic_detail: pubic and sacroiliac pain with difficulty turning in bed at twenty eight weeks and a soft uterus
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old woman in her second pregnancy at 28 weeks. She says she gets a grinding pain low down at the front when she rolls over in bed and when she climbs the stairs one leg at a time, and that it has built up over the last month rather than starting suddenly. She can walk about 200 metres before she has to stop.

She has had no tightenings, no loss of fluid, no bleeding and normal foetal movements. On examination the uterus is soft and non-tender with a symphysis fundal height of 28 cm. Pain is reproduced by the posterior pelvic pain provocation test on the right and by direct palpation over the symphysis pubis, and she has an antalgic waddling gait. There is no spinal tenderness and straight leg raising is negative bilaterally. Her pulse rate is 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in air and temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, with a foetal heart rate of 142 beats per minute. Urinalysis shows no blood, protein, nitrites or leucocytes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 142 beats per minute
data_table.Abdominal examination: Soft non-tender uterus with a symphysis fundal height of 28 cm
data_table.Provocation testing: Positive posterior pelvic pain provocation test on the right, tenderness over the symphysis pubis
data_table.Neurological examination: No spinal tenderness, straight leg raising negative bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for blood, protein, nitrites and leucocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for cardiotocography and a course of intramuscular betamethasone
options.rationale: Antenatal corticosteroids are given when birth within seven days is anticipated, and nothing here suggests that. Admitting a woman with a musculoskeletal problem for foetal monitoring treats the anxiety rather than the pelvis. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: Request a pelvic radiograph to measure the width of the symphysis pubis
options.rationale: Symphyseal width correlates poorly with symptoms, widening to around 10 mm is physiological in pregnancy, and the diagnosis is made on provocation testing rather than on imaging. Irradiating the pelvis in pregnancy for a clinical diagnosis is not justifiable. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy

options.text: Refer to women's health physiotherapy for a support belt and movement advice
options.rationale: Mechanical pain reproduced by pelvic provocation testing with a soft uterus and a normal urinalysis is pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain, and supervised physiotherapy with a pelvic support belt, activity modification and exercise is the evidence-based first-line treatment. It improves pain and function without any foetal exposure. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy

options.text: Arrange transvaginal ultrasound measurement of the cervical length today
options.rationale: Cervical length is measured when preterm labour or cervical insufficiency is suspected, which requires tightenings, pressure symptoms or a relevant history. A soft non-tender uterus with no contractions and pain reproduced by mechanical provocation does not raise that question. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy

options.text: Prescribe regular oral diclofenac and advise complete bed rest at home
options.rationale: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are avoided from 20 weeks because of foetal renal effects and oligohydramnios and are contraindicated after 30 weeks for ductal constriction. Bed rest additionally worsens deconditioning and raises venous thromboembolism risk in a condition treated by graded movement. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain affects around one in five pregnancies and arises from altered load transfer through the sacroiliac joints and symphysis under the influence of relaxin and a shifting centre of gravity. It is diagnosed clinically using reproducible provocation tests such as the posterior pelvic pain provocation test, the active straight leg raise and direct symphyseal palpation, with imaging reserved for atypical features. The important differentials are preterm labour, urinary tract infection, lumbar radiculopathy and, rarely, septic arthritis of the symphysis, each of which is excluded by the history, the urinalysis and the neurological examination. Management is physiotherapy-led, combining a pelvic support belt, individualised exercise, activity pacing and equipment such as crutches where needed, with paracetamol as the analgesic of choice. Most women improve substantially within weeks of birth, but a minority have persistent symptoms, and early referral rather than watchful waiting shortens the course.
key_points: The diagnosis is clinical, made on reproducible pelvic provocation tests.
A soft uterus with no contractions and a clear urinalysis excludes the urgent differentials.
Physiotherapy with a support belt and graded exercise is first-line treatment.
Bed rest is harmful and non-steroidal drugs are avoided from 20 weeks gestation.
explanation.pearls: Paracetamol is the analgesic of choice throughout pregnancy for pelvic girdle pain, while non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are avoided from 20 weeks because of foetal renal impairment and oligohydramnios and are contraindicated beyond 30 weeks because of premature ductal constriction.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: nocturnal hand numbness waking a woman at thirty two weeks with normal power and normal blood pressure
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29-year-old woman at 32 weeks in her first pregnancy. She says both hands go dead in the night and that she wakes two or three times and has to hang them over the side of the bed and shake them before the feeling comes back. It is worse in the right hand and she has started dropping her toothbrush in the mornings.

On examination there is reduced light touch over the pulp of the right thumb, index and middle fingers, with normal sensation over the little finger and over the skin of the thenar eminence itself. Abductor pollicis brevis power is 5 out of 5 on both sides and there is no wasting. Tapping over the flexor retinaculum reproduces the tingling in the same three digits. Neck movements are full and painless and the reflexes are symmetrical. Her pulse rate is 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in air and temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, with a foetal heart rate of 148 beats per minute. Urinalysis shows no protein.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 148 beats per minute
data_table.Sensory examination: Reduced light touch over the right thumb, index and middle finger pulps, sparing the little finger and the thenar skin
data_table.Motor examination: Abductor pollicis brevis power 5 out of 5 bilaterally with no thenar wasting
data_table.Provocation: Percussion over the flexor retinaculum reproduces tingling in the same three digits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies before any treatment is commenced now
options.rationale: Electrodiagnostic testing is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or for surgical planning, and it does not change management when the clinical picture is characteristic and treatment is conservative. The sparing of thenar skin sensation already confirms the lesion is at the wrist rather than proximal, since the palmar cutaneous branch leaves above the retinaculum. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Carpal tunnel syndrome)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Carpal tunnel syndrome

options.text: Refer to hand surgery for consideration of carpal tunnel decompression
options.rationale: Decompression is indicated for persistent symptoms after birth, or at any time for thenar wasting or progressive motor loss, neither of which is present. Operating for a condition that usually resolves spontaneously postpartum is disproportionate. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Carpal tunnel syndrome)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Carpal tunnel syndrome

options.text: Start oral pyridoxine and a low dose diuretic to reduce the fluid retention
options.rationale: Pyridoxine has not been shown to help and diuretics are not used in pregnancy for physiological oedema because they reduce plasma volume and placental perfusion. Neither addresses the mechanical compression that splinting relieves. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Fit neutral position wrist splints to be worn overnight and review after birth
options.rationale: Nocturnal median nerve symptoms with preserved power and no wasting are pregnancy-related carpal tunnel syndrome, which is driven by fluid retention and resolves in the great majority within weeks of birth. Night splinting the wrist in neutral is the first-line treatment and avoids any intervention during pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy

options.text: Refer for a corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel within the week
options.rationale: Local corticosteroid injection is a reasonable second-line option when splinting fails and symptoms are disabling, but it is not the first step in a self-limiting pregnancy-related presentation with normal motor function. Escalating before a trial of splinting exposes her to an invasive procedure she is unlikely to need. (Source: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal problems in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Carpal tunnel syndrome affects up to a third of pregnancies and typically appears in the third trimester as interstitial fluid accumulates within the fixed osseofibrous tunnel at the wrist. The classic picture is nocturnal or early morning paraesthesia in the median distribution relieved by shaking the hand, and the sparing of sensation over the thenar eminence is a useful sign because the palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the flexor retinaculum. Cervical radiculopathy, thoracic outlet syndrome and a proximal median neuropathy are the differentials, separated by neck signs, reflex changes and the distribution of sensory loss. The great majority of pregnancy-related cases resolve within weeks to a few months of birth, so conservative management with neutral night splints is appropriate first-line and reassurance about the natural history is a substantial part of the consultation. Thenar wasting, weakness of thumb abduction or constant rather than intermittent numbness indicate axonal loss and prompt specialist referral irrespective of gestation.
key_points: Third trimester onset with nocturnal median paraesthesia relieved by shaking is typical.
Sparing of thenar skin sensation localises the lesion to the wrist rather than proximally.
Neutral position night splinting is first-line and most cases resolve after birth.
Thenar wasting or weak thumb abduction indicates axonal loss and needs referral.
explanation.pearls: Test abductor pollicis brevis specifically by asking the woman to raise the thumb vertically against resistance with the palm flat: weakness there, or visible thenar wasting, converts a self-limiting pregnancy complaint into an indication for specialist referral regardless of gestation.
