subtopic_detail: fever and myalgia after soft cheese at twenty six weeks with no localising source of infection
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 34-year-old woman at 26 weeks who has felt feverish and achy for two days with a headache and some loose stools that have now settled. She mentions that she went to a wedding four days ago and ate the soft cheese because nobody told her not to.

On examination her chest is clear, the abdomen is soft with a non-tender uterus, there is no calf tenderness and no rash, and the throat and ears look normal. Her pulse rate is 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air and temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius, with a foetal heart rate of 165 beats per minute. Her white cell count is 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 68 mg/L (less than 5) and haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155). Midstream urine microscopy shows no organisms, no white cells and no growth on the previous day's specimen taken by her general practitioner.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 165 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Clear chest, soft non-tender uterus, no rash, no calf tenderness, normal throat and ears
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 68 mg/L (less than 5), haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155)
data_table.Urine: Midstream microscopy shows no organisms or white cells, no growth on the previous specimen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral cefalexin and review the result of a midstream urine sample
options.rationale: Cephalosporins have no useful activity against Listeria monocytogenes, which is the classic reason this organism is missed when a pregnant woman with fever is treated empirically for pyelonephritis. The urine is already clear, which removes the indication anyway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Send a stool culture and manage symptomatically with oral paracetamol
options.rationale: Stool culture is unreliable for Listeria because the organism is a normal transient gut coloniser and the diarrhoea has usually resolved by the time of presentation. Symptomatic management alone in a febrile woman with a foetal tachycardia risks intrauterine infection and stillbirth. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start oral azithromycin and arrange an ultrasound for foetal wellbeing
options.rationale: Macrolides do not reliably cover Listeria and oral therapy is inadequate for a bacteraemic illness in pregnancy. Ultrasound is a reasonable adjunct but it neither makes the diagnosis nor treats the mother. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take a high vaginal swab and start intravenous metronidazole overnight
options.rationale: Metronidazole covers anaerobes and has no activity against this Gram positive rod, and a vaginal swab addresses chorioamnionitis, which would present with uterine tenderness and offensive discharge. The near pair to keep in mind is intra-amniotic infection, distinguished here by the soft non-tender uterus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take blood cultures and start high dose intravenous benzylpenicillin
options.rationale: Fever with myalgia and no localising source in the second half of pregnancy after a high risk food exposure is listeriosis until excluded, and blood culture is the diagnostic test because stool culture is insensitive. High dose intravenous benzylpenicillin, or amoxicillin, is the treatment of choice and is started empirically because foetal loss follows delay. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Listeria monocytogenes is a facultative intracellular Gram positive rod that pregnant women acquire roughly twentyfold more often than the general population because of the cell-mediated immune shift of pregnancy. Maternal illness is often mild and non-specific, with fever, myalgia, headache and sometimes gastrointestinal upset, while the foetal consequences are severe and include miscarriage, preterm birth, stillbirth and early onset neonatal sepsis or meningitis. The high risk foods are soft and semi-soft cheeses, pre-prepared salads, cold cooked chicken, pate, smoked seafood and unpasteurised dairy, and the incubation period for invasive disease can extend to several weeks, which is why the dietary history reaches well beyond the preceding day or two. Blood cultures are the diagnostic test of choice, and because the organism is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins, empirical regimens chosen for urinary or respiratory sepsis will not cover it. Treatment is high dose intravenous benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin, with gentamicin added for severe disease, and trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole used where there is penicillin hypersensitivity.
key_points: Pregnancy raises the risk of invasive listeriosis roughly twentyfold.
Blood cultures make the diagnosis; stool culture is unreliable.
Listeria is intrinsically resistant to every cephalosporin.
High dose intravenous benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin is the treatment of choice.
explanation.pearls: The intrinsic cephalosporin resistance of Listeria monocytogenes is the trap: a febrile pregnant woman started on cefalexin or ceftriaxone for presumed pyelonephritis remains untreated, so ask about soft cheese, pate and cold cooked chicken before choosing the empirical agent.

subtopic_detail: palpitations and weight loss three months after birth with a suppressed thyrotropin and no eye signs
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 33-year-old woman 12 weeks after the birth of her first baby. She says her heart races when she walks up the drive, she feels hot when everyone else is comfortable, and she has lost 5 kg without trying while still fully breastfeeding. She has no past thyroid history and takes no medication other than an iodine-containing pregnancy multivitamin she has continued.

On examination there is a fine tremor of the outstretched hands and a small smooth painless goitre. The eyes show no lid retraction, no proptosis and a full range of movement, and there is no pretibial change. Her pulse rate is 104 beats per minute and regular, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in air and temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. Thyroid stimulating hormone is less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 28 pmol/L (10-20) and free triiodothyronine 7.1 pmol/L (3.5-6.0). Thyroid peroxidase antibody is strongly positive and thyrotropin receptor antibody is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, small smooth painless goitre, no lid retraction, proptosis or pretibial change
data_table.Thyroid function: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 28 pmol/L (10-20), free triiodothyronine 7.1 pmol/L (3.5-6.0)
data_table.Antibodies: Thyroid peroxidase antibody strongly positive, thyrotropin receptor antibody negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start propranolol for symptom control and repeat thyroid function in six weeks
options.rationale: A painless goitre with positive thyroid peroxidase antibody and negative thyrotropin receptor antibody within a year of birth is the thyrotoxic phase of postpartum thyroiditis, which is a destructive release of stored hormone rather than overproduction. Beta blockade controls symptoms while the phase runs its course, and propranolol is compatible with breastfeeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy and postpartum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy and postpartum

options.text: Start carbimazole and refer to endocrinology for ongoing specialist management
options.rationale: Thionamides block new hormone synthesis and are useless in a destructive thyroiditis, where the circulating hormone has already been made and stored. They would also drive her into hypothyroidism as the destructive phase ends. Graves disease is the near pair, distinguished here by the negative thyrotropin receptor antibody and the absence of orbitopathy. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy and postpartum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy and postpartum

options.text: Arrange radioactive iodine uptake scanning and cease breastfeeding today
options.rationale: Radioiodine is contraindicated during breastfeeding and requires cessation for a substantial period, which is a major intervention for a self-limiting condition. The antibody profile has already separated the destructive from the autoimmune hyperfunctioning cause without any radiation. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Start thyroxine replacement and recheck thyroid function in three months
options.rationale: Replacement is the treatment for the hypothyroid phase that typically follows, not for the current thyrotoxic phase, and giving it now would compound the excess circulating hormone. The timing of the phases is what makes the sequence matter. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy and postpartum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy and postpartum

options.text: Refer for total thyroidectomy after a period of medical pretreatment first
options.rationale: Definitive surgery is reserved for Graves disease with compressive symptoms, severe orbitopathy or failed medical therapy, and has no place in a transient self-limiting thyroiditis. Removing a gland that will recover normal function within months is not justifiable. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy and postpartum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy and postpartum

explanation.summary: Postpartum thyroiditis is an autoimmune destructive thyroiditis affecting around 5 per cent of women in the first year after birth, with much higher rates in those with type 1 diabetes or pre-existing thyroid autoimmunity. The classic course is a thyrotoxic phase between roughly one and four months postpartum, followed by a hypothyroid phase from about four to eight months, and then recovery of euthyroidism in most women by twelve months. Distinguishing it from Graves disease matters because the treatments are opposite, and the discriminators are a painless rather than tender gland, absent orbitopathy, a negative thyrotropin receptor antibody, a positive thyroid peroxidase antibody, and a low rather than high radionuclide uptake if scanning is ever needed. Beta blockade is the only treatment required in the thyrotoxic phase, with thyroxine reserved for symptomatic or profound hypothyroidism in the second phase. Around one in five women go on to permanent hypothyroidism, and recurrence in a subsequent pregnancy is common, so annual thyroid function testing is arranged after recovery.
key_points: The sequence is thyrotoxic then hypothyroid then recovery across the first postpartum year.
Negative thyrotropin receptor antibody with no orbitopathy separates this from Graves disease.
Thionamides do not work in a destructive thyroiditis; beta blockade is the treatment.
About one in five women develop permanent hypothyroidism and need annual testing.
explanation.pearls: Propranolol and metoprolol are the beta blockers of choice while breastfeeding because they transfer into milk in negligible amounts, whereas atenolol accumulates in the infant and has caused neonatal bradycardia and hypotension.

subtopic_detail: heavy painful periods with a diffusely bulky tender uterus and no focal lesion on imaging
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 42-year-old woman who has had progressively heavier and more painful periods over three years. She describes flooding through a pad in an hour on her two worst days, passing clots the size of a twenty cent piece, and a deep dragging ache that now starts a week before bleeding. She has two children, both born vaginally, and does not want any more. She has not had intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding.

On examination the uterus is smooth, symmetrically enlarged to about ten weeks size and tender on bimanual palpation, with no adnexal mass and no nodularity in the pouch of Douglas. Transvaginal ultrasound reports a globular uterus with asymmetrical myometrial wall thickening, indistinct junctional zone and small myometrial cysts, with no discrete fibroid, an endometrial thickness of 6 mm and normal ovaries. Her haemoglobin is 104 g/L (115-155) and ferritin 9 micrograms/L (30-200). Her cervical screening test six months ago was negative for human papillomavirus.

data_table.Pelvic examination: Smooth symmetrically enlarged tender uterus of about ten weeks size, no adnexal mass or nodularity
data_table.Ultrasound: Globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial wall thickening, indistinct junctional zone, small myometrial cysts, no discrete fibroid, endometrial thickness 6 mm, normal ovaries
data_table.Screening: Cervical screening test negative for human papillomavirus six months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Start tranexamic acid alone and review the bleeding chart in six months
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is a reasonable non-hormonal option that reduces blood loss by roughly a third, but it is taken only during bleeding, does not treat the dysmenorrhoea that dominates her symptoms and provides no contraception. It is the near pair to consider if she declined a hormonal device. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system after counselling
options.rationale: A globular tender uterus with an indistinct junctional zone and myometrial cysts but no discrete fibroid is adenomyosis, and the levonorgestrel intrauterine system is the first-line treatment because it reduces both bleeding and dysmenorrhoea by inducing endometrial and adenomyotic decidualisation. It also provides contraception, which she needs. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation as the first line interventional option
options.rationale: Embolisation has a role in adenomyosis refractory to medical management and is well established for fibroids, but it is a radiological intervention with a significant reintervention rate and is not a first-line choice. Medical therapy is offered before any procedure. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Start a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist for six months of therapy
options.rationale: Agonist therapy induces a hypo-oestrogenic state that shrinks adenomyosis effectively but causes bone loss and vasomotor symptoms, so it is used short term before surgery or when other options have failed. It is not sustainable as initial management for a woman who may be a decade from menopause. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Refer for hysteroscopic resection of the abnormal area of the endometrium
options.rationale: Hysteroscopic surgery treats intracavity pathology such as a polyp or submucosal fibroid, and the endometrial thickness here is normal with no focal lesion. Adenomyosis lies within the myometrium and is beyond the reach of a hysteroscopic resection. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium with surrounding smooth muscle hypertrophy, and it classically presents in the fourth and fifth decades with heavy menstrual bleeding, progressive secondary dysmenorrhoea and a symmetrically bulky tender uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound has largely replaced histology for diagnosis, with a globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial thickening, an indistinct or interrupted junctional zone, myometrial cysts and subendometrial echogenic lines being the recognised features. The main differential is uterine fibroids, which give an irregular rather than globular contour and discrete lesions, and endometriosis, which gives nodularity in the pouch of Douglas and adnexal findings. Levonorgestrel intrauterine systems are first-line because they address bleeding and pain simultaneously and provide contraception, with combined hormonal contraception, progestogens, tranexamic acid and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs as alternatives. Iron deficiency should be treated in parallel, since a ferritin this low will not correct through diet alone while the bleeding continues.
key_points: A globular tender uterus with an indistinct junctional zone on ultrasound suggests adenomyosis.
Fibroids give an irregular contour and discrete lesions rather than diffuse thickening.
The levonorgestrel intrauterine system is first-line for both bleeding and dysmenorrhoea.
Treat the coexisting iron deficiency rather than only the bleeding.
explanation.pearls: A ferritin below 30 micrograms/L confirms iron deficiency regardless of haemoglobin, and in heavy menstrual bleeding oral iron is given on alternate days rather than daily, because daily dosing raises hepcidin and reduces the fractional absorption of each subsequent dose.

subtopic_detail: household chickenpox contact at sixteen weeks in a woman with no recalled history of the illness
stem:
You are the general practitioner telephoned by a 27-year-old woman at 16 weeks in her first pregnancy. Her 4-year-old nephew, who stayed at her house for two nights and shared meals with her, developed a blistering rash yesterday and has been diagnosed with chickenpox. She last saw him 18 hours ago.

She grew up overseas, has no recollection of ever having had chickenpox and her mother is not contactable to confirm. Her antenatal booking bloods recorded rubella immunity and a negative hepatitis B surface antigen but no varicella serology was requested. She is well, has no rash and no fever, and she has taken no immunosuppressive medication. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated with a normal first trimester screen, and she asks whether there is anything she should be doing today rather than waiting for her next appointment in three weeks.

data_table.Exposure: Two nights of household contact with a child whose vesicular rash appeared yesterday, last contact 18 hours ago
data_table.Immune history: No recalled history of chickenpox, no varicella serology on the booking panel
data_table.Booking serology: Rubella immune, hepatitis B surface antigen negative
data_table.Current status: No rash, no fever, no immunosuppressive medication

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure her and arrange a detailed foetal morphology scan at twenty weeks
options.rationale: A morphology scan is already part of routine care and looking for limb hypoplasia or cicatricial scarring after the event does nothing to prevent congenital varicella syndrome. The opportunity to modify maternal disease closes within days. (Source: RANZCOG: Varicella in pregnancy)

options.text: Give zoster immunoglobulin now without waiting for any serology result back
options.rationale: This is the near pair to the correct answer and the distinction is that serology can be turned around well within the 96 hour window, so testing first avoids giving a limited plasma-derived product to the majority who are already immune. Immunoglobulin is given without serology only when the result cannot be obtained inside the window. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella)

options.text: Request urgent varicella serology and give zoster immunoglobulin if seronegative
options.rationale: A significant household exposure in a woman of uncertain immunity requires urgent varicella immunoglobulin G testing, because most adults with no recalled history are nonetheless immune and would gain nothing from a scarce blood product. If she is seronegative, zoster immunoglobulin is given as soon as possible and ideally within 96 hours of first exposure. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella)

options.text: Give the varicella vaccine today and repeat the dose four weeks later on
options.rationale: Varicella vaccine is a live attenuated preparation and is contraindicated during pregnancy, with vaccination deferred until after birth when it is safe even while breastfeeding. It would also be too slow to protect against an exposure that has already occurred. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella)

options.text: Start oral aciclovir today and continue it for the next seven days straight
options.rationale: Antiviral therapy is used to treat established maternal varicella, where it is started within 24 hours of the rash, and is considered as post-exposure prophylaxis only when immunoglobulin is unavailable or the window has passed. It is not the first-line post-exposure measure in pregnancy. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella)

explanation.summary: Around 95 per cent of Australian-born adults are varicella immune, and a substantial proportion of those with no recalled history of chickenpox are seropositive, which is why serology precedes immunoglobulin rather than following it. A significant exposure means face to face contact for at least five minutes, being in the same room for an hour or more, or household contact, with the infectious period running from 48 hours before the rash until all lesions have crusted. Maternal varicella in pregnancy carries appreciable maternal risk, since varicella pneumonia complicates around one in ten adult infections and is more severe in pregnancy, and foetal risk that depends on timing. Congenital varicella syndrome occurs in about 1 to 2 per cent of infections before 28 weeks and produces limb hypoplasia, cicatricial skin scarring, eye and neurological damage, while maternal rash from five days before to two days after birth threatens the neonate with severe disseminated disease. Zoster immunoglobulin is given to seronegative women as soon as possible after exposure and can still be offered up to ten days, and the woman is advised to present immediately if a rash develops so that aciclovir can be started within 24 hours.
key_points: Most adults with no recalled history of chickenpox are in fact seropositive, so test first.
Zoster immunoglobulin is given ideally within 96 hours and can be offered up to ten days.
Varicella vaccine is live attenuated and contraindicated during pregnancy.
Congenital varicella syndrome risk is about 1 to 2 per cent for infection before 28 weeks.
explanation.pearls: Maternal rash appearing between 5 days before and 2 days after birth is the highest risk window for the neonate, because the baby is delivered with virus but without transplacental antibody, and that infant needs zoster immunoglobulin at birth plus intravenous aciclovir if lesions appear.

subtopic_detail: breakthrough focal seizures at twenty four weeks in a woman stable on lamotrigine before conception
stem:
You are the obstetric physician seeing a 26-year-old woman at 24 weeks in her first pregnancy. She has focal epilepsy with impaired awareness and had been seizure free for three years on lamotrigine 300 mg daily before conception. She has had two seizures in the past fortnight, each lasting under two minutes with post-ictal confusion, and one occurred while she was making dinner.

She brings her dosette box and her partner confirms she has not missed a dose. She has not had vomiting, has not started any new medication including the combined oral contraceptive, and has not changed brand of tablet. She sleeps seven hours a night and has not been drinking alcohol. Her blood pressure is 106/64 mmHg with no proteinuria, her reflexes are normal and she has no headache or visual disturbance. The foetus is appropriately grown on ultrasound with normal liquor and umbilical artery Dopplers. A trough lamotrigine concentration is 2.1 mg/L, against a preconception baseline of 4.6 mg/L recorded in the same laboratory.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 106/64 mmHg with no proteinuria, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Seizure pattern: Two focal seizures with impaired awareness in a fortnight, each under two minutes, after three years seizure free
data_table.Adherence: Dosette box checked and adherence confirmed, no vomiting, no new medication, no brand change
data_table.Drug levels: Trough lamotrigine 2.1 mg/L against a preconception baseline of 4.6 mg/L in the same laboratory
data_table.Foetal assessment: Appropriate growth with normal liquor volume and umbilical artery Dopplers

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Switch her from lamotrigine to levetiracetam over the next two weeks now
options.rationale: Changing agent mid-pregnancy exposes the foetus to two drugs during the cross-titration and exposes the mother to a period of uncertain control, when the existing drug was working well before conception. Levetiracetam clearance also rises substantially in pregnancy, so the same problem would recur. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Maintain the current dose and reassess her seizures after she has given birth
options.rationale: Ongoing seizures carry real risks including trauma, foetal hypoxia and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, and the risk rises as clearance continues to increase into the third trimester. Waiting accepts a hazard that is straightforward to correct. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Add clobazam nightly and repeat an electroencephalogram within this month
options.rationale: Adding a second agent treats the symptom while leaving the pharmacokinetic cause uncorrected, and an electroencephalogram will not explain a fall in drug concentration. Clobazam is the near pair to a legitimate adjunct, but it is reserved for seizures that persist once the lamotrigine concentration has been restored. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Increase the lamotrigine dose guided by serial serum level monitoring
options.rationale: Oestrogen-driven induction of uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase markedly increases lamotrigine clearance in pregnancy, and a level that has fallen to under half the preconception baseline in an adherent woman explains the loss of seizure control. Increasing the dose against serial levels to restore the individual preconception concentration is the established approach. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Add sodium valproate at a low dose for the remainder of the pregnancy
options.rationale: Valproate carries the highest risk of major congenital malformation and of impaired neurodevelopment of any antiseizure medication and is avoided in pregnancy wherever an alternative exists. It also inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation, which would make the levels unpredictable. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Lamotrigine is eliminated almost entirely by glucuronidation, and rising oestrogen induces the responsible enzyme so strongly that clearance can more than double by the third trimester, with concentrations often falling to between a third and a half of preconception values. This is the commonest cause of breakthrough seizures in pregnancy in women who were previously well controlled, and it is managed by pre-emptive level monitoring roughly monthly with dose adjustment targeting the woman's own preconception concentration rather than a population range. Seizure control in pregnancy matters because generalised convulsions cause maternal trauma, placental abruption and foetal hypoxia, and epilepsy remains a leading indirect cause of maternal death through sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. The mirror image occurs after birth, when clearance returns to baseline within one to three weeks and toxicity develops unless the dose is tapered back on a prearranged schedule. All women with epilepsy who may become pregnant take high dose folic acid preconceptually, and valproate is avoided because of its dose-dependent malformation and neurodevelopmental risk.
key_points: Oestrogen induces glucuronidation, so lamotrigine clearance rises steeply in pregnancy.
Target the woman's own preconception concentration, not a population reference range.
Postpartum clearance normalises within one to three weeks, so the dose must be tapered back.
Valproate carries the highest teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk and is avoided.
explanation.pearls: Write the postpartum lamotrigine taper into the birth plan before the woman goes into labour: clearance falls back to preconception values within one to three weeks, and leaving a doubled pregnancy dose in place produces toxicity with ataxia and diplopia just as she is caring for a newborn.

subtopic_detail: maternal rash and joint pains at eighteen weeks after an outbreak of slapped cheek at a primary school
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 30-year-old primary school teacher at 18 weeks. Three weeks ago several children in her class had bright red cheeks and were sent home, and ten days ago she developed aching hands and knees along with a lacy pink rash on her upper arms that has now faded. She feels well today.

Her parvovirus B19 immunoglobulin M is positive and immunoglobulin G is positive, on a sample taken three days ago, and the booking sample from 10 weeks has been retrieved and tested as immunoglobulin G negative. Her full blood count shows haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155) with a normal white cell count and platelet count. Ultrasound today reports a structurally normal foetus with a normal liquor volume, no ascites, no pericardial effusion and no skin oedema. Her blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg with no proteinuria and she is afebrile. She asks what happens next.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg with no proteinuria, afebrile, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Serology: Parvovirus B19 immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G positive, with a booking sample at 10 weeks that was immunoglobulin G negative
data_table.Full blood count: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155) with normal white cell and platelet counts
data_table.Ultrasound: Structurally normal foetus, normal liquor volume, no ascites, pericardial effusion or skin oedema

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing management?

options.text: Arrange amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction within the next week
options.rationale: Amniotic fluid testing confirms foetal infection but does not quantify anaemia, which is what determines whether intervention is needed, and it carries a procedure-related loss risk. Maternal seroconversion has already established the exposure that matters. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Reassure her and continue routine antenatal care with no additional imaging
options.rationale: A single normal scan at three weeks does not exclude anaemia developing later, since the interval between maternal infection and hydrops is typically two to eight weeks and can extend to twelve. Discharging her from surveillance now would miss the window in which transfusion saves the foetus. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin to the mother to prevent vertical transmission
options.rationale: There is no evidence that maternal immunoglobulin prevents transplacental passage or foetal anaemia, and it is not recommended for this indication. Treatment when it is needed is directed at the foetus rather than the mother. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange fortnightly growth scans with umbilical artery Doppler assessment only
options.rationale: Growth and umbilical artery Dopplers assess placental insufficiency, which is a different pathology, and they are the near pair to the correct answer in that both are serial ultrasound. The umbilical artery does not reflect foetal haemoglobin, whereas the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity rises as blood viscosity falls in anaemia. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

options.text: Begin serial middle cerebral artery Doppler surveillance for the next twelve weeks
options.rationale: Documented seroconversion confirms recent maternal infection, and the foetal risk is anaemia from erythroid progenitor destruction, which precedes hydrops and is detected non-invasively by a rising middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity. Weekly or fortnightly surveillance for eight to twelve weeks after infection is the standard approach. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 targets the P antigen on erythroid progenitors and, when maternal infection occurs, can cross the placenta to cause foetal red cell aplasia, high output failure, hydrops and death. Vertical transmission occurs in roughly a third of maternal infections, with the greatest foetal risk before 20 weeks, and overall foetal loss is in the order of a few per cent, rising for infection in the first half of pregnancy. Around half of pregnant women are already immune, so serology is interpreted as a pair, with immunoglobulin M positivity plus documented seroconversion from a stored booking sample being the most secure evidence of recent infection. Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is the surveillance tool because anaemic foetal blood is less viscous and therefore flows faster, and a velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median for gestation identifies significant anaemia with high sensitivity. Intrauterine transfusion is the treatment when that threshold is crossed with or without hydrops, and it substantially improves survival, while hydrops from parvovirus can also resolve spontaneously, so a diagnosis is never a reason to offer termination on its own.
key_points: Transmission occurs in about a third of maternal infections, with highest risk before 20 weeks.
Foetal anaemia precedes hydrops and is detected by middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity.
Surveillance runs weekly to fortnightly for eight to twelve weeks after maternal infection.
Intrauterine transfusion is the treatment and markedly improves survival.
explanation.pearls: A middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median for gestational age is the threshold that triggers referral for intrauterine transfusion, and it detects significant foetal anaemia before any hydropic change is visible on the scan.

subtopic_detail: maternal toxoplasma seroconversion at fourteen weeks with a structurally normal foetus on ultrasound
stem:
You are the maternal foetal medicine registrar seeing a 32-year-old woman at 14 weeks who was investigated for three weeks of cervical lymphadenopathy and fatigue. She keeps two cats, empties the litter tray herself and has been gardening without gloves at a new house.

Toxoplasma immunoglobulin M is positive and immunoglobulin G is positive with a low avidity index, and her stored booking serum from 7 weeks is immunoglobulin G negative on retesting in the same reference laboratory. Her full blood count and liver function tests are normal and she is human immunodeficiency virus negative. Ultrasound today shows a structurally normal foetus with normal biometry, no intracranial calcification, normal ventricles and a normal liquor volume. Her blood pressure is 114/72 mmHg and she is afebrile. She is distressed and asks what can be done to protect the baby.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 114/72 mmHg, afebrile, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Serology: Toxoplasma immunoglobulin M positive, immunoglobulin G positive with low avidity, booking serum at 7 weeks immunoglobulin G negative
data_table.Other investigations: Normal full blood count and liver function tests, human immunodeficiency virus negative
data_table.Ultrasound: Structurally normal foetus with normal biometry, no intracranial calcification, normal ventricles and liquor volume
data_table.Exposure history: Two cats with owner-managed litter tray, gardening without gloves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start spiramycin now and arrange amniotic fluid testing after eighteen weeks
options.rationale: Spiramycin concentrates in the placenta without crossing it appreciably and is used to reduce vertical transmission while foetal infection status is unknown. Amniocentesis for toxoplasma polymerase chain reaction is deferred until after 18 weeks and at least four weeks after maternal infection to avoid false negatives, and its result determines whether therapy is escalated. (Source: RANZCOG: Toxoplasmosis in pregnancy)

options.text: Start pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and folinic acid immediately this week
options.rationale: This regimen treats established foetal infection and is the escalation once amniotic fluid polymerase chain reaction is positive or ultrasound shows foetal abnormality. Pyrimethamine is a folate antagonist and is avoided in the first trimester, so starting it before foetal infection is demonstrated exposes the pregnancy to unnecessary risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Toxoplasmosis in pregnancy)

options.text: Repeat the serology in four weeks and take no further action in the interim
options.rationale: Seroconversion has already been documented against a stored negative booking sample with a low avidity index, so the diagnosis is not in doubt and repeating the test adds nothing. The delay costs the weeks in which spiramycin reduces transmission. (Source: RANZCOG: Toxoplasmosis in pregnancy)

options.text: Offer termination of pregnancy given the risk of severe foetal damage now
options.rationale: Transmission risk at 14 weeks is only around 15 per cent, most infected infants are asymptomatic at birth, and treatment reduces both transmission and severity. Offering termination before foetal infection has even been established misrepresents the prognosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Toxoplasmosis in pregnancy)

options.text: Start azithromycin and arrange monthly ultrasound surveillance instead of this
options.rationale: Azithromycin has activity against Toxoplasma gondii and appears in some alternative regimens, but it is not the established first-line agent for reducing vertical transmission in Australian practice. Monthly ultrasound is a reasonable adjunct and is the near pair to the correct answer, but surveillance without treatment and without amniocentesis leaves both the transmission risk and the diagnosis unaddressed. (Source: RANZCOG: Toxoplasmosis in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Congenital toxoplasmosis follows primary maternal infection acquired from undercooked meat, soil, or cat faeces, and Australia does not screen universally because seroprevalence and incidence are both low. The relationship between gestation and outcome is inverse in two directions, since transmission risk rises with gestational age from roughly 5 per cent in the first trimester to over 60 per cent near term, while severity of foetal disease falls, so early infection is uncommon but devastating and late infection is common but usually subclinical. Diagnosis of recent infection rests on immunoglobulin M with a low immunoglobulin G avidity index, and ideally on documented seroconversion against a stored earlier sample, because immunoglobulin M can persist for a year or more and causes frequent misclassification. Spiramycin is given while foetal status is unknown, and pyrimethamine with sulfadiazine and folinic acid replaces it when amniotic fluid polymerase chain reaction confirms foetal infection or ultrasound shows hydrocephalus, intracranial calcification or hepatosplenomegaly. Infants born to infected mothers need paediatric infectious diseases follow-up with ophthalmological review, because chorioretinitis can present years after an apparently normal birth.
key_points: Transmission risk rises with gestation while severity of foetal disease falls.
Low immunoglobulin G avidity plus a stored negative sample confirms recent infection.
Spiramycin reduces transmission and does not cross the placenta appreciably.
Amniocentesis is deferred to after 18 weeks and at least four weeks after infection.
explanation.pearls: Amniotic fluid polymerase chain reaction for Toxoplasma gondii is timed to both 18 weeks gestation and at least four weeks after the estimated date of maternal infection, because sampling earlier than either threshold produces false negative results and a falsely reassuring plan.

subtopic_detail: acute focal abdominal pain over a known uterine mass at twenty two weeks with a soft uterus between episodes
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 36-year-old woman at 22 weeks who has had severe right sided abdominal pain for eighteen hours. A 7 cm intramural mass was documented on her first trimester scan and measured 11 cm at her morphology scan two weeks ago. She describes the pain as constant and burning, worst over one spot she can point to with a finger.

On examination there is marked localised tenderness over a firm mass palpable in the right side of the uterus, while the rest of the uterus is soft and relaxes completely between palpations. The cervix is long and closed on speculum examination with no bleeding or liquor. Her pulse rate is 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air and temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius, with a foetal heart rate of 150 beats per minute. White cell count is 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 32 mg/L (less than 5) and urinalysis is negative for nitrites and leucocytes. Cardiotocography shows a reactive trace with no contractions.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 150 beats per minute
data_table.Abdominal examination: Focal tenderness over a firm right-sided uterine mass, uterus soft and relaxed between palpations
data_table.Speculum examination: Long closed cervix with no bleeding and no liquor
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 32 mg/L (less than 5), urinalysis negative for nitrites and leucocytes
data_table.Serial imaging: Intramural mass 7 cm in the first trimester and 11 cm two weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange uterine artery embolisation to devascularise the fibroid immediately
options.rationale: Embolisation is contraindicated in pregnancy because it would interrupt the uterine blood supply the foetus depends on, and it involves significant ionising radiation. It is a postpartum or non-pregnant option only. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

options.text: Admit for analgesia, hydration and conservative management with review
options.rationale: Focal pain and tenderness localised to a rapidly enlarging fibroid, with a soft uterus between palpations and a low grade fever with modest inflammatory markers, is red degeneration caused by the fibroid outgrowing its blood supply. It is self-limiting over days to a fortnight and is managed with admission, analgesia and hydration. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange laparotomy and myomectomy to remove the degenerating fibroid now
options.rationale: Myomectomy during pregnancy carries substantial risks of haemorrhage, pregnancy loss and the need for hysterectomy, and it is reserved for a pedunculated torted fibroid or intractable pain that has failed all conservative measures. The natural history here is resolution without surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

options.text: Start intravenous antibiotics for a presumed intra-amniotic infection today
options.rationale: Chorioamnionitis is the near pair given the fever and raised inflammatory markers, and the distinction is anatomical rather than biochemical, since intra-amniotic infection produces generalised uterine tenderness, offensive discharge and foetal tachycardia rather than pain localised to one mass with a soft uterus elsewhere. Degeneration causes a low grade fever and a modest leucocytosis in its own right. (Source: RANZCOG: Fibroids in pregnancy)

options.text: Give nifedipine tocolysis and a course of intramuscular betamethasone today
options.rationale: Tocolysis and steroids are for threatened preterm labour, which requires contractions and cervical change, and the cardiotocograph shows no contractions with a long closed cervix. Treating for preterm labour here medicates a diagnosis she does not have. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

explanation.summary: Fibroids enlarge in pregnancy under oestrogen stimulation, and when growth outstrips the blood supply the central portion undergoes haemorrhagic or red degeneration, classically in the second trimester and in fibroids larger than about 5 cm. The presentation is acute severe pain localised precisely over the fibroid with focal tenderness, often with a low grade fever, a modest leucocytosis and a mildly raised C-reactive protein, all of which are explained by tissue necrosis rather than infection. The critical bedside discriminators are that the remainder of the uterus stays soft and non-tender, the cervix is closed, and the cardiotocograph shows no contractions, which separate this from chorioamnionitis, placental abruption and preterm labour. Management is conservative with opioid analgesia and hydration, since the process resolves spontaneously over several days to two weeks, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs may be used for a short course before 30 weeks but not beyond because of premature ductal closure. Surgery in pregnancy is reserved for torsion of a pedunculated fibroid or pain that fails every conservative measure, and the presence of fibroids raises the risks of malpresentation, obstructed labour and postpartum haemorrhage that the birth plan must anticipate.
key_points: Red degeneration causes focal pain over the fibroid with a soft uterus elsewhere.
Low grade fever, leucocytosis and a raised C-reactive protein come from necrosis, not infection.
A closed cervix with no contractions excludes preterm labour as the cause of the pain.
Management is conservative, with surgery reserved for torsion or intractable pain.
explanation.pearls: A short course of a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug is acceptable for red degeneration before 30 weeks but is stopped beyond that gestation and limited to about 48 hours, because prolonged exposure causes premature constriction of the ductus arteriosus and oligohydramnios.

subtopic_detail: seven centimetre ovarian cyst with fat and calcification in a nulliparous woman with normal tumour markers
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 24-year-old nulliparous woman referred after a scan arranged for six months of intermittent dull left iliac fossa discomfort. She has regular cycles, uses condoms for contraception, and has never been pregnant. She would like children in the future.

Transvaginal ultrasound describes a 7 cm left ovarian cyst containing an echogenic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing, layered echogenic material with a fluid level, and no solid vascular papillary projections on colour Doppler. The right ovary is normal and there is no free fluid in the pelvis. CA125 is 18 units/mL (less than 35), lactate dehydrogenase, alpha fetoprotein and beta human chorionic gonadotrophin are all within their reference intervals, and a urinary pregnancy test is negative. On examination the abdomen is soft with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no guarding, and her vital signs are within normal limits. The cyst measured 6.6 cm on a scan performed nine months earlier at another practice.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no guarding
data_table.Ultrasound: 7 cm left ovarian cyst with a shadowing echogenic focus, layered echogenic material with a fluid level, no vascular papillary projections, normal right ovary, no free fluid
data_table.Tumour markers: CA125 18 units/mL (less than 35), lactate dehydrogenase, alpha fetoprotein and beta human chorionic gonadotrophin within reference intervals
data_table.Serial imaging: Cyst measured 6.6 cm nine months earlier

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to gynaecological oncology for staging laparotomy and omental biopsy
options.rationale: Staging surgery is for a cyst with malignant features such as solid vascular components, thick septations, ascites or a raised risk of malignancy index, none of which are present. Referral here would subject a young woman to laparotomy for a benign lesion. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of ovarian cysts)

options.text: Perform ultrasound guided aspiration of the cyst and send fluid for cytology
options.rationale: Aspiration has a high recurrence rate, cannot remove the solid sebaceous and keratin contents of a teratoma, and risks chemical peritonitis from spillage of cyst contents into the peritoneal cavity. Cytology of aspirated fluid is also unreliable for excluding malignancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of ovarian cysts)

options.text: Perform laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy preserving the remaining ovarian tissue
options.rationale: The shadowing echogenic focus, layered fat-fluid level and absence of vascular papillary projections describe a mature cystic teratoma, and at 7 cm the torsion risk justifies removal in a young woman. Laparoscopic cystectomy with an endoscopic retrieval bag removes the lesion while preserving ovarian reserve and future fertility. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of ovarian cysts)

options.text: Perform laparoscopic salpingo-oophorectomy to avoid intraoperative spillage
options.rationale: Removing the whole ovary sacrifices reserve in a 24-year-old for a benign lesion, and spillage is managed by using a retrieval bag with copious irrigation rather than by removing more tissue. This is the near pair to the correct answer, and the distinction is that oophorectomy is reserved for suspected malignancy or an ovary destroyed by the lesion. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of ovarian cysts)

options.text: Observe with six monthly ultrasound surveillance and repeat tumour markers
options.rationale: Conservative surveillance is reasonable for an asymptomatic teratoma under about 5 cm, but this one is symptomatic, is larger than that threshold and has grown slowly over nine months. Torsion risk rises steeply with size and is the complication surveillance cannot prevent. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of ovarian cysts)

explanation.summary: Mature cystic teratoma is the commonest ovarian neoplasm in women under 40 and arises from a single germ cell, producing tissue from all three germ layers, which is why ultrasound shows fat, hair and calcific elements with characteristic acoustic shadowing and fat-fluid levels. Management balances the risks of surgery against the risks of leaving it, with torsion being the dominant concern because teratomas are heavy and mobile, and torsion risk rises appreciably beyond about 5 cm. Malignant transformation, usually to squamous cell carcinoma, occurs in well under 2 per cent and is concentrated in older women and larger lesions, so tumour markers are used to assess risk rather than to make the diagnosis. Surgery in a young woman wanting future fertility is ovarian-sparing cystectomy performed laparoscopically with a retrieval bag, because spilled sebaceous contents can cause a chemical peritonitis and because every fragment of preserved cortex counts towards later ovarian reserve. Bilateral teratomas occur in around 10 per cent, so the contralateral ovary is inspected at operation even when it looked normal on imaging.
key_points: Shadowing echogenic foci and fat-fluid levels are the ultrasound signature of a teratoma.
Torsion risk rises with size and drives the decision to operate rather than observe.
Ovarian-sparing cystectomy preserves reserve in a woman wanting future fertility.
A retrieval bag limits spillage, which can otherwise cause chemical peritonitis.
explanation.pearls: Around one in ten mature cystic teratomas are bilateral, so the contralateral ovary is directly inspected at laparoscopy even when preoperative ultrasound reported it as normal.

subtopic_detail: recurrent endometrioma in the only remaining ovary of a woman with a low antimullerian hormone
stem:
You are the fertility specialist seeing a 34-year-old woman who has been trying to conceive for two years. She had a left salpingo-oophorectomy at 26 for a torted ovary that was not salvageable, and a right ovarian cystectomy at 30 for a 5 cm endometrioma. She has severe dysmenorrhoea and deep dyspareunia and takes a combined oral contraceptive continuously for pain.

Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 4 cm right ovarian cyst with homogeneous low level ground glass echoes and no vascular solid components, with the left adnexa surgically absent. Her antimullerian hormone is 3.1 pmol/L (age related reference 8-30), her antral follicle count on the right is 3, and her day 3 follicle stimulating hormone is 12 IU/L (3-9). Her partner's semen analysis is normal on two occasions. A hysterosalpingogram shows a patent right tube. Her CA125 is 62 units/mL (less than 35) and she is otherwise well with normal vital signs.

data_table.Surgical history: Left salpingo-oophorectomy at 26, right ovarian cystectomy for endometrioma at 30
data_table.Ultrasound: 4 cm right ovarian cyst with homogeneous ground glass echoes and no vascular solid components, left adnexa surgically absent
data_table.Ovarian reserve: Antimullerian hormone 3.1 pmol/L (age related reference 8-30), right antral follicle count 3, day 3 follicle stimulating hormone 12 IU/L (3-9)
data_table.Other investigations: Patent right tube on hysterosalpingogram, normal partner semen analysis on two occasions, CA125 62 units/mL (less than 35)

lead_in: What would you recommend first?

options.text: Prescribe a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist for six months of therapy
options.rationale: Suppression shrinks endometriotic tissue and helps pain but does not improve spontaneous conception rates, and six months of anovulation is six months lost in a woman with declining reserve at 34. Her reserve markers make time the scarcest resource. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis and infertility)

options.text: Perform laparoscopic ablation of the cyst wall using bipolar diathermy energy
options.rationale: Ablation is the near pair to excision and it does preserve more cortex than stripping, but thermal energy applied to the ovarian surface still damages adjacent follicles and recurrence rates are higher. Neither approach is justified when the cyst is not obstructing retrieval and reserve is this low. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis and infertility)

options.text: Start continuous combined oral contraception and review her again in one year
options.rationale: She is already taking continuous combined contraception for pain, and continuing it prevents conception entirely, which is the opposite of what she has come for. Another year of delay at 34 with this reserve materially reduces her chance of a live birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis and infertility)

options.text: Refer directly for in vitro fertilisation without further ovarian surgery
options.rationale: Excising an endometrioma removes surrounding normal cortex and measurably lowers antimullerian hormone and antral follicle count, which is unacceptable when this is her only ovary and reserve is already markedly reduced. Proceeding straight to in vitro fertilisation preserves the follicles she has and gives the best chance of a pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis and infertility)

options.text: Perform a repeat laparoscopic cystectomy of the endometrioma before treatment
options.rationale: Repeat cystectomy causes greater reserve loss than a first procedure because the plane is scarred, and in a solitary ovary it risks premature ovarian insufficiency. Surgery before assisted reproduction is reserved for pain that has failed medical management, suspicious features, or a cyst obstructing oocyte retrieval. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis and infertility)

explanation.summary: Endometriomas are associated with reduced ovarian reserve both intrinsically, through local inflammation and pressure atrophy of adjacent cortex, and iatrogenically, because excisional surgery inevitably removes normal cortical tissue along with the cyst wall. The evidence that cystectomy lowers antimullerian hormone is consistent, and the loss is greater for bilateral disease, for larger cysts and for repeat procedures where the cleavage plane is scarred. That makes the decision context-dependent rather than reflexive, and the presence of a single remaining ovary inverts the usual teaching that a recurrent endometrioma should be excised. Surgery retains a clear place for pain refractory to medical treatment, for a cyst with suspicious features on imaging, for cysts obstructing access to follicles at oocyte retrieval, and where malignancy cannot be excluded. A CA125 modestly elevated into the 50 to 100 range is common in endometriosis and does not by itself indicate malignancy, though a rapidly rising value or solid vascular components on ultrasound would change that assessment entirely.
key_points: Endometrioma excision removes normal cortex and lowers antimullerian hormone measurably.
Repeat cystectomy costs more reserve than a first operation because the plane is scarred.
A solitary ovary with low reserve shifts the balance towards assisted reproduction first.
Surgery remains indicated for refractory pain, suspicious imaging or obstructed retrieval.
explanation.pearls: A CA125 in the 50 to 100 units/mL range is unremarkable in endometriosis and is not a reason to operate, whereas solid vascular papillary projections on ultrasound or a rapidly rising value in a postmenopausal woman warrant referral for a risk of malignancy index assessment.

subtopic_detail: multiple motor tics and one vocal tic for over a year in a nine year old with inattention
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 9-year-old boy referred by his general practitioner. His parents say he has been blinking hard and jerking his head to one side on and off since he was six, and that about a year ago he started making a repeated throat-clearing noise. The movements come in bouts, wax and wane in severity, and are worse when he is tired or excited.

He tells you he can feel a build-up like an itch just before each one and can hold them back for a short time in class, after which they come out in a burst at home. His teacher reports he is inattentive, loses his place and does not finish work, and this predates the vocal noise by two years. He has friends, enjoys swimming and is not being teased. The tics do not interfere with his handwriting or his sleep, and he says they do not bother him much. Neurological examination including gait, tone, power and coordination is normal, and he takes no medication and uses no substances.

data_table.Tic history: Multiple motor tics from age six and a vocal tic for one year, waxing and waning, worse with fatigue
data_table.Premonitory features: Describes a premonitory urge with temporary voluntary suppression followed by rebound
data_table.Functional impact: Handwriting, sleep and peer relationships unaffected, inattention predating the vocal tic by two years
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination including gait, tone, power and coordination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Start risperidone at a low dose and monitor his weight and prolactin level
options.rationale: Antipsychotics reduce tic severity but carry weight gain, metabolic and prolactin effects that are hard to justify for tics causing no functional impairment. They are reserved for severe or self-injurious tics that have not responded to behavioural treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders)

options.text: Start clonidine at night and titrate the dose against the frequency of the tics
options.rationale: Alpha-2 agonists are a reasonable pharmacological option and are particularly attractive where tics and inattention coexist, but they are second-line to behavioural therapy for tics that are not disabling. This is the near pair to the correct answer, and the distinction is that medication is reserved for impairment rather than for the presence of tics alone. (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is indicated for atypical features such as abrupt onset with fixed rather than waxing and waning course, focal neurological signs, or tics beginning in adulthood. A typical developmental course with a normal examination does not warrant a scan. (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders)

options.text: Start methylphenidate and review whether the tics become more frequent later
options.rationale: His inattention may well warrant assessment and treatment in its own right, and stimulants are not in fact contraindicated in tic disorders as was once taught, but the lead-in asks about the tics and no formal attention deficit diagnosis has yet been established. Treating a presumed comorbidity before assessing it puts the sequence the wrong way round. (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders)

options.text: Refer for comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics as first line therapy
options.rationale: Multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic present for more than a year with onset before 18 years meets criteria for Tourette syndrome, and behavioural therapy built on habit reversal training is first-line when tics are not severely disabling. It uses the premonitory urge he describes to train a competing response. (Source: RANZCP: Tic disorders)

explanation.summary: Tourette syndrome requires at least two motor tics and at least one vocal tic, not necessarily concurrent, persisting for more than a year with onset before 18 years, and it affects around 1 per cent of school aged children with a marked male predominance. The premonitory urge and the capacity for brief voluntary suppression followed by rebound are what distinguish tics from chorea, myoclonus, dystonia and stereotypies, and they are also the mechanism behavioural therapy exploits. Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics combines habit reversal training, in which a competing response is performed at the moment of the urge, with function-based assessment and relaxation, and it has the best evidence base of any first-line treatment. Comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception, with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder each affecting a substantial proportion, and the comorbidity usually causes more impairment than the tics. Tics typically peak in early adolescence and improve substantially by early adulthood, so a prognosis discussion is a therapeutic intervention in itself.
key_points: Two or more motor tics plus one vocal tic for over a year defines Tourette syndrome.
A premonitory urge with suppressibility and rebound distinguishes tics from other movements.
Behavioural therapy with habit reversal is first-line when tics are not disabling.
Comorbid attention and obsessive compulsive symptoms usually cause more impairment than the tics.
explanation.pearls: The old teaching that stimulants must be avoided in tic disorders has not held up: randomised evidence shows methylphenidate does not worsen tics overall, and untreated attention deficit hyperactivity disorder causes more functional harm in Tourette syndrome than the tics themselves.

subtopic_detail: a six year old who speaks freely at home but has not spoken at school for eight months
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old girl whose teacher has written asking for an assessment because the girl has not spoken a word at school since she started prep eight months ago. She nods, points and writes answers on a whiteboard, and completes written work at the expected standard.

Her parents say she chatters constantly at home, tells long stories to her grandmother on the phone, argues with her older brother and plays imaginative games with him involving reciprocal turn-taking and pretend. She spoke her first words at 11 months and put sentences together before she was two. At the surgery she sits close to her mother, makes brief eye contact with you, smiles at a joke and shakes her head when you ask a question, but does not speak. Her mother says she also goes silent with unfamiliar adults at the shops and at birthday parties. She passed her newborn hearing screen and has had no ear infections.

data_table.Speech pattern: Fluent age appropriate speech at home, no speech at school for eight months, silent with unfamiliar adults
data_table.Developmental history: First words at 11 months, sentences before two years, passed newborn hearing screen
data_table.Social functioning: Reciprocal imaginative play with her brother, brief eye contact, smiles responsively in the consultation
data_table.Academic function: Written work at the expected standard, communicates by nodding, pointing and writing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for graded exposure therapy delivered jointly with her school
options.rationale: Consistent failure to speak in specific social situations despite fluent speech elsewhere, lasting beyond a month of school and interfering with participation, is selective mutism, an anxiety disorder. Graded exposure with stimulus fading delivered in partnership with the school is the first-line treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders in children)

options.text: Refer for an autism spectrum diagnostic assessment before anything else
options.rationale: Autism is the near pair that families most often fear, and it is distinguished here by her reciprocal imaginative play, responsive smiling and normal social communication at home, since autistic social differences are present across all settings rather than confined to some. Situational specificity is the discriminating feature. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders in children)

options.text: Start fluoxetine at a low dose and review her response in six weeks time
options.rationale: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors have a role in selective mutism that has not responded to adequate behavioural therapy, or where severity prevents engagement with it. Starting medication before any psychological treatment has been tried inverts the recommended order. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders in children)

options.text: Arrange audiology and formal speech pathology assessment of her language
options.rationale: Hearing and language assessment would be essential if speech were delayed or abnormal in every setting, but she achieved milestones early and speaks fluently at home. A passed newborn screen with normal home speech makes a primary language or hearing disorder very unlikely. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders in children)

options.text: Advise the school to reward each spoken word with additional playtime
options.rationale: Contingent reward for speech raises the pressure on the very behaviour anxiety is blocking and commonly entrenches the silence. Effective behavioural programmes reward participation and graded approach steps rather than speech itself in the early stages. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders in children)

explanation.summary: Selective mutism is classified among the anxiety disorders and is defined by a consistent failure to speak in specific social situations where speaking is expected, despite speaking normally in others, lasting at least one month and not limited to the first month of school. It typically begins before age five but is usually identified when school entry makes the impairment visible, and it affects under 1 per cent of children with a female predominance. The core differentials are autism spectrum disorder, developmental language disorder, hearing impairment and the transient silence of a child learning a new language, each separated by whether communication is impaired across all settings or only some. Treatment is behavioural and collaborative, using stimulus fading, shaping and graded exposure delivered by the school and family with specialist guidance, and crucially it rewards brave approach behaviour rather than speech itself. Pressure, bribery and public attention to the silence reliably make it worse, so a substantial part of the intervention is coaching the adults around the child.
key_points: Situational specificity separates selective mutism from autism and language disorder.
The child speaks fluently at home, which excludes a primary language or hearing problem.
Graded exposure with stimulus fading and school partnership is first-line treatment.
Rewarding speech directly raises pressure; reward participation and approach instead.
explanation.pearls: Stimulus fading is the practical core of treatment: the child first speaks to a parent in an empty classroom, then a peer is quietly introduced into the room, then the teacher, with the audience widened only once speech is comfortable at the current step.

subtopic_detail: inner restlessness and pacing two days after a dose increase in a previously settled inpatient
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on the ward. A 24-year-old man admitted eleven days ago with a first episode of psychosis had his risperidone increased from 2 mg to 4 mg daily two days ago because he was still describing persecutory beliefs. Nursing staff have called you because he has been pacing the corridor since early morning and cannot sit through a meal.

He tells you the feeling is in his legs and that he has to keep moving or it becomes unbearable, and that it is worse when he sits still and eases when he walks. He says it started yesterday and that it is not the voices. His speech is normal in rate and form, he is not distractible, and his persecutory beliefs are described in the same terms and with the same conviction as at admission. There is no tremor, no cogwheel rigidity and no dystonia. His pulse rate is 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air and temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Creatine kinase is 140 units/L (40-200).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Mental state: Normal speech rate and form, not distractible, persecutory beliefs unchanged in content and conviction
data_table.Subjective report: Restlessness localised to the legs, worse at rest and relieved by walking, onset the day after the dose increase
data_table.Neurological examination: No tremor, cogwheel rigidity or dystonia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence diazepam and continue the current dose of risperidone unchanged
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do help akathisia and are a recognised second-line option, which makes this the near pair, but leaving the causative dose unchanged treats the symptom while the cause continues. Dose reduction addresses the mechanism and benzodiazepines are reserved for when propranolol is contraindicated or ineffective. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reduce the risperidone dose and start propranolol for symptom relief
options.rationale: A subjective inner restlessness localised to the legs, relieved by movement, beginning within days of a dose increase and with an unchanged mental state is akathisia. Reducing the offending dose is the primary intervention and propranolol is the best supported symptomatic treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Increase the risperidone dose to treat the worsening psychotic agitation
options.rationale: Mistaking akathisia for psychotic agitation and escalating the antipsychotic is the classic anti-pattern, because it worsens the akathisia in a self-reinforcing cycle. His delusional content and conviction are unchanged, which is the evidence that the psychosis has not worsened. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start benztropine to treat the emerging extrapyramidal adverse effects
options.rationale: Anticholinergics treat drug-induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia but are largely ineffective for akathisia, and they add cognitive impairment, constipation and urinary retention. The absence of tremor, rigidity and dystonia removes the indication anyway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add regular olanzapine at night in addition to his current treatment
options.rationale: Antipsychotic polypharmacy raises the total dopamine blockade and therefore the akathisia risk, while adding metabolic burden in a young man at the start of treatment. It compounds the cause rather than removing it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Akathisia is a subjective sense of inner restlessness, usually referred to the legs, accompanied by an objective inability to remain still, and it appears within days to weeks of starting or increasing a dopamine antagonist. It is among the most distressing of all antipsychotic adverse effects and carries a documented association with suicidal ideation and with treatment non-adherence, which is why recognising it matters more than its apparent mildness suggests. The diagnostic trap is that pacing, agitation and distress are also features of worsening psychosis, and the discriminators are the temporal relationship to a dose change, the patient's own localisation of the sensation to the limbs, relief with movement, and an otherwise unchanged mental state. Management begins with reducing or switching the antipsychotic, since akathisia is dose-related, with propranolol as the best supported symptomatic agent and benzodiazepines, mirtazapine or a switch to a lower-risk agent such as quetiapine or clozapine as further options. Anticholinergics, useful for parkinsonism and dystonia, are ineffective here and are a common prescribing error.
key_points: Onset within days of a dose increase with an unchanged mental state points to akathisia.
The sensation is localised to the limbs and relieved by movement, unlike psychotic agitation.
Dose reduction is primary; propranolol is the best supported symptomatic treatment.
Anticholinergics treat parkinsonism and dystonia but not akathisia.
explanation.pearls: Akathisia carries a recognised association with suicidal ideation, so a patient who becomes newly hopeless or impulsive within days of an antipsychotic dose increase is asked specifically whether the distress sits in the legs and eases when walking, before the agitation is attributed to the illness.

subtopic_detail: six months of feeling detached from oneself with fully retained awareness that the experience is not real
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 23-year-old apprentice electrician referred by his general practitioner. He says that since a frightening episode six months ago, when his heart pounded and he thought he was dying, he has felt as though he is watching himself from a few feet away, like a character in a film rather than the person doing the living.

He describes his hands as looking like they belong to someone else and says the street outside looks flat and drained of colour, as though painted on a backdrop. He is emphatic that he knows none of this is actually true and that it is his perception that has changed rather than the world, and he finds that distinction frustrating rather than reassuring. It is present for most of the day, most days. He smoked cannabis heavily for two years and stopped seven months ago, before the symptoms began, and uses no other substance and no alcohol. He has no hallucinations, no delusional beliefs and no thought disorder, his mood is anxious rather than low, and physical examination, thyroid function and a recent electroencephalogram are all normal.

data_table.Core symptoms: Persistent detachment from self with a sense of observing oneself, and a flat drained quality to the surroundings
data_table.Reality testing: Fully intact, with explicit awareness that the altered perception does not reflect external reality
data_table.Substance history: Cannabis ceased seven months ago before symptom onset, no other substance or alcohol use
data_table.Mental state: No hallucinations, delusions or thought disorder, anxious rather than depressed mood
data_table.Investigations: Normal physical examination, thyroid function and electroencephalogram

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start a benzodiazepine to be taken whenever the detachment occurs
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines can deepen dissociative symptoms as well as causing dependence, and an as-needed regimen for a symptom present most of the day would mean near continuous use. Symptom-contingent dosing also reinforces the checking and monitoring that maintain the disorder. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before any treatment
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is warranted where there are focal neurological signs, an abrupt onset in later life or a history of head injury, none of which applies to a young man with a normal examination. Scanning first would delay treatment and risks an incidental finding that generates further anxiety. (Source: RANZCP: Dissociative disorders)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy addressing the symptoms
options.rationale: Persistent detachment from the self and the surroundings with fully intact reality testing, causing distress and lasting months, is depersonalisation derealisation disorder. Psychological therapy with psychoeducation, grounding techniques and work on the catastrophic appraisals that maintain the symptoms is the first-line treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Dissociative disorders)

options.text: Start a low dose antipsychotic given the persistent unreal quality
options.rationale: Antipsychotics treat psychosis, which requires loss of reality testing, and he retains it completely by insisting the change is in his perception rather than in the world. Antipsychotics have no established efficacy in this disorder and add metabolic and extrapyramidal burden. (Source: RANZCP: Dissociative disorders)

options.text: Arrange electroencephalography to exclude temporal lobe epilepsy
options.rationale: Focal epilepsy can produce brief episodic dissociative experiences and is worth considering, which makes this the near pair, but seizure-related symptoms are stereotyped, last seconds to minutes and occur in discrete episodes rather than continuously for six months. The study has also already been performed and was normal. (Source: RANZCP: Dissociative disorders)

explanation.summary: Depersonalisation derealisation disorder is classified among the dissociative disorders and is defined by persistent or recurrent experiences of detachment from one's own thoughts, body or actions, or from the surroundings, with reality testing remaining fully intact throughout.
