Transient depersonalisation is extremely common, reported by up to half of the population at some point and particularly during panic, sleep deprivation or intoxication, but the disorder requires persistence and clinically significant distress or impairment. Onset is typically in adolescence or early adulthood and is frequently triggered by a panic attack, severe stress or cannabis use, and it can persist for years after the trigger has gone, as here. The intact reality testing is the feature that separates it from psychosis and is worth stating explicitly to the patient, because many fear they are developing schizophrenia and that fear itself amplifies the symptom. Treatment is primarily psychological, with cognitive behavioural approaches targeting symptom monitoring, avoidance and catastrophic interpretation, while medication is reserved for comorbid anxiety or depression since no agent has established efficacy for the dissociative symptoms themselves.
key_points: Intact reality testing separates this disorder from psychosis and should be named for the patient.
Panic, severe stress and cannabis are common triggers, and symptoms outlast them.
Cognitive behavioural therapy targeting appraisal and monitoring is first-line.
No medication has established efficacy for the dissociative symptoms themselves.
explanation.pearls: Fear of impending madness maintains this disorder more than any other factor, so explicitly naming the condition and explaining that intact insight rules out psychosis is itself therapeutic and often reduces symptom intensity before any formal therapy begins.

subtopic_detail: recurrent replicative nightmares waking a veteran nightly despite improvement in his daytime symptoms
stem:
You are the psychiatrist reviewing a 44-year-old former soldier who has been taking sertraline 150 mg daily for nine months for post-traumatic stress disorder following a deployment. He has completed a course of trauma-focused therapy.

He tells you his daytime symptoms have improved substantially, with far fewer intrusive daytime images, less avoidance and a return to part-time work. What has not changed is that five or six nights a week he wakes between one and three in the morning from the same dream, which replays a specific incident almost exactly as it happened, and he then lies awake for two hours. His partner says he does not shout, thrash, kick or leave the bed, and neither of them has ever been injured during the night. He drinks no alcohol, uses no cannabis and takes no other medication. His mood is reactive, he is not suicidal, and his physical examination and blood tests including thyroid function are normal.

data_table.Nightmare pattern: Replicative trauma-specific dreams waking him five or six nights weekly between 0100 and 0300 with two hours of subsequent wakefulness
data_table.Daytime symptoms: Substantially improved intrusions, reduced avoidance, returned to part-time work
data_table.Collateral from partner: No vocalisation, thrashing, kicking or leaving the bed, no injury to either partner
data_table.Treatment to date: Sertraline 150 mg daily for nine months, completed course of trauma-focused therapy
data_table.Investigations: Normal physical examination and blood tests including thyroid function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe nightly temazepam to consolidate sleep and reduce awakenings
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are specifically discouraged in post-traumatic stress disorder because they impair the emotional processing that trauma-focused therapy depends on, carry dependence risk in a population with high comorbid substance use, and have been associated with worse outcomes. They also do not reduce nightmare frequency. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD guidelines)

options.text: Start quetiapine at night for its sedating and dream suppressing effect
options.rationale: Low dose antipsychotics are sometimes used off label for this purpose but the evidence is weak and the metabolic burden in a middle-aged man is real. Pharmacological augmentation follows rather than precedes a trial of the psychological treatment with the best evidence. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD guidelines)

options.text: Refer for polysomnography to assess for rapid eye movement behaviour
options.rationale: Rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder is the near pair worth excluding, since it also produces dramatic nocturnal events, and it is distinguished by dream enactment with vocalisation, thrashing and injury to the patient or bed partner, which the collateral history explicitly rules out here. Trauma nightmares occur without loss of atonia and do not need a sleep study. (Source: RANZCP: Sleep disorders)

options.text: Refer for imagery rehearsal therapy targeting the recurrent nightmares
options.rationale: Nightmares frequently persist as a residual symptom after daytime post-traumatic symptoms have responded, and imagery rehearsal therapy, in which the patient rewrites and rehearses an altered dream narrative while awake, has the strongest evidence of any treatment for them. It is recommended ahead of adding further medication. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD guidelines)

options.text: Increase the sertraline dose and review his sleep diary in six weeks
options.rationale: He has already had a substantial response at this dose across nine months, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors have a modest effect on nightmares specifically, with some evidence that they suppress rapid eye movement sleep and can worsen dream disturbance. Further escalation is unlikely to target the residual symptom. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD guidelines)

explanation.summary: Nightmares are among the most persistent symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder and commonly outlast the daytime intrusions, avoidance and hyperarousal that respond first to treatment, which makes residual nightmare disorder a distinct treatment target rather than evidence of overall failure. Trauma nightmares differ from ordinary bad dreams in that they frequently replicate the index event with unusual fidelity, occur in the second half of the night during rapid eye movement sleep, and produce full awakening with clear recall and autonomic arousal. The differential that must be excluded on collateral history is rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder, in which loss of the normal muscle atonia allows the dream to be acted out with vocalisation, movement and injury, and which carries entirely different implications as a prodrome of synucleinopathy. Imagery rehearsal therapy is the treatment with the strongest evidence and works by having the patient select a recurrent nightmare, rewrite the narrative with a changed ending while awake, and rehearse the new version daily for around ten to twenty minutes. Australian guidance places it ahead of pharmacological options, with prazosin remaining a second-line consideration whose supporting evidence has become less consistent since the larger negative trials.
key_points: Nightmares often persist after daytime post-traumatic symptoms have responded to treatment.
Dream enactment with vocalisation or injury indicates rapid eye movement behaviour disorder instead.
Imagery rehearsal therapy rewrites and rehearses the dream while awake and is first-line.
Benzodiazepines are discouraged in post-traumatic stress disorder and do not reduce nightmares.
explanation.pearls: Ask the bed partner specifically whether he moves, shouts or has ever hurt either of them during a dream: dream enactment points to rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder and a synucleinopathy prodrome, while a man who lies still and wakes to the same replayed scene has trauma nightmares.

subtopic_detail: confusion and unsteadiness three weeks after starting an antidepressant in a woman of seventy nine
stem:
You are the general practitioner called to see a 79-year-old woman at home by her daughter, who says her mother has been muddled about the day of the week for three days and had a near fall in the kitchen. She was started on sertraline 50 mg daily three weeks ago for a depressive episode and reports her mood has lifted slightly.

Her other medications are amlodipine, atorvastatin and a thiazide she has taken for eight years without incident. She has had no cough, no urinary symptoms, no fever and no vomiting. On examination she is alert but disorientated to time, with normal power and no focal neurological signs, moist mucous membranes, no postural drop and no peripheral oedema. Her pulse rate is 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg lying and standing, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in air and temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. Sodium is 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urea 3.1 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), serum osmolality 258 mmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 420 mmol/kg and urine sodium 52 mmol/L. Her sodium was 138 mmol/L eight weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg lying and standing, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert but disorientated to time, moist mucous membranes, no postural drop, no oedema, no focal neurological signs
data_table.Electrolytes: Sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urea 3.1 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90)
data_table.Osmolality studies: Serum osmolality 258 mmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 420 mmol/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the sertraline and start hypertonic saline in a monitored setting
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures, marked obtundation or coma, and confusion with unsteadiness at 122 mmol/L does not meet that threshold. Continuing the causative drug would also guarantee recurrence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Halve the sertraline dose and repeat the sodium level again in two weeks
options.rationale: The effect is idiosyncratic rather than reliably dose-dependent, so dose reduction does not dependably correct it, and a two week interval is far too long to monitor a sodium of 122 mmol/L. This is the near pair to the correct answer and the distinction is that partial measures leave a symptomatic patient at risk of further falls. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Switch her to mirtazapine today and recheck the sodium in three days time
options.rationale: Switching antidepressant is a reasonable plan once the sodium has recovered and the depression still needs treatment, and mirtazapine carries a lower though not absent risk. Starting the replacement on the same day removes the ability to attribute any ongoing abnormality and skips the fluid restriction that actually corrects the sodium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start demeclocycline and continue the sertraline at her current daily dose
options.rationale: Demeclocycline is a third-line agent for chronic syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis where the cause cannot be removed, with nephrotoxicity and photosensitivity as recognised problems. Here the cause is entirely removable, which makes pharmacological antagonism unnecessary. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Cease the sertraline and commence fluid restriction with daily sodium checks
options.rationale: A euvolaemic hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and a urine sodium above 30 mmol/L appearing three weeks after starting a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is drug-induced syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis. Withdrawal of the causative drug with fluid restriction and close biochemical monitoring is the treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are among the commonest drug causes of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, with the risk concentrated in the first four weeks of treatment and rising steeply with age, female sex, low body weight and concurrent diuretic use. The diagnosis requires hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia in a clinically euvolaemic patient with inappropriately concentrated urine, a urine sodium above about 30 mmol/L, and normal thyroid and adrenal function, and a low urea with a low urate supports it. The main alternative in this age group is thiazide-induced hyponatraemia, which is why an eight year history of stable sodium on the same thiazide followed by an abrupt fall three weeks after a new antidepressant points to the newer drug. Correction must be controlled, with a rise of no more than 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours, because faster correction of chronic hyponatraemia risks osmotic demyelination with devastating and often irreversible consequences. Once the sodium normalises, an antidepressant with lower risk can be introduced with a sodium check at one to two weeks, and the depression itself still requires treatment.
key_points: Risk is highest in the first four weeks and rises with age, female sex and diuretic use.
Euvolaemia with concentrated urine and urine sodium above 30 mmol/L defines the syndrome.
A stable sodium for years on the same thiazide points to the newly added drug.
Correction is limited to 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.
explanation.pearls: Check the sodium two weeks after starting any selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor in a patient over 65 who is also taking a thiazide, because the combination multiplies the risk and the presentation is usually a fall or confusion rather than anything that looks biochemical.

subtopic_detail: abdominal distension with absent bowel sounds in a man in his fourth year of clozapine treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 41-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia who has taken clozapine 500 mg daily for four years with good symptomatic control. Community staff report he has been off his food for five days, has vomited twice today and that his belly looks swollen.

He is drowsy but rousable and tells you his tummy has been aching and that he has not opened his bowels for nine days, which he says is not unusual for him. He takes no regular aperient. On examination the abdomen is grossly distended and tympanitic with generalised tenderness but no guarding, and bowel sounds are absent over four minutes of auscultation. There is no rigidity of the limbs and no tremor. His pulse rate is 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 102/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent in air and temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius. White cell count is 11.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 6.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), creatine kinase 180 units/L (40-200), lactate 3.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2) and creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 102/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent in air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Abdominal examination: Grossly distended tympanitic abdomen with generalised tenderness, no guarding, absent bowel sounds over four minutes
data_table.Neurological examination: Drowsy but rousable, no limb rigidity, no tremor
data_table.Bowel history: No bowel action for nine days, no regular aperient, two episodes of vomiting today
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 11.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), absolute neutrophil count 6.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), creatine kinase 180 units/L (40-200), lactate 3.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent abdominal imaging, withhold clozapine and involve the surgical team
options.rationale: Absent bowel sounds with gross distension, vomiting, tachycardia and a raised lactate in a patient on long-term clozapine is clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility progressing to ileus, which carries a high mortality once obstruction or ischaemia develops. Urgent imaging, withholding the drug and surgical involvement are simultaneous rather than sequential steps. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)

options.text: Continue clozapine and start a stimulant laxative with review tomorrow morning
options.rationale: Aperients are the mainstay of prevention and of mild hypomotility, but giving a stimulant laxative into a possibly obstructed bowel with absent sounds risks perforation. Overnight review is far too slow for a patient with a raised lactate and hypotension. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)

options.text: Check the clozapine level and reduce the dose by a quarter this same evening
options.rationale: A clozapine concentration is useful in working out subsequent dosing but takes days to return and does nothing about a distended obstructed abdomen tonight. Dose reduction is too slow an intervention for an acute surgical problem. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)

options.text: Start an antiemetic and encourage oral fluids with a high fibre diet on the ward
options.rationale: Oral intake is contraindicated in a patient with absent bowel sounds and vomiting, and fibre without adequate transit worsens distension. Fibre supplementation is for prevention in an ambulant patient, not for an acute presentation. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)

options.text: Withhold clozapine and repeat the full blood count before any imaging is done
options.rationale: Neutropenia is the clozapine adverse effect that monitoring programmes are built around, and it is the near pair here, but his absolute neutrophil count is normal and haematological toxicity does not cause a silent distended abdomen. Deferring imaging to chase a normal blood count delays the diagnosis that matters. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility results from potent antagonism at muscarinic, serotonergic and adrenergic receptors in the enteric nervous system, and it affects a substantial minority of patients on the drug, with slowed colonic transit demonstrable in most. It is far less famous than agranulocytosis but kills more people, since case series consistently show gastrointestinal complications causing several times as many clozapine-related deaths as haematological ones, largely because it is recognised late. Late recognition has specific causes, in that patients on clozapine often have blunted pain perception and impaired symptom reporting, constipation is normalised by both patient and team, and no mandatory monitoring framework exists for bowel function in the way it does for the neutrophil count. Presentation ranges from chronic constipation to faecal impaction, paralytic ileus, toxic megacolon, ischaemia and perforation, and the transition can be rapid. Prevention is the practical message, with a baseline and regular bowel history, prophylactic aperients for anyone with reduced frequency, avoidance of additional anticholinergic drugs, and a low threshold for imaging when a patient on clozapine reports abdominal symptoms.
key_points: Gastrointestinal hypomotility causes more clozapine deaths than agranulocytosis does.
Blunted pain perception and normalised constipation lead to late presentation.
Absent bowel sounds with distension mandates imaging and surgical involvement, not laxatives.
Prevention relies on routine bowel history and prophylactic aperients rather than monitoring bloods.
explanation.pearls: Ask every clozapine patient how often they open their bowels at each review and start a regular osmotic aperient if it is less than every second day, because there is no blood test that detects the complication that most often kills them.

subtopic_detail: partition delusions about a neighbour in a woman of seventy eight with intact cognition and normal imaging
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 78-year-old widow referred after she called the police three times in a fortnight. She believes the man in the next unit comes through the wall of her bedroom at night to move her belongings and put chemicals in her tea, and she has stopped drinking anything he might have reached.

She describes hearing his voice through the wall commenting on what she is doing. She lives alone, manages her own finances and medications accurately, cooks and shops independently, and her daughter confirms she has been sharp and organised until this began four months ago. On examination her Montreal Cognitive Assessment is 27 out of 30, attention and digit span are normal, and there is no fluctuation in her conscious level across a one hour interview. She has no visual hallucinations, no parkinsonism and no dream enactment. She wears two hearing aids that her daughter says stopped working months ago. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function, B12 and inflammatory markers are all normal.

data_table.Psychotic symptoms: Persecutory partition delusions involving the adjacent unit, auditory hallucinations through the wall, onset four months ago
data_table.Cognition: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 27 out of 30, normal attention and digit span, no fluctuation in conscious level
data_table.Neurological examination: No visual hallucinations, no parkinsonism, no dream enactment behaviour
data_table.Functional status: Independent with finances, medications, cooking and shopping
data_table.Investigations: Normal magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function, B12 and inflammatory markers
data_table.Sensory status: Wears two hearing aids that have not worked for months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy without any change to her medication
options.rationale: Psychological therapy is a useful adjunct for distress and for coping with residual symptoms, but as sole treatment for florid persecutory delusions that have led to police involvement and to her refusing fluids it is inadequate. Her refusal to drink creates a physical risk that needs faster resolution. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis in older people)

options.text: Start low dose amisulpride and arrange formal audiology assessment
options.rationale: Partition delusions with auditory hallucinations, preserved cognition and function, normal imaging and onset after 60 years describe very late onset schizophrenia-like psychosis. Low dose antipsychotic treatment combined with correction of the sensory deprivation that contributes to symptom formation is the established approach. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis in older people)

options.text: Start donepezil and refer to the memory clinic for cognitive follow up
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors treat the psychosis of Alzheimer disease and dementia with Lewy bodies, both of which require cognitive impairment that is absent here with a Montreal Cognitive Assessment of 27 and full independence. Treating a dementia she does not have delays effective treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis in older people)

options.text: Treat as a delirium and screen for infection with cultures and further imaging
options.rationale: Delirium requires an acute onset over hours to days with impaired attention and a fluctuating conscious level, whereas this evolved over four months with normal attention and no fluctuation. The screening bloods and imaging are already normal. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis in older people)

options.text: Start quetiapine at a low dose given her likely Lewy body sensitivity
options.rationale: Quetiapine is the correct choice when antipsychotic sensitivity from dementia with Lewy bodies is a concern, and this is the near pair to the correct answer. The distinction is that Lewy body disease requires fluctuating cognition, recurrent formed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism or dream enactment, and all four are explicitly absent, so the sensitivity concern that drives the choice does not apply. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis in older people)

explanation.summary: Psychosis presenting for the first time after the age of 60 is classified as very late onset schizophrenia-like psychosis, and it differs from earlier onset schizophrenia in several consistent ways. Women predominate, negative symptoms and formal thought disorder are uncommon, cognition and premorbid function are typically preserved, and the delusional content is characteristically persecutory and spatially organised around the home, with partition delusions about people or substances passing through walls, floors and ceilings being close to pathognomonic. Sensory deprivation, particularly uncorrected hearing loss and to a lesser extent visual impairment, is a well replicated risk factor, and social isolation compounds it, so correcting the sensory deficit is a therapeutic intervention rather than an afterthought. The essential differentials are delirium, separated by the time course and by attention, dementia with psychosis, separated by cognitive testing and functional history, and dementia with Lewy bodies, separated by fluctuation, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and dream enactment. Response to antipsychotics is generally good but doses are a quarter to a half of those used in younger adults, and the increased mortality associated with antipsychotics in dementia makes accurate diagnosis before prescribing important.
key_points: Partition delusions involving walls, floors and ceilings are characteristic of the syndrome.
Preserved cognition and function separate it from dementia with psychosis.
Uncorrected hearing loss is a replicated risk factor and correcting it is part of treatment.
Antipsychotic doses are a quarter to a half of those used in younger adults.
explanation.pearls: Check whether the hearing aids actually work rather than whether they are worn: uncorrected hearing loss is one of the few modifiable risk factors in very late onset psychosis, and a dead battery has been the treatable contributor in more than one referral.

subtopic_detail: recurrent unexplained hypoglycaemia in a toddler that stops entirely during a supervised admission
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see the family of a 2-year-old girl admitted for the fourth time in three months with hypoglycaemic episodes. Each previous admission followed an ambulance call from home, and each time she recovered promptly and was discharged after a normal work-up.

During this nine-day admission, in which a nurse has been present at all cares and no food or drink has come from home, her glucose has remained between 4.2 and 6.8 mmol/L with no episodes. A sample taken during the last documented episode at home has now returned showing glucose 1.8 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), insulin 42 mIU/L, C-peptide less than 0.05 nmol/L (0.3-1.5) and beta-hydroxybutyrate suppressed. Cortisol and growth hormone responses were appropriate. Her mother, who trained as an enrolled nurse, has stayed at the bedside throughout, has asked repeatedly for further tests and has told several staff that a specialist interstate suspects a rare metabolic disorder. The treating team has been unable to verify that referral.

data_table.Inpatient course: Nine days with supervised cares and no external food, glucose 4.2 to 6.8 mmol/L with no episodes
data_table.Critical sample from home: Glucose 1.8 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), insulin 42 mIU/L, C-peptide less than 0.05 nmol/L (0.3-1.5), suppressed beta-hydroxybutyrate
data_table.Counter-regulatory testing: Appropriate cortisol and growth hormone responses
data_table.Collateral: Unverifiable account of an interstate specialist referral, repeated requests for further investigation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with a continuous glucose monitor and review her in one week
options.rationale: Discharging the child back into the environment where the episodes occur, on the strength of a device that can be removed or its data disputed, returns her to a situation with a documented mortality. Covert surveillance and monitoring are not substitutes for statutory protection. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Offer the mother psychological therapy and arrange community follow up
options.rationale: Treatment for the perpetrating parent may well be part of the eventual plan, but it follows rather than replaces protection of the child, and engaging therapeutically first risks alerting the parent before safeguarding is in place. The child's safety is not contingent on the parent accepting help. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Report to child protection services and keep the child in hospital
options.rationale: High insulin with a suppressed C-peptide is chemically impossible in endogenous hyperinsulinism and proves administration of exogenous insulin, and episodes that occur only at home and cease under supervision complete the picture of factitious disorder imposed on another. Mandatory reporting with the child kept in a place of safety is the immediate step. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Arrange a supervised fast with paired insulin and cortisol sampling now
options.rationale: A diagnostic fast is how endogenous hypoglycaemia is investigated, and it would be the right test if the mechanism were unknown. The paired sample already obtained has answered the question definitively, and a further fast exposes the child to deliberate hypoglycaemia for no diagnostic gain. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Refer to paediatric endocrinology for insulinoma localisation imaging
options.rationale: An insulinoma is the near pair to consider, and it is excluded by the C-peptide, because a tumour secreting endogenous insulin releases C-peptide in equimolar amounts and the level would be high rather than undetectable. Insulinoma is also vanishingly rare at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Factitious disorder imposed on another, historically called Munchausen syndrome by proxy and described in child protection frameworks as fabricated or induced illness, involves a carer falsifying or inducing symptoms in a dependent for psychological rather than material gain. The perpetrator is usually the mother, health care backgrounds are over-represented, and the pattern typically includes recurrent presentations, symptoms witnessed only by the carer, findings that resolve when the carer is absent, unverifiable accounts of other specialists, and persistent pressure for further investigation. Insulin administration is one of the most commonly reported induction methods and is uniquely easy to prove biochemically, because exogenous insulin raises measured insulin while suppressing endogenous secretion and therefore C-peptide, a dissociation that no endogenous cause can produce. Mortality in reported series runs at around 6 to 10 per cent and long-term morbidity from unnecessary investigation and treatment is substantial, so protection precedes psychiatric formulation. The correct process is a mandatory report to the statutory agency with the child kept in a place of safety, a multidisciplinary meeting, a documented chronology assembled from source records rather than from the carer's account, and assessment of siblings, who are also at risk.
key_points: Raised insulin with suppressed C-peptide proves exogenous insulin administration.
Symptoms witnessed only by one carer and resolving under supervision is the pattern.
Mandatory reporting and a place of safety precede any therapeutic engagement with the parent.
Siblings are assessed too, and the chronology is built from source records not carer report.
explanation.pearls: Insulin and C-peptide are released in equimolar amounts from the beta cell, so a high insulin with an undetectable C-peptide during hypoglycaemia can only mean exogenous insulin, and in a two year old that single pairing is a child protection finding rather than an endocrine one.

subtopic_detail: a specific threat against a named person disclosed in a session by a patient with a history of violence
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 38-year-old man in an outpatient clinic for the eighth time. He has been attending for help with anger and relationship difficulties following separation from his partner. He has two previous convictions for assault, the most recent four years ago.

Today he tells you that his former partner's new boyfriend, whom he names and whose workplace and shift pattern he describes, is going to be dealt with this week. He says he has bought a knife for the purpose and that he has driven past the workplace twice. He is calm, coherent and consistent as he describes this and he repeats it when you check you have understood. On mental state examination his speech is normal in rate and form, there is no evidence of any delusion, hallucination or thought disorder, his mood is euthymic with a congruent affect, and his cognition is intact. He has taken no alcohol or other substance today. He tells you he has said this to you in confidence and asks you not to repeat it.

data_table.Disclosure: Named intended victim with described workplace and shift pattern, weapon obtained, two reconnaissance visits, stated timeframe of this week
data_table.Mental state: Normal speech rate and form, no delusions, hallucinations or thought disorder, euthymic mood with congruent affect, intact cognition
data_table.Substance use: No alcohol or other substance taken today
data_table.History: Two previous convictions for assault, most recent four years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Arrange an involuntary admission under the mental health legislation today
options.rationale: Involuntary treatment criteria across Australian jurisdictions require a mental illness for which treatment is necessary, and his mental state examination shows no illness, with the risk arising from intent rather than from symptoms. This is the near pair to the correct answer, and the distinction is that the mental health act manages risk arising from treatable illness whereas criminal justice manages risk arising from intent. (Source: RANZCP: Confidentiality and disclosure)

options.text: Discuss the disclosure with the treating team at the next case meeting
options.rationale: Team discussion is valuable and a second opinion is always worth having, but the stated timeframe is this week and a scheduled meeting introduces a delay the situation does not tolerate. Urgency is what converts a discussable concern into an immediate duty. (Source: RANZCP: Confidentiality and disclosure)

options.text: Contact the medical defence organisation before taking any other action
options.rationale: Medicolegal advice is worth obtaining and defence organisations are available urgently, but seeking it first places the clinician's exposure ahead of a named person's safety. The advice, when it comes, will be to disclose. (Source: RANZCP: Confidentiality and disclosure)

options.text: Notify the police and take steps to warn the person who was named
options.rationale: Australian privacy and health records legislation permits disclosure without consent where there is a serious and imminent threat to the life or safety of an identifiable individual, and every element that makes a threat credible is present. Warning the intended victim and notifying police is the recognised discharge of that duty. (Source: RANZCP: Confidentiality and disclosure)

options.text: Maintain confidentiality and document the disclosure fully in the case notes
options.rationale: Confidentiality is a strong obligation but it is not absolute, and it yields where disclosure is necessary to lessen a serious threat to an identifiable person. Thorough documentation is necessary but it protects the record rather than the person named. (Source: RANZCP: Confidentiality and disclosure)

explanation.summary: Confidentiality in Australian practice is governed by the Privacy Act and its Australian Privacy Principles together with state and territory health records legislation, all of which permit use or disclosure of health information without consent where the clinician reasonably believes it is necessary to lessen or prevent a serious threat to the life, health or safety of any individual. Australia has no direct statutory equivalent of the Tarasoff duty developed in American case law, but the professional and legal expectation converges on the same practical step when a threat is specific, credible and imminent. The features that make a threat actionable are a named or readily identifiable victim, expressed intent, a formulated plan, access to means, preparatory behaviour such as reconnaissance or weapon acquisition, and a stated timeframe, all of which are present in this presentation. Importantly the absence of mental illness does not remove the duty, and it does narrow the options, because involuntary treatment legislation cannot be used to detain a person who has no mental illness requiring treatment, leaving police notification and victim warning as the available routes. Practically the clinician informs the patient of the intended disclosure where it is safe to do so, discloses only the minimum information necessary, documents the reasoning contemporaneously, and seeks medicolegal and senior advice in parallel rather than beforehand.
key_points: Privacy legislation permits disclosure to lessen a serious threat to an identifiable person.
A named victim, a plan, access to means, reconnaissance and a timeframe make a threat actionable.
Absence of mental illness removes the mental health act as an option but not the duty to act.
Disclose the minimum necessary, document the reasoning, and seek advice in parallel.
explanation.pearls: Tell the patient you are going to disclose, unless doing so would increase the risk: it preserves what remains of the therapeutic relationship, it is expected under the privacy principles, and it is one of the first things asked about if the decision is later reviewed.

sources.label: Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice

subtopic_detail: repeated requests for rhinoplasty in a man who spends four hours a day checking mirrors
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 27-year-old man referred by a plastic surgeon who has declined to operate. He has had two previous rhinoplasties, the first at 21 and the second at 24, and says neither achieved what he wanted.

He tells you his nose is crooked and too wide and that people look at it on the train. He checks his profile in reflective surfaces for what he estimates as four hours a day, photographs his face from fixed angles each morning to compare, wears a cap pulled low and has stopped going to the gym or on dates. He resigned from a job requiring video meetings. He accepts that others tell him his nose looks normal but says they are being kind, and when you ask whether it is possible they are right he pauses and says probably not but he cannot be sure. There is no belief that he is being watched or persecuted, no hallucination, and no thought disorder. His mood is low with initial insomnia and he has thought about suicide if no surgeon will operate. The referring surgeon documented an anatomically normal nose.

data_table.Preoccupation: Estimated four hours daily of mirror checking and photographic comparison of a surgeon-documented normal nose
data_table.Functional impact: Resigned from work requiring video meetings, ceased gym attendance and dating, camouflages with a cap
data_table.Insight: Accepts reassurance is offered sincerely but cannot be certain his perception is mistaken
data_table.Mental state: Low mood with initial insomnia, no persecutory belief, hallucination or thought disorder, suicidal ideation contingent on surgical refusal
data_table.Surgical history: Two previous rhinoplasties at 21 and 24 with no relief of distress

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Support the referral for rhinoplasty given the distress that he describes
options.rationale: Cosmetic procedures in body dysmorphic disorder leave the great majority no better or worse, the preoccupation commonly migrates to another feature, and dissatisfaction with surgeons is associated with litigation and rarely with violence. His two previous operations already demonstrate this pattern. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Start a low dose antipsychotic for the overvalued ideas about his nose
options.rationale: Insight in this disorder runs on a spectrum and around a third hold their belief with delusional intensity, but that specifier does not change first-line treatment, which remains a serotonin reuptake inhibitor rather than an antipsychotic. Antipsychotic augmentation is considered only for inadequate response. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Refer for supportive counselling and review his progress again in six months
options.rationale: Generic supportive counselling is markedly less effective than structured cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention, and a six month interval is unsafe given the suicidal ideation he describes. This is the near pair to the correct answer, and the distinction is that the specific therapy targets the checking and reassurance-seeking that maintain the disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Start a benzodiazepine for the anxiety and reassess him after four weeks
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines provide short-lived relief, do not treat the underlying disorder and risk dependence in a chronic condition. They may also function as a safety behaviour that maintains avoidance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start a high dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor with cognitive therapy
options.rationale: Preoccupation with a defect that others do not perceive, repetitive checking and camouflage behaviours and marked functional impairment define body dysmorphic disorder. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors at the higher end of the dose range, combined with cognitive behavioural therapy including exposure and response prevention, are the established first-line treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

explanation.summary: Body dysmorphic disorder sits within the obsessive compulsive and related disorders and affects around 2 per cent of the population, with far higher rates in cosmetic surgery and dermatology clinics where prevalence estimates reach 10 to 15 per cent. The diagnosis requires preoccupation with one or more perceived defects not observable or appearing slight to others, repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, grooming, skin picking, reassurance seeking or comparison, and clinically significant distress or impairment. Insight is specified as good, poor or absent, and roughly a third hold the belief with delusional conviction, which does not alter the treatment pathway and should not be reclassified as a psychotic disorder. Suicidality is the reason this diagnosis matters so much in practice, since rates of suicidal ideation and attempts are among the highest of any psychiatric disorder, and the ideation is frequently contingent on whether a procedure will be performed. Cosmetic intervention is not effective treatment, with the great majority reporting no improvement or worsening and the preoccupation commonly shifting to a new body area, so declining surgery while actively offering psychiatric treatment is the clinically and ethically correct position.
key_points: Preoccupation with a slight or unobservable defect plus repetitive behaviours defines the disorder.
Around a third hold the belief with delusional conviction without changing first-line treatment.
Suicidality is high and is often contingent on whether a procedure is performed.
Cosmetic surgery rarely helps and the preoccupation commonly migrates to another feature.
explanation.pearls: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors for body dysmorphic disorder are titrated to the upper end of the licensed range, as with obsessive compulsive disorder, and a trial is judged inadequate before 12 weeks at the maximum tolerated dose rather than at the four to six weeks used in depression.
