subtopic_detail: raised corrected calcium with an unsuppressed parathyroid hormone after fifteen years of mood stabiliser treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatrist reviewing a 58-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has taken lithium for 15 years. She had three manic admissions before lithium was started and none since, and two previous attempts to switch her to other agents both ended in relapse within four months.

She feels well and has no bone pain, abdominal pain, polyuria or constipation. Her routine annual bloods show total calcium 2.72 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), albumin 32 g/L (35-50), phosphate 0.74 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), parathyroid hormone 7.2 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), lithium 0.72 mmol/L (0.60-0.80), creatinine 94 micromol/L (45-90) and estimated glomerular filtration rate 58 mL/min/1.73m2. Thyroid function is normal. A repeat set taken a fortnight later shows the same pattern. Her full blood count, liver function and serum protein electrophoresis are normal, and a myeloma screen is negative. She takes no thiazide, no calcium supplement and no vitamin D preparation, and she has had no recent immobilisation.

data_table.Calcium studies: Total calcium 2.72 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), albumin 32 g/L (35-50), phosphate 0.74 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), parathyroid hormone 7.2 pmol/L (1.6-6.9)
data_table.Lithium and renal: Lithium 0.72 mmol/L (0.60-0.80), creatinine 94 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 58 mL/min/1.73m2
data_table.Other investigations: Normal thyroid function, full blood count, liver function and serum protein electrophoresis, negative myeloma screen
data_table.Confounders excluded: No thiazide, calcium supplement or vitamin D preparation, no recent immobilisation
data_table.Psychiatric history: Three manic admissions before lithium, none in 15 years, two failed switches with relapse within four months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for endocrine assessment and parathyroid imaging while continuing lithium
options.rationale: A corrected calcium near 2.88 mmol/L with an unsuppressed parathyroid hormone, low-normal phosphate and a negative malignancy screen is parathyroid-driven hypercalcaemia, which in this setting is lithium-associated hyperparathyroidism. Endocrine referral with localisation imaging while lithium continues allows the parathyroid problem to be treated surgically without destabilising a mood disorder that has responded to nothing else. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease lithium abruptly and substitute sodium valproate at an equivalent dose
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium withdrawal carries a well documented rebound risk of mania within weeks, and hyperparathyroidism frequently persists after lithium is stopped because the glands have become autonomous. Stopping therefore risks relapse without reliably fixing the calcium. (Source: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder)

options.text: Start cinacalcet now and continue lithium at the current dose and interval
options.rationale: Cinacalcet lowers calcium by increasing calcium-sensing receptor sensitivity and is genuinely useful when surgery is not an option, which makes this the near pair to the correct answer. The distinction is that it is a medical holding measure rather than definitive treatment, and it is prescribed after endocrine assessment has established whether the disease is single-gland and operable rather than before. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Reassure her, since the measured calcium is close to the reference range
options.rationale: Correcting for an albumin of 32 g/L adds roughly 0.02 mmol/L for every gram below 40, giving a corrected calcium near 2.88 mmol/L, which is clearly elevated rather than borderline. Reading the uncorrected value in a hypoalbuminaemic patient systematically understates the true calcium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Reduce the lithium dose and repeat both results in one month before acting
options.rationale: Her lithium concentration is within the therapeutic range and the hypercalcaemia is not a dose-related toxic effect, so reducing the dose risks relapse without correcting the calcium. In a woman who has relapsed on two previous attempts to change treatment, that is a poor trade. (Source: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder)

explanation.summary: Lithium raises the set point at which calcium suppresses parathyroid hormone release by acting on the calcium-sensing receptor, so parathyroid hormone remains inappropriately unsuppressed in the face of a rising calcium, and with prolonged exposure the glands can become autonomous with multiglandular hyperplasia. Prevalence rises with duration of treatment and reaches roughly 10 to 15 per cent after a decade or more, yet it is frequently missed because calcium is not always included in routine lithium monitoring and because mild hypercalcaemia is asymptomatic. The biochemical trap in this case is albumin, since roughly 40 per cent of serum calcium is protein bound and a low albumin lowers the measured total calcium while leaving the physiologically active ionised fraction untouched, so a value that looks near-normal can conceal clear hypercalcaemia. An unsuppressed parathyroid hormone with hypercalcaemia localises the problem to the parathyroid glands and excludes the malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia that would suppress it, which matters because the alternative diagnoses have entirely different urgency. The management dilemma is that stopping lithium is not reliably curative once autonomy is established, while continuing it leaves the calcium elevated, and in a woman whose bipolar illness has failed two alternative agents the resolution is to treat the parathyroid disease surgically and keep the lithium.
key_points: Lithium raises the parathyroid calcium set point, leaving parathyroid hormone unsuppressed.
Correct calcium for albumin by about 0.02 mmol/L per gram below 40 before interpreting it.
An unsuppressed parathyroid hormone excludes malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia.
Hyperparathyroidism often persists after lithium cessation, so stopping is not reliably curative.
explanation.pearls: Add corrected calcium to the annual lithium monitoring panel alongside renal and thyroid function, because lithium-associated hyperparathyroidism affects roughly one in eight patients after a decade of treatment and is asymptomatic until renal stones or bone loss have already occurred.

subtopic_detail: a prolonged repolarisation interval on opioid substitution therapy after a second drug was added
stem:
You are the addiction medicine registrar reviewing a 46-year-old man who has been stable on methadone 130 mg daily for three years, with no heroin use on supervised urine testing for 18 months and steady employment. Four weeks ago another doctor started escitalopram 20 mg daily for depression. He has had two days of vomiting and loose stools from a gastrointestinal illness that is now settling.

He has had no syncope, no palpitations and no seizures, and there is no family history of sudden cardiac death. His electrocardiogram today shows sinus rhythm at 52 beats per minute with a measured QT interval of 520 milliseconds. His potassium is 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L (2.15-2.55) and creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110). His liver function and thyroid function are normal, and he takes no other prescribed or over the counter medication. He tells you that stopping methadone is the one thing he does not want, because the last time his dose was cut he relapsed within a fortnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 52 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm at 52 beats per minute with a measured QT interval of 520 milliseconds
data_table.Electrolytes: Potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.28 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110)
data_table.Medications: Methadone 130 mg daily for three years, escitalopram 20 mg daily started four weeks ago
data_table.Symptoms: No syncope, palpitations or seizures, two days of vomiting and diarrhoea now settling
data_table.Other investigations: Normal liver and thyroid function, no family history of sudden cardiac death

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for cardiology review and insertion of an implantable defibrillator
options.rationale: Device therapy is for inherited or structural arrhythmia syndromes with sustained ventricular arrhythmia or high predicted risk, not for reversible acquired prolongation from drugs and electrolytes. Treating the reversible causes is expected to normalise the interval entirely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Correct the potassium and magnesium, cease escitalopram and repeat the tracing
options.rationale: At a rate of 52 beats per minute the RR interval is 1.15 seconds, so the rate-corrected interval is about 484 milliseconds rather than the alarming 520 measured, placing him below the 500 millisecond threshold at which methadone reduction is usually mandated. The reversible contributors, namely hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and a recently added serotonergic drug with its own repolarisation effect, are corrected first because doing so preserves the opioid treatment that is keeping him well. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Halve the methadone dose today and review the electrocardiogram next week
options.rationale: Halving a stable maintenance dose would precipitate withdrawal and, on his own history, relapse to injecting, which carries a far higher mortality than the arrhythmic risk being avoided. Dose reduction is the answer once the corrected interval exceeds 500 milliseconds with reversible causes already addressed. (Source: RANZCP: Opioid dependence)

options.text: Cease methadone and transfer him to buprenorphine over the next few days
options.rationale: Buprenorphine has a much smaller effect on cardiac repolarisation and transfer is the right move for genuinely refractory prolongation, which makes this the near pair to the correct answer. The distinction is that transfer destabilises a patient stable for three years and is reserved for when the interval remains prolonged after reversible contributors have been corrected. (Source: RANZCP: Opioid dependence)

options.text: Continue all current treatment and repeat the electrocardiogram in six months
options.rationale: Leaving a potassium of 3.1 mmol/L and a magnesium of 0.62 mmol/L untreated in a patient on a repolarisation-prolonging opioid accepts an avoidable risk of torsades de pointes. Electrolyte depletion after vomiting is precisely the setting in which these arrhythmias occur. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Methadone blocks the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current and prolongs cardiac repolarisation in a dose-related way, with risk rising appreciably above roughly 100 mg daily, which is why baseline and follow-up electrocardiography is part of Australian opioid substitution practice. The interval that matters is the rate-corrected one, and at bradycardic rates the Bazett formula, which divides the measured QT by the square root of the RR interval in seconds, corrects downwards, so a raw QT of 520 milliseconds at 52 beats per minute yields a corrected value near 484 rather than the value that appears on first reading. Thresholds are conventionally an interval above 500 milliseconds, or a rise of more than 60 milliseconds from baseline, as the point at which dose reduction, drug substitution or specialist referral becomes necessary. Risk is multiplicative rather than additive, so a moderately prolonged interval matters far more in the presence of hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia, hepatic impairment, cytochrome inhibitors or a second prolonging drug, and escitalopram has its own dose-related effect that is greatest at 20 mg. The decision is genuinely a trade-off, since cutting or stopping methadone in a stable patient carries a real and quantified risk of relapse to injecting drug use with its own substantial mortality, so reversible contributors are corrected before the opioid is touched.
key_points: Bazett correction at a slow heart rate lowers the corrected interval below the measured QT.
Above 500 milliseconds corrected, or a rise over 60 milliseconds, triggers dose change or transfer.
Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia and a second prolonging drug multiply the risk.
Destabilising effective opioid substitution carries its own substantial mortality.
explanation.pearls: Replace magnesium even when the level is only borderline in drug-induced repolarisation prolongation, because intravenous magnesium suppresses the early afterdepolarisations that trigger torsades de pointes independently of whether the serum magnesium was low to begin with.

subtopic_detail: a shuffling wide based gait preceding urinary urgency and mental slowing with enlarged ventricles
stem:
You are the geriatric medicine registrar seeing a 76-year-old man whose daughter says his walking has changed over about nine months. She describes his feet as looking stuck to the floor when he sets off and when he turns in the hallway, and says he takes several small steps to get around a corner.

The walking came first. Over the past three months he has begun rushing to the toilet and has twice not made it, and in the last month she has noticed he is slower to answer questions and has stopped doing the crossword. On examination his stride is short and his feet are wide apart, and he takes six steps to turn 180 degrees. There is no tremor at rest, no bradykinesia of repetitive finger tapping, no cogwheel rigidity and no asymmetry of limb tone. Power, reflexes and sensation are normal and the plantar responses are flexor. His Montreal Cognitive Assessment is 23 out of 30, losing points on attention and executive tasks with preserved delayed recall. Computed tomography shows enlarged lateral ventricles disproportionate to the degree of cortical sulcal widening.

data_table.Gait: Short stride with a wide base, hesitation on initiation, six steps to turn 180 degrees
data_table.Symptom sequence: Gait disturbance for nine months, urinary urgency for three months, cognitive slowing for one month
data_table.Movement examination: No rest tremor, bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity or asymmetry of tone
data_table.Neurological examination: Normal power, reflexes and sensation with flexor plantar responses
data_table.Cognition: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 23 out of 30, deficits in attention and executive function with preserved delayed recall
data_table.Imaging: Enlarged lateral ventricles disproportionate to cortical sulcal widening

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer directly for ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion on these findings
options.rationale: Shunting is the definitive treatment and this is the near pair to the correct answer, but imaging and clinical features alone predict response poorly and the operation carries risks of subdural haematoma, infection and shunt failure. Demonstrating reversibility first is what selects the patients who benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start an anticholinergic for the urinary symptoms and review in two months
options.rationale: Treating the bladder in isolation ignores the gait and cognitive features that share a single cause, and anticholinergic drugs worsen cognition in older adults and add falls risk. The urinary urgency here is a central rather than a bladder problem. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Perform a high volume lumbar puncture with gait testing before and after
options.rationale: Gait disturbance preceding urinary and cognitive symptoms, with ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy, is the picture of normal pressure hydrocephalus. Removing 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid with timed and videoed gait assessment either side is the standard test of reversibility and predicts response to shunting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start levodopa and assess the gait response after six weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Parkinson disease is the principal differential because both cause a shuffling gait with start hesitation and turning difficulty, and it is separated here by the absence of rest tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity and asymmetry, and by a wide rather than narrow base. A levodopa trial would delay a potentially reversible diagnosis by six weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start donepezil and refer to the memory clinic for cognitive follow up
options.rationale: Alzheimer disease impairs delayed recall early and affects gait only late, whereas his memory is preserved and the gait changed first by many months. Treating this as a primary dementia misses the reversible cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a communicating hydrocephalus in which cerebrospinal fluid pressure measured at a single point is within the normal range, and it matters disproportionately because it is one of the few treatable causes of gait disturbance and cognitive decline in older people. The classic triad of gait apraxia, urinary incontinence and cognitive impairment is present in full in only a minority, and the sequence carries more diagnostic weight than the completeness, since gait almost always comes first and a case where cognition leads should be doubted. The gait is broad based, short strided and magnetic with marked start hesitation and difficulty turning, and it is distinguished from parkinsonian gait by the wide base and by the absence of rest tremor, rigidity and asymmetry, although the overlap is real enough that the two are often confused. Imaging shows ventriculomegaly disproportionate to sulcal atrophy, conventionally with an Evans index above 0.3, but imaging alone cannot distinguish it from the ventricular enlargement of cerebral atrophy, so a cerebrospinal fluid drainage trial is used to demonstrate reversibility. Gait improvement after high volume drainage is the best predictor of benefit from ventriculoperitoneal shunting, and gait responds better than cognition, so realistic expectations are set before surgery.
key_points: Gait disturbance almost always precedes the urinary and cognitive features.
A wide base with no rest tremor, rigidity or asymmetry separates it from Parkinson disease.
Ventriculomegaly alone cannot be distinguished from atrophy without a drainage trial.
Gait responds to shunting better than cognition does, which shapes expectations.
explanation.pearls: Time and video the gait over a fixed distance before and immediately after removing 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid, because a measurable improvement in walking speed and turning is the best available predictor of who will benefit from a shunt, and unrecorded clinical impression is unreliable.

subtopic_detail: fever ten days after chemotherapy with a neutrophil count below half a billion per litre
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 58-year-old woman who finished her second cycle of chemotherapy for breast cancer ten days ago. She has felt shivery since this morning and recorded a temperature of 38.4 degrees Celsius at home.

She has no cough, no dysuria, no diarrhoea and no rash. Her central venous access device site is clean with no erythema, tenderness or discharge. On examination her chest is clear, her abdomen is soft and non-tender, and the mouth shows no ulceration or thrush. Her pulse rate is 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in air and temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius. Her white cell count is 1.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 0.3 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-155), platelets 88 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90), lactate 1.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2) and C-reactive protein 94 mg/L (less than 5).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Clear chest, soft non-tender abdomen, no oral ulceration, clean central line site with no erythema or discharge
data_table.Full blood count: White cell count 1.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), absolute neutrophil count 0.3 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-155), platelets 88 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Other investigations: Creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90), lactate 1.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), C-reactive protein 94 mg/L (less than 5)
data_table.Treatment history: Second cycle of chemotherapy completed ten days ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and review again in the morning
options.rationale: Oral therapy with amoxicillin and clavulanate plus ciprofloxacin is an option only for carefully selected low-risk outpatients with a favourable risk score, adequate support and reliable follow-up. This regimen also lacks pseudomonal cover, which is the reason antipseudomonal agents are mandated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give granulocyte colony stimulating factor and observe her on the ward
options.rationale: Colony stimulating factor shortens the duration of neutropenia and has a place in primary and secondary prophylaxis, but it does not treat established infection and has no demonstrated mortality benefit in this setting. It is an adjunct, never the initial intervention. (Source: eviQ: Febrile neutropenia)

options.text: Start intravenous vancomycin alone and add gentamicin if she deteriorates
options.rationale: Vancomycin covers Gram positive organisms only and leaves the Gram negative bacilli, particularly Pseudomonas aeruginosa, that cause the most rapidly fatal episodes entirely untreated. It is the near pair to correct empirical therapy, and the distinguishing point is that it is added to a beta lactam for suspected line infection, skin or soft tissue infection or haemodynamic instability rather than used alone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take blood cultures and give intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam now
options.rationale: Fever with an absolute neutrophil count below 0.5 x10^9/L is febrile neutropenia, a medical emergency in which empirical broad spectrum antipseudomonal beta lactam therapy is given within an hour of presentation. Cultures are drawn immediately before the first dose, from both a peripheral vein and each lumen of the central device, but they must not delay it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Await the blood culture result before starting any antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: Cultures take 24 to 48 hours and are negative in around 70 per cent of episodes, while mortality in untreated neutropenic sepsis rises sharply with every hour of delay. Waiting for microbiological confirmation is the central error this presentation tests. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Febrile neutropenia is defined as a single oral temperature of 38.3 degrees Celsius or more, or 38.0 degrees Celsius sustained for an hour, together with an absolute neutrophil count below 0.5 x10^9/L or below 1.0 x10^9/L and predicted to fall. The nadir typically falls between seven and fourteen days after cytotoxic chemotherapy, which makes the timing in the history a diagnostic feature in its own right. Clinical signs of infection are attenuated because the inflammatory response depends on the neutrophils that are absent, so pus, consolidation on auscultation and localised erythema may all be missing, and no source is identified in around half of episodes. Empirical therapy is an antipseudomonal beta lactam such as piperacillin with tazobactam or cefepime given within an hour, with vancomycin added for suspected line or skin infection, for haemodynamic instability or for known resistant Gram positive colonisation, and an aminoglycoside added for shock or known resistant Gram negative organisms. Risk stratification tools such as the Multinational Association for Supportive Care in Cancer score identify a low-risk subgroup suitable for oral therapy and early discharge, but that decision follows the first dose rather than preceding it.
key_points: Fever with a neutrophil count below 0.5 x10^9/L is an emergency requiring antibiotics within an hour.
Signs of infection are blunted because the inflammatory response requires neutrophils.
Empirical cover must include Pseudomonas aeruginosa; vancomycin alone is inadequate.
No source is found in around half of episodes and cultures are often negative.
explanation.pearls: The chemotherapy nadir at 7 to 14 days after treatment means a patient who telephones with fever in that window is told to come in immediately rather than to take paracetamol and see how they go, since antipyretics mask the only reliable sign they have.

subtopic_detail: strictly unilateral periorbital pain with lacrimation and agitation in nightly attacks lasting an hour
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 34-year-old man who has come in at two in the morning with severe pain behind his right eye. He says it has woken him about ninety minutes after falling asleep every night for the past eighteen days, lasts around an hour and then goes completely.

He cannot sit still during the attack and paces the cubicle, rocking and pressing his palm into the socket, and tells you he would rather be doing anything than lying down. His right eye is watering and red, the right nostril is running, and the right upper lid is drooping with a smaller pupil on that side. There is no photophobia, no phonophobia and no vomiting, and he says he has been completely well between attacks and has kept working. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and drinks a beer most evenings, which he has noticed now sets off an attack. Neurological examination including fundoscopy is otherwise normal and he is afebrile with no neck stiffness.

data_table.Attack pattern: Nightly strictly right sided periorbital pain waking him 90 minutes after sleep onset, lasting about one hour, for 18 days
data_table.Autonomic features: Right conjunctival injection, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, partial ptosis and miosis
data_table.Behaviour in attack: Restless and pacing, unable to lie still
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination including fundoscopy, no neck stiffness, afebrile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate acute treatment?

options.text: Prescribe oral sumatriptan to be taken at the onset of each further attack
options.rationale: Oral triptans take 30 to 60 minutes to act, by which time an attack is already resolving, and the same drug given subcutaneously acts within about ten minutes. This is the near pair to the correct answer, and the distinction is entirely one of route and pharmacokinetics rather than of drug choice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start carbamazepine and titrate the dose against the attack frequency
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia, which produces brief electric shock-like paroxysms lasting seconds, triggered by touching the face, and without autonomic features or nocturnal periodicity. The attack duration alone separates the two conditions. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Prescribe regular oral prednisolone for the duration of the current cluster
options.rationale: A tapering corticosteroid course is a legitimate transitional treatment used to suppress attacks while a preventive agent is titrated, but it does not abort the attack he is having now. Its place is bridging rather than acute relief. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start propranolol as preventive treatment and review him in eight weeks
options.rationale: Propranolol prevents migraine and has no established role in cluster headache, where verapamil is the preventive agent of choice. Eight weeks is also longer than the bout is likely to last, so the review would follow spontaneous remission. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Give high flow oxygen by non rebreather mask and subcutaneous sumatriptan
options.rationale: Strictly unilateral periorbital pain with ipsilateral cranial autonomic features and agitation in circadian nocturnal attacks is cluster headache, and high flow oxygen with subcutaneous sumatriptan are the two acute treatments with the strongest evidence. Both work within minutes, which matters when attacks peak in under a quarter of an hour. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Cluster headache is the commonest trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia and is defined by severe strictly unilateral orbital, supraorbital or temporal pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes untreated, occurring from every other day to eight times daily, with ipsilateral cranial autonomic features or a sense of restlessness. Three features separate it from migraine at the bedside, namely the restlessness and pacing where migraine sufferers lie still in the dark, the prominent ipsilateral autonomic signs, and the striking circadian and circannual periodicity that wakes patients at the same time each night. A partial Horner syndrome is common and usually resolves between attacks, although it can persist. Acute treatment must act within minutes, which restricts the effective options to oxygen at 12 to 15 litres per minute by non-rebreather mask and to subcutaneous or intranasal triptans, and oral agents of any kind are too slow. Verapamil is the preventive of choice with electrocardiographic monitoring during titration because of dose-related atrioventricular block, a tapering corticosteroid course or greater occipital nerve block can bridge the gap, and smoking cessation and alcohol avoidance during a bout are advised.
key_points: Restlessness during attacks distinguishes cluster headache from migraine, where patients lie still.
Attacks last 15 to 180 minutes with ipsilateral autonomic features and circadian periodicity.
Acute treatment must act in minutes: high flow oxygen and subcutaneous or nasal triptan.
Verapamil is the preventive of choice and requires electrocardiographic monitoring.
explanation.pearls: Oxygen for cluster headache must be 12 to 15 litres per minute through a non-rebreather mask with a reservoir bag, because nasal prongs or a simple mask deliver too low a fraction of inspired oxygen to abort the attack and are the usual reason a patient reports that oxygen did not work.

subtopic_detail: a rising creatinine during a diarrhoeal illness in a woman taking three drugs that each impair renal autoregulation
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 72-year-old woman three days into a diarrhoeal illness that her whole family has had. She has hypertension and osteoarthritis, and takes perindopril, indapamide and ibuprofen, the last of which she buys herself and has been taking regularly for knee pain.

She has kept drinking cordial but has passed urine only twice today. On examination her mucous membranes are dry, the jugular venous pressure is not visible, and there is a postural drop from 128/74 mmHg lying to 104/62 mmHg standing with a pulse rate of 96 beats per minute. There is no rash, no fever, no loin tenderness and no palpable bladder. Creatinine is 186 micromol/L (45-90), up from 76 micromol/L six weeks ago, urea 16.8 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), potassium 5.5 mmol/L (3.5-5.2) and sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145). Urinalysis shows no blood, protein, nitrites or leucocytes, and microscopy shows no casts, no eosinophils and no crystals. A renal tract ultrasound reports normal sized unobstructed kidneys with no hydronephrosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 128/74 mmHg lying and 104/62 mmHg standing, pulse rate 96 beats per minute, afebrile, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, jugular venous pressure not visible, no rash, no loin tenderness, no palpable bladder
data_table.Renal function: Creatinine 186 micromol/L (45-90) from 76 micromol/L six weeks ago, urea 16.8 mmol/L (3.0-8.0)
data_table.Urine: No blood, protein, nitrites or leucocytes, microscopy showing no casts, eosinophils or crystals
data_table.Imaging: Normal sized unobstructed kidneys with no hydronephrosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold the perindopril, indapamide and ibuprofen and rehydrate her
options.rationale: Volume depletion with a bland urinary sediment and an unobstructed tract indicates prerenal acute kidney injury, and all three drugs are contributing by different mechanisms that each disable glomerular autoregulation. Withholding the whole combination while restoring volume is the treatment, with reintroduction once renal function has recovered. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury)

options.text: Withhold the perindopril only and continue the other two medications
options.rationale: Stopping one agent leaves the other two mechanisms operating, with the diuretic continuing to deplete volume and the anti-inflammatory continuing to constrict the afferent arteriole. This is the near pair to the correct answer, and the distinction is that the injury arises from the combination rather than from any single drug. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury)

options.text: Start prednisolone for a presumed acute interstitial nephritis today
options.rationale: Drug-induced interstitial nephritis is worth considering with any new medication, but it typically produces sterile pyuria, white cell casts, eosinophiluria, a rash or fever, and her sediment and examination are bland. Corticosteroid would add hyperglycaemia and immunosuppression without addressing the volume deficit. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury)

options.text: Insert a urinary catheter and arrange renal tract imaging this evening
options.rationale: Catheterisation and imaging are the right moves when obstruction is suspected, and obstruction has already been excluded by an ultrasound showing no hydronephrosis with a non-palpable bladder. An unnecessary catheter carries a real risk of urinary infection in this age group. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury)

options.text: Refer for urgent renal biopsy to establish the underlying diagnosis
options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for suspected intrinsic glomerular or interstitial disease where the cause remains unclear after non-invasive assessment, particularly with an active sediment or systemic features. A clear precipitant with a bland sediment does not warrant an invasive procedure with a bleeding risk. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury)

explanation.summary: The combination of a renin angiotensin system inhibitor, a diuretic and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug is often called the triple whammy and is one of the commonest preventable causes of community-acquired acute kidney injury in older Australians. The three act at different points on the same autoregulatory system, since the diuretic depletes intravascular volume, the non-steroidal blocks the prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar vasodilatation that maintains glomerular perfusion when volume is low, and the angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor blocks the efferent arteriolar constriction that would otherwise preserve filtration pressure. Each is well tolerated alone in a euvolaemic patient, which is why the combination is so often overlooked until an intercurrent illness removes the volume reserve, and gastroenteritis, vomiting, febrile illness and hot weather are the usual triggers. A bland urinary sediment with an unobstructed tract and clinical volume depletion establishes a prerenal picture without further investigation, and management is to withhold all three agents and restore volume. Sick day guidance is the durable lesson, with patients on these agents told which medicines to pause during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever, and over-the-counter anti-inflammatory purchase asked about directly since it will not appear on the medication list.
key_points: Diuretic, renin angiotensin inhibitor and non-steroidal disable renal autoregulation together.
An intercurrent illness removing volume reserve is the usual precipitant.
A bland sediment with no obstruction establishes a prerenal cause without further tests.
Over-the-counter anti-inflammatory use must be asked about, as it is absent from the list.
explanation.pearls: Give written sick day guidance to every patient on a renin angiotensin inhibitor plus a diuretic, naming the medicines to pause during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever and when to restart them, because the combination is safe until the day the patient cannot keep fluids down.

subtopic_detail: a falling phosphate on the third day of nutritional support after a fortnight of minimal oral intake
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 74-year-old man admitted eight days ago after a fall at home, where he had been living alone and eating almost nothing for a fortnight because of low mood after his wife died. He weighs 48 kg and his body mass index is 16.2 kg/m2.

Nasogastric feeding was started three days ago at his full estimated energy requirement. This morning he is more short of breath than yesterday, has new peripheral oedema and says his legs feel weak going to the toilet. On examination there are bibasal crackles and a raised jugular venous pressure. His pulse rate is 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 93 per cent in air and temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Phosphate is 0.38 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), having been 0.82 mmol/L on admission, potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.58 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.26 mmol/L (2.15-2.55) and creatinine 74 micromol/L (60-110). His thiamine status was not assessed before feeding began.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 93 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bibasal crackles, raised jugular venous pressure, new peripheral oedema, proximal weakness
data_table.Nutritional status: Weight 48 kg, body mass index 16.2 kg/m2, minimal oral intake for a fortnight before admission
data_table.Electrolytes: Phosphate 0.38 mmol/L (0.75-1.50) from 0.82 mmol/L on admission, potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.58 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.26 mmol/L (2.15-2.55)
data_table.Feeding history: Nasogastric feeding at full estimated requirement from day three of admission, thiamine status not assessed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Change to parenteral nutrition and add an insulin infusion for tight control
options.rationale: The route of feeding is not the problem and parenteral nutrition carries higher refeeding risk along with line-related complications. Adding exogenous insulin would drive further intracellular shift of the very electrolytes that are already dangerously low. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Reduce the feeding rate, replace phosphate intravenously and give thiamine
options.rationale: A falling phosphate with hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and new fluid overload after reintroducing nutrition to a severely malnourished patient is refeeding syndrome. Management is to reduce the caloric load, aggressively replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium, and give thiamine, which is consumed rapidly as carbohydrate metabolism resumes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Continue the current feeding rate and replace phosphate by the oral route
options.rationale: Oral phosphate is slow, causes diarrhoea at the doses needed and is inadequate for a level of 0.38 mmol/L with respiratory and cardiac manifestations. Continuing full-rate feeding sustains the insulin-driven intracellular shift that caused the problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Stop feeding entirely and recommence once the phosphate has normalised
options.rationale: Stopping feeding altogether prolongs malnutrition and sets up a repeat episode when it is restarted, and the evidence supports continuing at a reduced rate while replacing electrolytes. This is the near pair to the correct answer, and the distinction is between reducing and abandoning the feed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Increase the feeding rate to correct the underlying malnutrition more quickly
options.rationale: Increasing the caloric load intensifies the insulin surge that drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells and will deepen every abnormality present. Starting at full requirement was itself the precipitant in this case. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is the constellation of fluid and electrolyte shifts that follows reintroduction of nutrition after a period of starvation, driven by the switch from fat and protein catabolism back to carbohydrate metabolism and the resulting insulin surge. Insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells at a time when total body stores are already depleted despite normal or near-normal admission levels, and it simultaneously promotes sodium and water retention, producing the oedema and cardiac failure seen here. Hypophosphataemia is the biochemical hallmark and it causes the clinical syndrome, since adenosine triphosphate and 2,3-diphosphoglycerate synthesis both fail, producing respiratory muscle weakness, cardiac failure, rhabdomyolysis, haemolysis, seizures and arrhythmia. Thiamine is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and is consumed rapidly as carbohydrate metabolism restarts, so it is given before or with the first feed to prevent precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy. Prevention is what matters most, with identification of high-risk patients by body mass index, weight loss, duration of negligible intake and pre-existing electrolyte abnormality, starting feeds at a fraction of the requirement and building up over days, with daily electrolyte monitoring throughout the first week.
key_points: Insulin release after refeeding drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells.
Hypophosphataemia impairs adenosine triphosphate synthesis, causing cardiac and respiratory failure.
Thiamine is given before or with the first feed to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
Prevention means starting at reduced calories and building up with daily monitoring.
explanation.pearls: Start feeding a patient at high refeeding risk at about 5 to 10 kcal per kilogram per day and build to full requirement over four to seven days, with daily phosphate, potassium and magnesium for the first week, since normal admission electrolytes say nothing about total body stores.

subtopic_detail: excessive daytime sleepiness with witnessed apnoeas in a heavy vehicle driver awaiting a sleep study
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 52-year-old man who drives a semi-trailer on overnight interstate runs. He has come for a repeat prescription and mentions that he nodded off at the wheel for a moment approaching a roundabout last week and put it down to a long shift.

His partner says he snores loudly, stops breathing and then gasps several times a night. His Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 17 out of 24. His body mass index is 37 kg/m2, his neck circumference is 45 cm and his blood pressure is 152/94 mmHg on two occasions despite perindopril. He has fallen asleep watching television and while sitting in the waiting room today. Examination shows a crowded oropharynx, clear lung fields and no peripheral oedema, and his oxygen saturation is 95 per cent in air. A polysomnogram has been requested and the next available appointment in the public system is in fourteen weeks. He asks you to sign his commercial driving medical certificate today.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 152/94 mmHg on two occasions, SpO2 95 per cent in air, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Sleep history: Loud snoring with witnessed apnoeas and gasping, Epworth Sleepiness Scale 17 out of 24
data_table.Anthropometry: Body mass index 37 kg/m2, neck circumference 45 cm
data_table.Recent event: Episode of falling asleep at the wheel while driving a heavy vehicle last week
data_table.Examination: Crowded oropharynx, clear lung fields, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Pending investigation: Polysomnogram requested with a fourteen week wait

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Start modafinil to control the sleepiness while he awaits the sleep study
options.rationale: Wake-promoting agents are reserved for residual sleepiness that persists despite adequate treatment of the underlying disorder, and using one to mask sleepiness in an untreated driver is unsafe. It also has no effect on the apnoeas, the hypoxaemia or the blood pressure. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for bariatric surgery assessment and continue his current work duties
options.rationale: Weight loss is genuinely disease-modifying and bariatric referral is reasonable in the longer term, but surgery is months away at best and does nothing about tomorrow night's shift. The immediate hazard is not addressed. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Advise him to stop commercial driving now and document that advice clearly
options.rationale: Severe excessive daytime sleepiness with a recent episode of falling asleep at the wheel means he does not meet the commercial vehicle standard, and the advice to cease driving applies immediately rather than after the sleep study. Australian practice places the reporting obligation on the driver, with the doctor responsible for giving and documenting clear advice. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Allow him to keep driving until the sleep study result becomes available
options.rationale: A fourteen week wait means fourteen more weeks of overnight heavy vehicle driving by a man who has already fallen asleep at the wheel, and fitness to drive turns on demonstrated sleepiness rather than on a numerical apnoea index. Deferring the decision to the test misunderstands what the standard measures. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Notify the driver licensing authority today without informing the patient
options.rationale: Reporting to the licensing authority is permitted where a driver continues to drive against advice and is the near pair to the correct answer, but it follows rather than replaces giving the advice, and doing it covertly is not supported. The first step is always an explicit conversation with the patient. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

explanation.summary: Obstructive sleep apnoea affects a substantial proportion of commercial drivers and is associated with a two to threefold increase in motor vehicle crash risk, concentrated in those with excessive daytime sleepiness rather than in everyone with a raised apnoea hypopnoea index. The Australian standard set out in Assessing Fitness to Drive is stricter for commercial vehicle drivers than for private drivers and turns primarily on symptoms, so a driver reporting sleepiness while driving, or a recent episode of falling asleep at the wheel, does not meet the standard regardless of what a sleep study eventually shows. The legal framework places the obligation to report a relevant medical condition on the driver, while the treating doctor is responsible for assessing fitness, giving clear advice, and documenting both, with direct notification to the licensing authority permitted and appropriate where a driver continues to drive against advice. Continuous positive airway pressure is the definitive treatment and drivers can usually return to commercial driving once symptoms are controlled and adherence is demonstrated objectively, typically with downloaded device data showing regular use. Weight loss, positional therapy, mandibular advancement splints and treatment of contributory hypothyroidism or alcohol use are adjuncts, and the associated hypertension frequently improves with effective treatment.
key_points: Commercial driving standards turn on daytime sleepiness rather than on the apnoea index alone.
Falling asleep at the wheel means the standard is not met, before any sleep study is done.
The driver holds the reporting obligation; the doctor advises, documents and may notify.
Return to commercial driving requires symptom control with demonstrated device adherence.
explanation.pearls: An Epworth Sleepiness Scale of 16 or more, or any episode of falling asleep at the wheel, disqualifies a commercial driver under the Austroads standard immediately, so the certificate is withheld on the day rather than held open pending the polysomnogram.

subtopic_detail: a rapidly enlarging ulcer with a violaceous undermined edge that worsened after surgical debridement
stem:
You are the medical registrar asked to review a 44-year-old woman on the surgical ward. A small pustule on her left shin three weeks ago broke down into an ulcer, and she was taken to theatre for debridement eight days ago because it was thought to be infected. The wound has enlarged from 3 cm to 9 cm since the operation.

On examination the ulcer has a deep necrotic base with a raised violaceous overhanging border and a surrounding rim of erythema, and the skin at the edges of the surgical incision has itself broken down. Pedal pulses are easily palpable and the ankle brachial index is 1.05 bilaterally. Two wound swabs and two sets of blood cultures have grown no organisms despite eight days of intravenous flucloxacillin, and a punch biopsy from the edge shows a dense neutrophilic infiltrate with no organisms on special stains and no vasculitis. She has had intermittent bloody diarrhoea for two years that she has not sought help for. Her temperature is 37.2 degrees Celsius, white cell count 12.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) and C-reactive protein 78 mg/L (less than 5).

data_table.Vital signs: Temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Wound examination: 9 cm ulcer with necrotic base, raised violaceous overhanging border, breakdown at the surgical incision edges
data_table.Vascular assessment: Easily palpable pedal pulses, ankle brachial index 1.05 bilaterally
data_table.Microbiology: Two wound swabs and two sets of blood cultures with no growth after eight days of intravenous flucloxacillin
data_table.Histology: Dense neutrophilic infiltrate, no organisms on special stains, no vasculitis
data_table.Other history: Two years of intermittent bloody diarrhoea, white cell count 12.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 78 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin and repeat the wound swab in two days
options.rationale: She has already completed eight days of exactly this treatment with sterile cultures and a deteriorating wound, and the biopsy shows no organisms on special stains. Repeating a failed antimicrobial strategy delays the immunosuppression that will stop the ulcer extending. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Apply negative pressure wound therapy and continue regular sharp debridement
options.rationale: Negative pressure therapy has a role once the disease is immunologically controlled, but combining it with ongoing sharp debridement continues the mechanical trauma that drives pathergy. It is the near pair to reasonable wound care, and the distinguishing point is that the timing relative to immunosuppression is what makes it helpful or harmful. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum

options.text: Refer for arterial duplex imaging and consideration of revascularisation
options.rationale: An arterial ulcer is a legitimate differential for a necrotic leg ulcer but is excluded by easily palpable pedal pulses and a normal ankle brachial index. Arterial ulcers also have a punched-out rather than undermined violaceous border. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Leg ulcers)

options.text: Start systemic corticosteroid therapy and avoid any further debridement
options.rationale: Enlargement of the ulcer after surgery and breakdown at the incision edges is pathergy, which with a violaceous undermined border, sterile cultures and a neutrophilic infiltrate on biopsy indicates pyoderma gangrenosum. High dose systemic corticosteroid with strict avoidance of further surgical trauma is first-line treatment. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum

options.text: Arrange a further wider debridement with split skin grafting to follow it
options.rationale: Surgery is the single most harmful intervention in this condition because pathergy causes the wound to extend along every new incision, which is exactly what has already happened. Grafting without immunosuppression reliably fails and creates a second pathergic wound at the donor site. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Pyoderma gangrenosum

explanation.summary: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic dermatosis rather than an infection, despite a name that has misled clinicians for a century, and it typically begins as a pustule or nodule that breaks down into a rapidly enlarging painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined border. It is a diagnosis of exclusion with no confirmatory test, so infection, vasculitis, malignancy, venous and arterial disease and calciphylaxis are ruled out by culture, biopsy and vascular assessment before it is accepted. Around half of cases are associated with a systemic disease, most often inflammatory bowel disease, inflammatory arthritis or a haematological disorder, and the undisclosed bloody diarrhoea here points to an underlying colitis that needs investigation in its own right. Pathergy, in which minor trauma provokes new or extending lesions, is the feature that makes the condition dangerous in surgical hands, because each debridement enlarges the wound and the deterioration is then misread as worsening infection prompting yet more surgery. Treatment is immunosuppression, beginning with high dose systemic corticosteroid or ciclosporin, with tumour necrosis factor inhibitors used for refractory disease or where inflammatory bowel disease coexists, alongside meticulous non-traumatic wound care and adequate analgesia.
key_points: Pathergy means the ulcer extends after surgery, which is often misread as infection.
It is a diagnosis of exclusion; biopsy shows neutrophils and excludes other causes.
Around half of cases have an associated systemic disease, often inflammatory bowel disease.
Treatment is systemic immunosuppression with strict avoidance of further debridement.
explanation.pearls: A leg ulcer that gets dramatically bigger in the days after debridement, with sterile cultures despite adequate antibiotics, is pyoderma gangrenosum until proven otherwise, and the next operation will make it worse rather than better.
