subtopic_detail: recurrent oral and genital ulceration with blurred vision and a positive skin prick response
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 29-year-old man born in Turkey who has had crops of painful mouth ulcers for three years, occurring six or seven times a year and taking a fortnight to heal. Over the past year he has also had two episodes of painful scrotal ulceration that left scars.

He now reports three days of blurred vision and floaters in the right eye with some aching around it. On examination there are four shallow ulcers with erythematous rims on the buccal mucosa and two healed scars on the scrotum, and there are several tender erythematous nodules on both shins. A cannula inserted in the emergency department yesterday has developed a sterile pustule at the puncture site. Herpes simplex polymerase chain reaction from an ulcer base is negative, coeliac serology is negative, and his full blood count, iron studies, B12 and folate are all normal. C-reactive protein is 42 mg/L (less than 5) and he is afebrile with otherwise normal vital signs.

data_table.Mucocutaneous findings: Four shallow buccal ulcers with erythematous rims, two healed scrotal scars, tender erythematous nodules on both shins
data_table.Needle site: Sterile pustule at a cannula puncture site inserted the previous day
data_table.Ocular symptoms: Three days of blurred vision, floaters and periocular ache in the right eye
data_table.Investigations: Negative herpes simplex polymerase chain reaction and coeliac serology, normal full blood count, iron studies, B12 and folate, C-reactive protein 42 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start topical corticosteroid eye drops and review him in the clinic next month
options.rationale: Topical therapy penetrates adequately for anterior uveitis only, and posterior segment inflammation requires systemic treatment. A month of observation in a condition that causes irreversible visual loss within days is the central hazard here. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Behcet disease)

options.text: Start valaciclovir and swab both ulcer sites for herpes simplex virus again
options.rationale: Recurrent herpetic ulceration is the near pair for oral and genital ulcers occurring together, and it is excluded here by a negative polymerase chain reaction from the ulcer base, by the scarring pattern and by the accompanying erythema nodosum and pathergy, which herpes does not produce. Repeating a negative test delays treatment of the eye. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start colchicine alone and review the ulcer frequency in three months time
options.rationale: Colchicine is a reasonable first-line agent for mucocutaneous and joint manifestations and would be appropriate if ulcers were the only problem. It is inadequate as sole therapy once sight-threatening ocular disease is present. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Behcet disease)

options.text: Refer for gastroenterology assessment and colonoscopy before any treatment
options.rationale: Inflammatory bowel disease can produce oral ulceration and erythema nodosum and warrants consideration, but he has no bowel symptoms and endoscopy will take weeks. The eye cannot wait for a differential diagnosis to be narrowed by an unrelated investigation. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Behcet disease)

options.text: Refer urgently for ophthalmology review and start systemic corticosteroid
options.rationale: Recurrent oral and genital ulceration with erythema nodosum, a positive pathergy response and new ocular symptoms indicates Behcet disease with probable posterior uveitis, which is sight-threatening and can destroy vision within days. Same-day ophthalmological assessment with systemic corticosteroid, followed by a steroid-sparing agent, is the appropriate response. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Behcet disease)

explanation.summary: Behcet disease is a variable vessel vasculitis affecting arteries and veins of all sizes, with a marked geographic distribution along the historical Silk Road from the eastern Mediterranean through to East Asia, and a strong association with HLA-B51. The International Study Group criteria require recurrent oral ulceration at least three times a year plus two of recurrent genital ulceration, eye lesions, skin lesions and a positive pathergy test, in which a sterile pustule forms at a needle prick site within 48 hours. Ocular involvement occurs in around half of patients, is typically a bilateral relapsing panuveitis with retinal vasculitis rather than isolated anterior uveitis, and was historically a leading cause of blindness in young adults in endemic regions. Other major manifestations are venous thrombosis, arterial aneurysm including the pulmonary arteries, central nervous system parenchymal and venous sinus disease, and gastrointestinal ulceration that can perforate. Treatment is stratified by organ involvement, with colchicine and topical measures for mucocutaneous disease, and systemic corticosteroid combined with azathioprine, ciclosporin, interferon alfa or a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor for ocular, neurological and vascular disease.
key_points: Recurrent oral ulceration plus two of genital ulcers, eye, skin or pathergy meets criteria.
Pathergy is a sterile pustule forming at a needle prick site within 48 hours.
Ocular disease is a relapsing panuveitis with retinal vasculitis, not isolated anterior uveitis.
Sight-threatening or neurological disease requires systemic immunosuppression, not colchicine alone.
explanation.pearls: Look at the cannula sites before ordering a pathergy test: a sterile pustule that appeared at a venepuncture or cannulation site within 48 hours is the same phenomenon and is often already documented in the nursing notes as a line-site reaction.

subtopic_detail: progressive headache with papilloedema and a focal seizure in a woman taking combined oral contraception
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 31-year-old woman with eight days of headache that has become steadily worse. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and returned from a long-haul flight a fortnight ago.

She describes the headache as a constant band that is worse when she lies flat, worse when she coughs or strains, and worst on waking. This afternoon her left arm jerked rhythmically for about ninety seconds while she remained aware throughout, and afterwards the arm felt weak for twenty minutes. On examination there is bilateral papilloedema with blurred disc margins and absent venous pulsation, and visual acuity is 6/6 in each eye. Power, tone, reflexes and sensation are now normal in all four limbs and she is fully oriented. There is no neck stiffness, no fever and no rash. An unenhanced computed tomography scan of the brain shows a small area of haemorrhage in the right parietal region with surrounding low attenuation that does not conform to an arterial territory. Her vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Headache pattern: Eight days of progressive headache worse lying flat, on coughing and straining, and on waking
data_table.Seizure: Focal motor seizure of the left arm lasting 90 seconds with retained awareness and 20 minutes of postictal weakness
data_table.Fundoscopy: Bilateral papilloedema with blurred disc margins and absent venous pulsation, visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally
data_table.Neurological examination: Normal power, tone, reflexes and sensation in all four limbs, fully oriented, no neck stiffness
data_table.Computed tomography: Small right parietal haemorrhage with surrounding low attenuation not conforming to an arterial territory
data_table.Risk factors: Combined oral contraceptive use and recent long-haul flight

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange venographic imaging and start therapeutic anticoagulation
options.rationale: Progressive positional headache with papilloedema, a focal seizure and a parenchymal haemorrhage that crosses arterial boundaries in a woman on oestrogen indicates cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Venography confirms it and therapeutic anticoagulation is the established treatment, since the haemorrhage is venous infarction caused by the clot rather than a contraindication to treating it. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Withhold anticoagulation because of the intracranial haemorrhage present
options.rationale: This is the central trap of the presentation, and randomised and observational evidence both support anticoagulating despite haemorrhagic venous infarction, because relieving the venous outflow obstruction is what stops the bleeding from extending. Withholding treatment allows the thrombus to propagate and the infarct to enlarge. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Start intravenous mannitol and refer for decompressive craniectomy now
options.rationale: Decompressive surgery is reserved for impending herniation from a large venous infarct with a deteriorating conscious state, and she is fully oriented with normal limb power. Osmotic therapy also does not address the underlying occlusion. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Load with levetiracetam and repeat the unenhanced scan in 24 hours
options.rationale: An antiseizure medication is appropriate after a seizure with a supratentorial lesion and is part of the plan, which makes this the near pair to the correct answer. The distinction is that it treats a complication while leaving the thrombosis undiagnosed and untreated, and a repeat unenhanced scan cannot demonstrate the occluded sinus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start high dose aspirin and arrange carotid duplex ultrasound tomorrow
options.rationale: Antiplatelet therapy and carotid imaging belong to the workup of arterial ischaemic stroke, which this is not, since the lesion crosses arterial territory boundaries and the presentation is dominated by raised intracranial pressure. Carotid disease is also vanishingly rare at this age. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

explanation.summary: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis accounts for under 1 per cent of strokes but occurs in a much younger population, with a median age around 35 and a marked female predominance driven by oestrogen-containing contraception, pregnancy and the puerperium. Presentation is protean and often subacute, and the four recognised syndromes are isolated intracranial hypertension with headache and papilloedema, focal deficits, seizures, and encephalopathy, with headache the presenting symptom in around 90 per cent. Two features on plain imaging should raise the diagnosis, namely a parenchymal haemorrhage or infarct that does not respect arterial territory boundaries, particularly when parasagittal or temporal, and a hyperdense cord or delta sign, though the unenhanced scan is normal in up to a third of cases so a negative scan does not exclude it. Confirmation is by computed tomography venography or magnetic resonance venography, and treatment is therapeutic anticoagulation with low molecular weight heparin even in the presence of haemorrhagic venous infarction, a counterintuitive principle supported by trial and registry data because the bleeding is a consequence of venous congestion that anticoagulation relieves. Endovascular thrombectomy is reserved for deterioration despite anticoagulation, and thrombophilia screening, cessation of oestrogen-containing contraception and three to twelve months of oral anticoagulation follow.
key_points: Oestrogen-containing contraception, pregnancy and the puerperium are the major risk factors.
A haemorrhage or infarct crossing arterial territory boundaries suggests a venous cause.
Anticoagulation is given despite haemorrhagic venous infarction, which is the key principle.
A normal unenhanced scan occurs in up to a third of cases and does not exclude the diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: A headache that is worse lying flat, worse on coughing or straining and worst on waking is the raised intracranial pressure pattern, and in a young woman on the combined pill it should trigger venographic imaging rather than a diagnosis of migraine, whatever the unenhanced scan shows.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

subtopic_detail: new back pain with brisk lower limb reflexes and a sensory level in a man with known metastatic disease
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department at ten at night to see a 71-year-old man with prostate cancer and known bone metastases, on androgen deprivation therapy. He has had mid back pain for three weeks that is worse lying flat and wakes him, and today he has found the stairs difficult and nearly fell twice.

He says his legs feel heavy rather than painful and that he has had to strain to start passing urine since yesterday. On examination hip flexion is 4 out of 5 bilaterally with normal power in the arms, both knee and ankle reflexes are brisk with sustained ankle clonus, and both plantar responses are extensor. There is a band of reduced pinprick sensation below the level of the umbilicus. The bladder is palpable to three finger breadths above the pubic symphysis. There is percussion tenderness over the mid thoracic spine. His observations are normal, his prostate specific antigen has risen from 12 to 68 micrograms/L over four months, and his corrected calcium is 2.44 mmol/L (2.15-2.55).

data_table.Motor examination: Hip flexion 4 out of 5 bilaterally with normal upper limb power
data_table.Reflexes and tone: Brisk knee and ankle reflexes with sustained ankle clonus, extensor plantar responses bilaterally
data_table.Sensory examination: Band of reduced pinprick sensation below the umbilicus
data_table.Other findings: Palpable bladder three finger breadths above the pubic symphysis, mid thoracic percussion tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Prostate specific antigen risen from 12 to 68 micrograms/L over four months, corrected calcium 2.44 mmol/L (2.15-2.55)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine within the next week
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is the correct modality, which makes this the near pair to the correct answer, and it fails on two counts. The whole spine must be imaged because a third of patients have compression at more than one level, some of it remote from the symptomatic site, and the timeframe must be hours rather than a week. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

options.text: Give high dose dexamethasone and arrange urgent whole spine imaging
options.rationale: Back pain with upper motor neuron signs, a sensory level and urinary retention in a man with bone metastases is malignant spinal cord compression, and neurological outcome depends almost entirely on how much function remains when treatment begins. High dose dexamethasone is given immediately to reduce peritumoural oedema while magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine is arranged. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

options.text: Arrange a plain radiograph of the lumbar spine and review the result first
options.rationale: Plain films miss around a fifth of compressive lesions, cannot show the cord or the epidural space, and would be imaging the wrong region given a sensory level at the umbilicus corresponding to the tenth thoracic dermatome. A normal film would falsely reassure. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

options.text: Start opioid analgesia and refer to outpatient radiation oncology clinic
options.rationale: Analgesia is necessary but does nothing for the compression, and an outpatient referral introduces a delay measured in days when the window for preserving ambulation is measured in hours. Established paraplegia is rarely reversible. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

options.text: Arrange a radionuclide bone scan and refer for palliative radiotherapy later
options.rationale: A bone scan shows osseous metastatic activity but gives no information about the epidural space or the degree of cord compression, and it cannot guide the radiotherapy field or a surgical decision. It answers a question that has already been answered. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

explanation.summary: Malignant spinal cord compression complicates around 5 per cent of cancers, most often from prostate, breast, lung, myeloma and renal primaries, and results from vertebral metastasis expanding into the epidural space or from vertebral collapse. Back pain precedes neurological signs by a median of several weeks and has characteristic features, being worse on lying flat, waking the patient at night and worsened by coughing or straining, which together distinguish it from mechanical pain that eases with rest. The single strongest predictor of whether a patient walks afterwards is whether they were walking when treatment started, so this is a presentation where hours matter and where waiting for the morning list costs function that does not return. Dexamethasone is given immediately at high dose to reduce vasogenic oedema, whole spine magnetic resonance imaging is obtained urgently because multilevel disease is common and changes the treatment field, and definitive treatment is decided jointly between radiation oncology and spinal surgery. Surgical decompression with stabilisation followed by radiotherapy gives better ambulatory outcomes than radiotherapy alone in selected patients with a single level of compression, good performance status, a reasonable prognosis and spinal instability or a radioresistant tumour.
key_points: Pain worse lying flat and waking the patient is the warning that precedes neurological signs.
Ambulatory status at the start of treatment is the strongest predictor of final function.
Image the whole spine, since around a third of patients have multilevel compression.
Dexamethasone is given before imaging, not after it.
explanation.pearls: The sensory level in cord compression sits at or below the compressive lesion and never above it, so a level at the umbilicus corresponding to the tenth thoracic dermatome means imaging the thoracic and cervical spine as well, and a lumbar-only request will miss the lesion entirely.

subtopic_detail: a platelet fall of more than half on day seven of low molecular weight heparin with a new limb thrombosis
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 66-year-old woman who is day seven after an elective total knee replacement and has been on prophylactic enoxaparin since the operation. The nursing staff have called you because her left calf has become swollen and painful overnight.

On examination the left calf is 4 cm larger than the right with pitting oedema and tenderness along the deep veins, and the surgical wound is clean and dry with no erythema or discharge. There is no bleeding from the wound, no bruising and no petechiae anywhere. Her platelet count is 68 x10^9/L today, having been 198 x10^9/L on the day of surgery and 186 x10^9/L on day three. Haemoglobin is 112 g/L (115-155), white cell count 8.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), fibrinogen 4.1 g/L (2.0-4.0), prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time are both normal and the blood film shows no schistocytes and no platelet clumping. Compression ultrasound confirms occlusive thrombus in the left popliteal vein. Her temperature is 36.9 degrees Celsius and the remaining vital signs are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Left calf 4 cm larger than the right with pitting oedema and deep venous tenderness, clean dry surgical wound, no bleeding, bruising or petechiae
data_table.Platelet trend: 198 x10^9/L on the day of surgery, 186 x10^9/L on day three, 68 x10^9/L today on day seven
data_table.Other haematology: Haemoglobin 112 g/L (115-155), white cell count 8.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), fibrinogen 4.1 g/L (2.0-4.0), normal prothrombin and activated partial thromboplastin times
data_table.Blood film: No schistocytes and no platelet clumping
data_table.Imaging: Compression ultrasound showing occlusive thrombus in the left popliteal vein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease heparin and start warfarin at a loading dose on the same evening
options.rationale: Warfarin given before the platelet count has recovered depletes protein C faster than the procoagulant factors and can precipitate venous limb gangrene and skin necrosis, which makes this the most dangerous of the wrong answers. Warfarin is introduced only once the platelet count exceeds 150 x10^9/L, overlapped with the non-heparin agent. (Source: HSANZ: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Continue enoxaparin and give intravenous immunoglobulin for the low count
options.rationale: High dose immunoglobulin has a role in severe or refractory disease by saturating the Fc receptors that mediate platelet activation, which makes it the near pair to a legitimate adjunct. The distinction is that it never substitutes for stopping the heparin, and continuing the causative drug guarantees progression. (Source: HSANZ: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Cease all heparin and start a non heparin parenteral anticoagulant
options.rationale: A platelet fall of more than 50 per cent beginning on day five to ten of heparin exposure with new thrombosis and no alternative cause gives a high 4Ts score, and the disorder is profoundly prothrombotic despite the low count. Stopping every heparin preparation and starting a full therapeutic dose of a non-heparin agent such as danaparoid, argatroban or fondaparinux is the immediate step. (Source: HSANZ: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Cease heparin and transfuse platelets before starting any anticoagulation
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion adds substrate to a process that is driving thrombosis rather than bleeding and has been associated with arterial thrombotic events in this setting. It is reserved for active major bleeding, which is absent here. (Source: HSANZ: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Change to unfractionated heparin and monitor the platelet count each day
options.rationale: The antibody is directed against platelet factor 4 bound to heparin and cross-reacts across all heparin preparations, so unfractionated heparin perpetuates rather than resolves the process. Unfractionated heparin in fact carries a higher risk of causing the syndrome than the low molecular weight form. (Source: HSANZ: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia)

explanation.summary: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia is an immune reaction in which antibodies form against complexes of platelet factor 4 and heparin, and those immune complexes cross-link platelet Fc receptors to cause platelet activation, thrombin generation and thrombosis, with the thrombocytopenia arising from consumption rather than from impaired production. The paradox that defines it clinically is that bleeding is rare while thrombosis occurs in up to half of untreated patients, so a falling platelet count on heparin is a thrombotic emergency rather than a bleeding one. The 4Ts score structures the pretest assessment using the degree of thrombocytopenia, the timing at five to ten days after first exposure or sooner with recent prior exposure, the presence of thrombosis or skin necrosis, and the absence of other causes, and a high score mandates immediate action before any laboratory confirmation. Confirmatory testing proceeds in two steps, with a sensitive but non-specific immunoassay for platelet factor 4 antibodies followed by a functional assay such as serotonin release or heparin induced platelet activation, but results take days and treatment cannot wait. Anticoagulation continues for at least four weeks in isolated thrombocytopenia and three months where thrombosis has occurred, and the event is documented prominently as an adverse drug reaction because re-exposure years later can provoke rapid-onset recurrence.
key_points: It causes thrombosis rather than bleeding despite a falling platelet count.
The 4Ts score drives immediate management before laboratory confirmation returns.
All heparin preparations cross-react, so switching to unfractionated heparin is futile.
Warfarin before platelet recovery risks venous limb gangrene through protein C depletion.
explanation.pearls: Delay warfarin until the platelet count is above 150 x10^9/L and overlap it with the non-heparin anticoagulant for at least five days, because starting it early depletes protein C before the procoagulant factors fall and has caused venous limb gangrene requiring amputation.

subtopic_detail: tender shin nodules with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and ankle arthritis in a woman of thirty
stem:
You are the respiratory registrar seeing a 30-year-old woman referred after a chest radiograph taken for two weeks of ankle pain and swelling. She has crops of tender red raised lumps over both shins that came up ten days ago.

She has had no cough, no breathlessness on climbing two flights, no fever, no night sweats and no weight loss. She was born in Australia, has not travelled overseas, and has had no known contact with anyone with tuberculosis. On examination there are six tender erythematous nodules on both shins, both ankles are warm and swollen with painful dorsiflexion, and the chest is clear on auscultation. There is no lymphadenopathy palpable in the neck, axillae or groins, and there are no skin lesions elsewhere, no red eye and no facial rash. The chest radiograph shows symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields. An interferon gamma release assay is negative, corrected calcium is 2.44 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), and her spirometry and gas transfer are normal.

data_table.Skin examination: Six tender erythematous nodules over both shins present for ten days
data_table.Joint examination: Both ankles warm and swollen with painful dorsiflexion
data_table.Respiratory examination: Clear chest on auscultation, no palpable lymphadenopathy
data_table.Chest radiograph: Symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields
data_table.Investigations: Negative interferon gamma release assay, corrected calcium 2.44 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), normal spirometry and gas transfer

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start standard four drug antituberculous therapy while cultures are awaited
options.rationale: Tuberculous lymphadenopathy is characteristically unilateral or asymmetrical and accompanied by constitutional symptoms, and her interferon gamma release assay is negative with no exposure history. Empirical antituberculous therapy carries substantial hepatotoxicity for a diagnosis that is not supported. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start high dose oral prednisolone and taper it over the next six months
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are reserved for organ-threatening disease such as significant pulmonary impairment, cardiac or neurological involvement, hypercalcaemia or sight-threatening uveitis, none of which is present given normal lung function and a normal calcium. Steroids may also prolong the course in an otherwise self-limiting presentation. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis

options.text: Refer to haematology for excision biopsy to exclude a lymphoproliferative cause
options.rationale: Lymphoma typically produces asymmetrical or bulky mediastinal nodes with constitutional symptoms rather than symmetrical hilar enlargement with erythema nodosum and periarticular ankle inflammation. Surgical biopsy would subject her to a general anaesthetic for a clinical diagnosis. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis

options.text: Treat symptomatically with a nonsteroidal drug and review her in six weeks
options.rationale: Erythema nodosum with symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and ankle periarthritis in a well patient is Lofgren syndrome, an acute presentation of sarcoidosis with a distinctive natural history of spontaneous remission in around 90 per cent within two years. The constellation is sufficiently specific that tissue diagnosis is not required, and symptomatic treatment with observation is appropriate. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis

options.text: Arrange endobronchial ultrasound guided lymph node sampling within the week
options.rationale: Tissue sampling is indicated where the presentation is atypical, where lymphoma or malignancy is a genuine concern, or where treatment decisions depend on it, and it is the near pair to the correct answer because it is the standard route to a sarcoidosis diagnosis in other presentations. The distinguishing point is that this specific triad is diagnostic on its own and biopsy adds procedural risk without changing management. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis

explanation.summary: Lofgren syndrome is an acute form of sarcoidosis defined by the combination of erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and periarticular ankle inflammation, often with fever, and it is one of the few presentations in which the clinical picture alone is considered diagnostic without histology. That exception exists because the specificity of the triad approaches 95 per cent and because the prognosis is excellent, with spontaneous resolution in around 90 per cent within two years, particularly in those carrying HLA-DRB1 03. The ankle involvement is a periarthritis of the soft tissues around the joint rather than a true synovitis, which is why it is warm and tender but not destructive. Initial assessment still includes chest radiography, lung function with gas transfer, serum calcium, renal and liver function, an electrocardiogram and ophthalmological review, because asymptomatic cardiac, renal and ocular involvement determine whether treatment is needed. Corticosteroids are reserved for organ-threatening disease rather than given routinely, and in this presentation non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs with rest and planned review are sufficient, with colchicine or a short steroid course used if symptoms are severe.
key_points: Erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and ankle periarthritis define the syndrome.
The triad is diagnostic without biopsy, unlike other presentations of sarcoidosis.
Around 90 per cent remit spontaneously within two years.
Steroids are reserved for organ-threatening disease, not for the syndrome itself.
explanation.pearls: Symmetry of the hilar lymphadenopathy is what earns the clinical diagnosis: asymmetrical or unilateral hilar nodes, or any accompanying weight loss and night sweats, take the presentation out of Lofgren syndrome and back to tissue sampling for lymphoma and tuberculosis.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis

subtopic_detail: a rising urate and potassium after induction chemotherapy in a man whose brother haemolysed on primaquine
stem:
You are the medical registrar on call. A 34-year-old man received the first dose of induction chemotherapy for a bulky high grade lymphoma fourteen hours ago and has been on intravenous fluids with allopurinol since admission. He feels nauseated and has cramp in both hands but is otherwise comfortable.

His family came to Australia from Sardinia. He tells you his older brother was admitted with dark urine and jaundice after taking an antimalarial before a trip, and that he was told to avoid the same tablet and fava beans. He has never been tested himself. On examination he has a positive Trousseau sign and is otherwise unremarkable. His pulse rate is 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air and temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Potassium is 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urate 0.68 mmol/L (0.20-0.42), phosphate 2.4 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), corrected calcium 1.82 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-110) from 82 micromol/L on admission and lactate dehydrogenase 1840 units/L (120-250). His electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with normal T wave morphology and a QRS duration of 88 milliseconds. Urine output has been 30 mL per hour for the last three hours.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give intravenous calcium gluconate to correct the low calcium immediately
options.rationale: The hypocalcaemia here is secondary to hyperphosphataemia, and giving calcium while the phosphate is 2.4 mmol/L promotes calcium phosphate precipitation in the renal tubules and soft tissues, worsening the kidney injury. Calcium is reserved for cardiac membrane stabilisation with electrocardiographic changes or for symptomatic tetany or seizures, and a Trousseau sign alone does not meet that threshold. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Start urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate and add a loop diuretic
options.rationale: Alkalinisation increases urate solubility but simultaneously reduces calcium phosphate solubility, promoting nephrocalcinosis in a patient whose phosphate is already markedly raised, and it is no longer recommended. A diuretic in a patient who is becoming oliguric with a rising creatinine risks compounding hypovolaemia. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Arrange urgent haemodialysis before starting any further medical measures
options.rationale: Renal replacement therapy is indicated for refractory hyperkalaemia, severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia, fluid overload or oliguria persisting despite adequate volume expansion, and none of those thresholds has yet been reached with a normal electrocardiogram and fluids not yet maximised. It remains a real possibility over the next hours if the response is inadequate. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Give intravenous rasburicase and continue the high volume intravenous fluids
options.rationale: Rasburicase is the standard agent for established tumour lysis with a urate this high, and it would be the answer in almost any other patient, which is what makes it the tempting branch here. Its metabolism generates hydrogen peroxide, and in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, which this family history strongly suggests, it precipitates severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia and is contraindicated. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Escalate the intravenous fluids, continue allopurinol and test for enzyme deficiency
options.rationale: With urine output falling and creatinine rising, intensified volume expansion is the immediate priority, and allopurinol is continued because it blocks further urate formation without the oxidative risk. Testing glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase status is what determines whether rasburicase can ever be used, and treatment proceeds on the safe assumption of deficiency until it returns. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

explanation.summary: Tumour lysis syndrome follows massive release of intracellular contents from rapidly dividing cells, classically in bulky high grade lymphoma and acute leukaemias within 12 to 72 hours of treatment, producing hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and secondary hypocalcaemia, with acute kidney injury from urate and calcium phosphate deposition. Prevention rests on risk stratification, aggressive hydration and a urate-lowering agent, with allopurinol for intermediate risk and rasburicase for high risk or established disease. Rasburicase is a recombinant urate oxidase that converts urate to the far more soluble allantoin, and because that reaction generates hydrogen peroxide it causes severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in people who cannot regenerate reduced glutathione, making glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency an absolute contraindication. The deficiency is X-linked and common in people of Mediterranean, African, Middle Eastern and Southeast Asian ancestry, and a family history of haemolysis after primaquine or fava beans is strong enough evidence to withhold the drug while testing proceeds. The management of hypocalcaemia in this syndrome is also counterintuitive, since correcting it in the face of a high phosphate drives calcium phosphate deposition, so calcium is given only for arrhythmia, tetany or seizures rather than for the number.
key_points: Rasburicase generates hydrogen peroxide and is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.
Hypocalcaemia is treated only for arrhythmia, tetany or seizures, not for the value alone.
Urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended as it promotes calcium phosphate deposition.
Volume expansion with allopurinol is the safe route when enzyme status is unknown.
explanation.pearls: A family history of haemolysis after primaquine, dapsone, nitrofurantoin or fava beans is enough to withhold rasburicase before any test result is available, because the resulting haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia are more dangerous than the hyperuricaemia the drug was going to treat.
